## Publisher’s Preface

Anyone with an interest in culture will know the historical and intellectual importance of the publication of the late scholar Husayn Muruwwa’s *Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy*. They will also know the gap this book filled in the Arabic library. Muruwwa intended it to be an encyclopedic work. It became especially important to democratic and progressive readers and institutions, as well as to individual intellectuals in general and progressive intellectuals in particular, not to mention university students and everyone with a broader interest in culture.

The problem was that this very large book was originally published by Dār al-Fārābī in only two volumes. The first ran to more than a thousand pages, while the second was around eight hundred pages.

Edition followed edition, and the book became an essential reference for intellectuals, university researchers, and students across the Arab world. Today, however, many readers may be interested in only one part of it. One may be concerned mainly with pre-Islamic Arabia, another only with questions of method, and another with the materialist analysis of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy, regardless of the other sections. Buying only the part one needs also costs less than buying the whole work.

For these reasons, we decided to issue a new edition in four volumes:

**Volume I:** the book’s methodological introduction, followed by studies of pre-Islamic Arabia and the rise and early period of Islam.

**Volume II:** *kalām*, or Islamic theology, especially the Muʿtazila and Ashʿarism, followed by Aristotelian formal logic, since the Muʿtazila were the first to make use of it.

**Volume III:** Sufism, represented through only two examples, Ibn ʿArabī and al-Suhrawardī; the *Epistles of the Brethren of Purity*; and a short account of the development of the sciences among the Arabs.

**Volume IV:** the mature stage of philosophy: al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.

**The Publisher**

# Introduction

- Theoretical and methodological theses on the question of intellectual heritage
- The ideological setting of the struggle over heritage
- The Arab liberation struggle requires a clear position on the problem of heritage
- How should we read our philosophical heritage, both old and new?
- Arab-Islamic thought in the Middle Ages: its distinctive features and historical role

## 1

This book presents a way of approaching the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage[^V1-1] based on a scientific method that Arab authors have only recently begun to use.

From the Middle Ages, when this intellectual heritage took shape in its many forms, down to our own time, most studies of it have shared the same basic weakness. Despite the differences between their schools and tendencies, they have generally looked at the intellectual achievements of the medieval Arab-Islamic world from only one side.

They have treated those achievements as though they existed independently of their own history.

In other words, they have failed to uncover the real and objective, though indirect, relationship between the internal laws governing intellectual development and the broader laws governing the movement of society. As a result, the history of Arab-Islamic thought has remained a closed and static history, almost a history without history, because it has been cut off from its social roots—that is, from its real and objective historical setting.

Only the materialist view of history can uncover this relationship. It allows us to see the heritage in its historical movement, understand the relative value of its different parts, and decide which of them still deserve to remain present in our own time.

Some parts of that heritage still matter because they show a genuine historical connection between the progressive and democratic elements of our cultural past and the progressive and democratic elements of our national culture today.

Yet Arab thinkers and researchers have only very recently begun to bring the materialist view of history into the study of medieval Arab-Islamic thought, whether at the level of theory or in practical research.

Their efforts therefore remain limited. As far as we know, there are only a handful of applied studies. Some offer broad accounts of “scientific thought among the Arabs”[^V1-2]. Others deal with particular parts of the philosophical heritage[^V1-3]. At the time of writing, we know of only one work that has tried to place the philosophy of this heritage within a complete overall framework[^V1-4].

The theoretical study of the heritage as a general problem is even more limited. On the basis of this same method, we know of only one study[^V1-5] that fully meets its requirements and treats the intellectual heritage as a problem for **present-day Arab thought**, rather than simply as a problem belonging to the past.

That study is a systematic and scientific attempt to uncover “the relationship between thought within the present Arab social structure and the thought that came before it within the previous social structure.”

The present book is another link in this still-new chain of practical attempts.

It is not pure coincidence that these efforts began at roughly the same historical moment. They did not arise simply because a number of individuals happened to become interested in the same question.

They arose from a historical necessity: an objective national need for this kind of systematic and scientific engagement with the intellectual heritage of the Arab peoples at the present stage of their struggle for liberation.

The conditions have now matured for us to solve the problem of the relationship between present-day Arab thought and its inherited past on a new basis—one that fits the revolutionary direction of the Arab liberation movement at this stage in its development.

The attempt to reconsider this heritage is not new. It did not begin only in our own recent period.

The efforts we have just mentioned therefore did not arise in a historical vacuum. They represent a new stage in a problem that began more than a century ago.

It began with a group of Arab thinkers and intellectuals who emerged as pioneers of what came to be called the modern **Arab Renaissance**, or *Nahda*. In the field of thought, they expressed—at first spontaneously—the beginnings of an objective loosening in the relationship between Arab feudal social structures and the military-feudal rule of the Turkish Ottoman caliphate.

At the beginning, this loosening was an almost direct effect of the growing crisis known in nineteenth-century international politics as the **Eastern Question**, which developed as capitalism was moving into its imperialist stage.

The meaning of this term reveals the heart of the matter. It refers to the way the capitalist West of Europe sought to establish imperial control over the countries of the East that made up the greater part of the Ottoman Empire. These were largely the Arab countries.

The European powers exploited the weakness and decline of the Ottoman Empire at a stage when that particular form of feudal relations had historically reached its end.

The “Eastern Question” was therefore one expression of the rivalry between the ambitions of the European imperial powers over the inheritance of the “sick man,” as they then called the Ottoman state—in other words, over access to the East and the Arab countries.

Alongside this weakening of the relationship between Arab social structures and the backward and historically decaying military-feudal rule of the Ottomans, another factor also helped push this group of Arab thinkers and intellectuals toward the ideas that would later be called the Arab Renaissance.

That second factor was their intellectual contact with the social, political, and intellectual movements of nineteenth-century Western Europe.

The Renaissance movement grew and became more clearly defined among Arab intellectuals, army officers, and students, though the two factors we have just described affected them in different ways.

It also developed among the growing commercial bourgeoisie in Lebanon, Egypt, and Syria. Here the driving force was the conflict between the interests of this bourgeoisie and the feudal relations tied to the rule of the collapsing Ottoman Turkish state. This was combined with the bourgeoisie’s desire to link its interests to the capitalist West.

At the same time, the first seeds of national feeling were growing among the Arab masses, together with a desire to free themselves from Ottoman Turkish rule, which had lasted for several centuries.

At first, these feelings appeared as a form of national pride in the achievements of the flourishing periods of medieval Arab civilization. That pride became an early source of awareness of a national existence in the present. Later, it would develop into a force for national liberation.

This change became especially clear after the First World War, as Western imperial powers increasingly moved to impose colonial control over the countries of the East—the Arab countries—in economic, political, military, and cultural forms.

As national feeling among the Arab masses began to take the form of pride in the past, that pride also appeared in literature and other forms of thought as a renewed interest in the different cultural achievements of that past.

At first, however, this return to the heritage took the form of imitating its styles, defending it fanatically, and boasting about it to an extreme degree. People tried to revive its original forms through teaching, publication, and commentary.

In practice, they were often repeating the heritage in a distorted form, without adding to it, developing it, or reconsidering its methods and ideas.

For this reason, the early return to the heritage was backward-looking in its method but progressive in its motives. Its driving force was national resistance to the older colonial challenge of Turkish rule and, later, to the newer challenge of Western imperialism.

After the First World War, the earlier national impulses developed into uprisings and armed national revolutions. The powerful Renaissance movement increasingly became a movement of national liberation with deeper roots among the masses.

At the same time, the movement toward the heritage also began to change.

It was no longer simply a matter of repeating the traditional heritage. It became an attempt to reconsider not only the achievements of that heritage, but also the racist European colonial theories about the heritage of colonized peoples.

Those theories tried to belittle the national history and culture of colonized peoples, cut them off from both, and empty their past of anything that might give them reason to take pride in it.

They also presented these peoples as racially and historically incapable of belonging to the family of peoples able to create civilization or culture—not only in the past, but in the present and future as well.

The move toward this new way of dealing with the heritage was, in itself, progressive.

Yet the practical work carried out in its name was often tied to positions that did not match its progressive aim. In some cases, they directly worked against it.

These positions looked at the heritage from a bourgeois point of view. They took the form of chauvinistic nationalism and stood against a democratic view of culture, both in their understanding of the heritage itself and in their view of its relationship with other cultures.

Internally, the bourgeois approach ignored the social character of the heritage. It stressed its individual side instead, treating it as the work of gifted members of an “elite,” separate from their historical social surroundings and from the human forces of production whose labour created the material basis on which the achievements of the heritage rested.

This bourgeois position also concentrated almost entirely on the visible and finished forms of the heritage.

Externally, it not only tried to ignore the mutual links between the national cultural heritage and other national and world cultures. It also tended to replace European racist theories with new racist theories of its own when judging the national heritage of Asian and African peoples.

One example was the “theory” developed by the ideologues of colonial rule about Black Africans. According to this theory, Black people suffered from biological and creative deficiencies that left them without history and without cultural traditions of their own.

In constructing this “theory,” its authors exploited the fact that historical and colonial conditions had prevented some African peoples from developing a philosophical form of social consciousness[^V1-6].

In connection with this colonial theory, we can recall an observation by the British historian Basil Davidson:

> “... The effect of colonial administration proved so overwhelming that many Africans came to believe the slanders directed against their own historical achievements. Inside and outside the continent, Africans accepted—or, out of fear, were forced to accept—the statement of a former governor of Kenya that Africans were so primitive that, in relation to civilization, they were almost like a blank sheet of paper. Yet an important part of the African renaissance in its later years was its rejection and dismissal of this judgment, and its insistence that Africa possessed forms of social thought, organization, and belief that were distinctive and valuable to civilization.”[^V1-7]

Another example of a European theory with a racist character appeared in the nineteenth century. It claimed that there were two different ways of thinking: an Eastern way and a Western way.

According to this view, Eastern thought was instinctive and synthetic, while Western thought was logical and analytical.

This racial “theory” appeared in Western bourgeois literature in statements such as the famous line by the English poet: “East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet.”

The intellectual imperialism that accompanied European colonial policy in the East also produced another theory of this kind: the theory of **Eurocentrism**.

In this case, the claim was that philosophy existed only in Europe, and that philosophical thought was centered entirely in that continent[^V1-8].

The bourgeois reaction in the East to such Western racist theories often reproduced the same basic logic. Its answer was racist in character as well.

Under the influence of this reaction, together with other nationalist factors, positions toward the heritage appeared that reflected bourgeois nationalist thought.

We moved from a theory of the “European center of philosophy” to a theory of an “Eastern center”[^V1-9].

The heritage was now viewed in a way that exaggerated both its relative value and the extent of its influence on world and Western cultures and philosophies.

One example can be found in a report presented by the Pakistani philosopher Muhammad Sharif to the Twelfth World Congress of Philosophy. He argued that Islamic philosophy gave humanism[^V1-10] its first principles, introduced the West to historical sciences and the scientific method, laid the foundations of the Italian Renaissance, and influenced modern European thought all the way to Immanuel Kant[^V1-11].

There is undoubtedly a historical basis for some of these conclusions.

But when they are presented in such absolute terms, with other historical factors ignored, they become open to scientific criticism. They also take on the character of a new form of bias replacing the rejected bias of the West.

There is another form of this bourgeois nationalist position toward the heritage. It appears in new Salafi or revivalist currents dressed in the language of “modernity.”

Some of these currents introduced the idea of **“modernizing” the heritage**.

By this they meant interpreting ideas from the past as though they were identical with ideas from the present.

This jumps over every stage of history and ignores the radical changes that took place in inherited ideas over time. It also ignores the economic and social conditions and the scientific discoveries that created ideas in the modern world which could not historically have arisen outside those conditions and discoveries.

We have seen several examples of this kind of “modernization.”

At one time people spoke of “Arab socialism,” and at another of “Islamic socialism”[^V1-12].

Others tried to find “principles of capitalism” in Islam[^V1-13].

Books were written searching for “materialism” in Islamic texts[^V1-14], for “Islamic personalism”[^V1-15], or for “humanism and existentialism in Arab thought”[^V1-16].

Some even claimed to derive the natural sciences from the Qurʾān in the same form in which those sciences are known in our own age[^V1-17].

Bourgeois nationalist thought produced this new form of revivalism as another expression of the ideology of the modern Arab bourgeoisie.

To “modernize” ancient or medieval ideas and philosophies in this way, as we have said, is to treat ideas from the past as though they were identical with the ideas of the present—in this case, the twentieth century itself.

That is a metaphysical view. It denies that thought has a history and changes over time. Instead, it treats thought as static and frozen.

It also takes conditions such as capitalism, socialism, existentialism, and personalism, together with their modern meanings, out of the social relations and objective conditions that produced them in our age and transfers them into a historical setting in which they could not possibly have had any reason to exist.

This idea of complete similarity between past and present also reduces modern philosophy to something crude and simplistic.

How much would Leibniz’s mathematical thought be cheapened, for example, if we said it was simply identical with the mathematical thought of Pythagoras?

And how much would Marxist dialectical materialism be reduced if we treated it as identical with the simple materialism found among the earliest Greek materialists?

It is certainly true that no philosophy has ever appeared in a vacuum or out of nothing.

Every new philosophy has drawn on the philosophical heritage that came before it and has taken part of that earlier heritage into itself.

But this is very different from saying that old and new ideas are identical.

Hegel’s lectures on the history of philosophy help make this difference clear.

Hegel also says that contemporary philosophy is the result of all the principles that came before it. But he understands the relationship between modern philosophy and earlier philosophies—or between any later philosophy and one that came before it—through the law of the **negation of the negation**.

Hegel illustrates this through the natural development of a tree.

The flower, he says, negates the leaf because it shows that the leaf was not the highest stage or the full reality of the tree. The fruit then negates the flower.

Yet the fruit could never exist if all the earlier stages—root, leaf, and flower—had not come before it.

The appearance of these currents and others like them in an age of national liberation movements and the collapse of imperialism, together with the growing intensity of ideological struggle, has pushed the question of our position toward the national intellectual heritage to the front of the issues facing our time.

We now have to evaluate this heritage, understand it, and put it to use within that ideological struggle itself.

For this reason, the question has become more complex at the same time as it has become one of the central problems of modern thought.

At the present stage, it can no longer be solved without an ideological basis.

Arab bourgeois thought is trying to solve the problem through the kinds of answers we have just described, in keeping with its own ideological position.

It is therefore time for revolutionary Arab thought to offer its own answers, based on its own revolutionary ideology: the ideology of the classes and social groups standing against the camp of the reactionary right-wing bourgeoisie, which opposes the development of the national liberation movement in a socially democratic and revolutionary direction.

As we have seen from some of the examples above, bourgeois solutions to the problem of heritage reveal not only the ideological confusion of the bourgeoisie. They also reveal its inability to come to terms with the spirit of modern science.

This failure may itself reflect the ideological confusion into which the profound changes of our age have thrown it.

From our point of view, a genuinely scientific and objective attempt to evaluate the national intellectual heritage and absorb it in the true spirit of our age must lead to the conclusion that this problem can be solved correctly only on the basis of the Marxist-Leninist method.

This method requires us to bring out the democratic content that lies within every national intellectual heritage and connect it with the international democratic content of modern culture.

That modern democratic content is itself a real reflection of the international democratic content of today’s national liberation revolutions and of the socialist revolution that has become one of the defining features of our age.

## 2

From these conclusions, we can see that a scientific solution to the relationship between our Arab present—with all its national, social, and intellectual dimensions—and the intellectual heritage of our past depends on our having a clear scientific understanding of two facts.

The first is the revolutionary content of the Arab national liberation movement today and the direction of its future development.

The second is the deep connection between the revolutionary character of that movement and the need for a revolutionary position toward the heritage.

In other words, our position toward the heritage must begin from the present itself—from the revolutionary side of that present.

The first point becomes clear when we look closely at the overall direction of the Arab national liberation movement, especially from the period after the Second World War down to the present.

If we drew a graph of its recent course, we would see that its upward movement has generally been stronger than its downward movement.

We would also see that the upward curve is revolutionary in its basic character.

It gains this character from the growing national and social awareness of liberation among the Arab popular masses. This awareness appears in several ways.

**First**, there is a deepening hostility toward colonialism and imperialism, and toward the forces that cooperate with them, depend on them, or take part with them in seizing the national rights of peoples, taking their land and resources, and suppressing their national aspirations for liberation.

This includes international Zionism and the state it established through the seizure of Palestine.

**Second**, through different forms and levels of struggle, this hostility is increasingly becoming hostility toward the social system represented by colonialism and imperialism—that is, the system of capitalist exploitation.

**Third**, under the influence of these two factors and of social conditions in most Arab countries, this awareness has increasingly taken the form of class consciousness as well.

The national character of the struggle of the Arab masses is therefore increasingly joined by a social character, to the point that the dividing line between the two is becoming difficult to see.

In recent years, we have therefore seen the struggles of the masses in different places rise to a more advanced level, where the goals of national liberation and social liberation increasingly overlap and become inseparable. Lebanon provides one example.

**Fourth**, the development of national and political awareness in this way has begun to produce a noticeable change inside the Arab national liberation movement itself.

The relationship between two of its main sides is beginning to break apart.

The first consists of some senior leaders of certain Arab regimes and the supporters they draw from the “new class” created by those regimes.

The second consists of workers, poor peasants, revolutionary intellectuals, soldiers, and broad sections of the lower and middle bourgeoisie, influenced by the work of national and progressive parties and forces.

The developments we have described did not take place in isolation.

They were connected with the victories won by many national liberation movements in Southeast Asia and Africa, with the struggles of the international revolutionary movement in the capitalist countries, and with the deep social, intellectual, and political influence exercised across the world by the victorious leading force of that movement: the socialist system of states.

Taken together, these conditions have produced a clear difference in position between the two main sides of the Arab national liberation movement over the national causes to which that movement is committed, above all the complete national liberation of the Palestinian Arab people.

This difference became especially visible during the 1970s.

Signs began to appear that the first side might lay down the weapons of struggle against imperialism—especially American imperialism—and against the forces allied with or dependent on it, including Zionism and Arab reaction.

It had begun, or was close to beginning, to abandon its position in the Arab liberation struggle and move toward the position of its real enemies.

Yet opposition to imperialism and its allies and dependents had originally formed the basis of the temporary alliance between the different forces within the Arab national liberation movement as a whole.

The popular, national, and progressive forces that make up the other side have moved in the opposite direction.

As the struggle develops, they become more firmly rooted in their position and more deeply committed to its revolutionary demands.

At the same time, the leaders of the first side and the forces supporting them increasingly redirect their main conflict away from the enemies of national liberation and toward the friends of those same national causes.

This growing difference in position has revealed the social and class foundations behind it.

It has also brought more clearly to the surface the meaning of the close and inseparable connection between national struggle and social struggle within the Arab national liberation movement.

In doing so, it has confirmed the revolutionary content that is becoming ever more deeply rooted within that movement.

**Fifth**, there are the continuing changes taking place within fighting groups that form part of the Arab national liberation movement.

Some of these groups originally emerged at an earlier stage with chauvinistic, racial, and isolationist nationalist ideas, along with ways of thinking closer to a new form of revivalism.

Their response to the later changes, both in theory and in practice, means two things.

First, they are freeing themselves from their earlier ideas and tendencies.

Second, through revolutionary conviction, they are choosing to merge themselves into the scientific course of the revolutionary movement and into the practical struggle that follows that course.

**Sixth**, the main forces of the Arab national liberation movement increasingly understand that there is an unavoidable and fundamental connection of principle and destiny between themselves and the other national liberation movements of the world, as well as with the international revolutionary movement as a whole and its firm leading force: the system of socialist countries.

These are the main elements that make up the content of the Arab national liberation movement at its present stage.

As we can see, this content contains a number of revolutionary elements.

This does not mean that we ignore, overlook, or underestimate the negative elements that also exist within the movement.

It means only that we are identifying its general direction and the future possibilities contained within it: a conscious revolutionary development rather than a merely spontaneous one.

## 3

We now come to the second point: the deep connection between the revolutionary content of the Arab national liberation movement at its present stage and a revolutionary position toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.

What do we mean by this?

And why do we call it a **fact**?

Something does not become true simply because we want it to be true.

Truth is not subjective. It is objective. Otherwise it is not truth at all, but an illusion, an idea, an opinion, or a vision.

This is the heart of the issue before us.

The connection we are talking about is a real and objective one. It is therefore genuinely a fact.

It would be unnatural—if not impossible—for us to take a revolutionary position toward the problems of the present while taking a non-revolutionary position toward the heritage of the past.

A revolutionary outlook cannot be divided up in that way.

To divide it here is to destroy the whole position and reveal that the claimed “revolutionary” outlook is only something artificially attached to the field to which it claims to belong.

A revolutionary position toward the problems of the present requires us to begin from that same position when looking at the heritage.

That means knowing the heritage in a revolutionary way and building that knowledge on the ideology of the revolutionary forces of the present.

These are the forces that have an objective historical relationship with the social basis on which the intellectual heritage of the past was produced.

By this we mean the earlier social forces that produced the material foundations reflected in the forms of social consciousness—philosophy, science, literature, and art—that make up this heritage[^V1-18].

Building our knowledge of the heritage on this ideological basis is not something we are forcing onto reality from outside, nor is it something produced by pure abstract reasoning.

It comes from the nature of reality itself.

If we examine—as we will later in this introduction—the different ways in which people have understood our intellectual heritage through history, interpretation, or study in the various periods that came after it, we will find many different forms of knowledge.

Some differ from one another. Some directly contradict one another. Others resemble one another.

How do we explain this?

Why does one historian understand the heritage differently from another? Why does one interpreter or researcher reach a different understanding from another, when the inherited intellectual work itself remains the same historical reality?

Its texts have been handed down in fixed form to later generations, whether those texts have already been discovered or are still unknown to us.

To explain this, we must first distinguish between the heritage itself and our **knowledge of the heritage**.

We are dealing with two things, not one.

Knowledge of the heritage is something added to it from outside and produced from different sources.

This is why such knowledge can take many forms and change, while the heritage itself remains one and the same.

Since we clearly see many different forms of knowledge about the same heritage, the people who produce those different forms must differ from one another in some important way.

What is that difference?

Is it simply a difference between individuals—their personal ability to understand, their temperament, or other private and subjective qualities?

Or is something broader at work?

If these different forms of knowledge came only from private and individual factors, then similarity between them would either be extremely rare or impossible.

Purely subjective personal qualities rarely resemble one another closely, and complete identity between them is impossible.

Yet when we classify the different ways our intellectual heritage has been understood in one period or another, we find many examples that resemble one another and sometimes come very close to being identical.

At the same time, we find examples that differ sharply or directly contradict one another.

This leads us to conclude that the similarities, differences, and contradictions between these forms of knowledge come from social rather than merely individual starting points, and from objective rather than merely subjective conditions.

This conclusion brings us closer to the root of the issue.

Here again, we can turn to the different forms of knowledge that have been produced, from various periods down to the present, about the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.

Examining these forms is one of the main tasks of this introduction, although we have not yet reached the proper place for that discussion.

Nothing prevents us, however, from anticipating its results here and using them as part of our search for a scientific solution to the relationship between the Arab present and the heritage.

We will find that behind every form of “knowledge” about this heritage produced by a historian, interpreter, or researcher, ancient or modern, there is an ideological position.

At its root, an ideological position is a **class position**.

This class position does not have to appear openly in every individual case. It may instead be hidden within the intellectual foundation from which a particular interpretation of the heritage begins.

This is not something unique to the Arab-Islamic heritage.

It is a rule, or something close to a general law, that applies here just as it applies to every attempt to understand any part of humanity’s heritage in any period of civilization.

We can begin with an example close to us.

Among contemporary Arab writers who study the history of philosophy, we find different attempts to understand the ancient Greek philosophical heritage.

When they try to identify the main philosophical direction of a great Greek thinker such as Aristotle, two major and very different forms of interpretation appear.

One tries with great effort to bring out the idealist sides of Aristotle’s teachings and hide their materialist sides. At times, it even distorts or misrepresents those sides in order to turn the basic direction of Aristotle’s philosophy away from its materialist tendency and toward pure idealism.

Against this, we find another kind of interpretation.

It concentrates on the materialist tendencies in Aristotelian philosophy without ignoring the idealist weaknesses that are also present in it.

Nor does it overlook the lack of consistency within Aristotle’s philosophical system.

On the one hand, Aristotle deals with the problem of matter and form in an idealist way. On the other, he puts forward the materialist principle that being exists prior to consciousness[^V1-19].

We understand the difference between these two ways of reading the same philosophical heritage of the same philosopher as a difference in intellectual and ideological starting point.

This becomes even clearer when we remember the relationship between Aristotle’s heritage and the heritage of Arab-Islamic philosophy.

Arab-Islamic philosophy built its relationship with Aristotle on the basis of central principles in his thought.

Historically, those principles opened a path toward questioning the carefully organized idealist structure Plato had built in opposition to the seeds of philosophical materialism planted before him by thinkers such as Thales, Anaximander, and Democrates among the Ionian philosophers, and by Democritus, one of the founders of atomism.

A particular intellectual and ideological starting point lies behind the concentrated attacks on the relationship between Aristotle’s logical and philosophical heritage and the heritage of the leading Muslim logicians and philosophers of the medieval Arab-Islamic world.

The same starting point lies behind the completely dismissive view that some revivalists, both old and modern, have taken toward that relationship—a view that conflicts with both historical and scientific reasoning[^V1-20].

In this total rejection, we can detect hostility toward some of the materialist sides of Aristotle’s philosophy.

This is especially clear in the distinctly materialist character of his criticism of Plato’s theory of Forms, and in the even clearer materialist basis of his theory of knowledge.

It is useful here to make a brief side observation about the sharply different, and sometimes completely opposite, positions taken toward Aristotle’s heritage in Europe during the Middle Ages and at the beginning of the Renaissance.

These differences appeared among intellectual and philosophical schools that were subject to Christian theological authority, especially those that held powerful positions within the universities.

Anyone familiar with the history of this period knows how attitudes toward Aristotle’s philosophy moved between two extremes.

At one point, studying Aristotle could be forbidden, with severe punishments imposed on anyone who “committed” the offense.

At another, the study of Aristotle could itself become compulsory, with equally severe punishments imposed on anyone who “committed” the offense of refusing it.

What explains such different and contradictory positions toward the philosophical heritage of one and the same philosopher?

The reason was that “knowledge” of that heritage took on the character of the intellectual and ideological foundation that governed how this knowledge was produced.

To confirm this point, we can look at another striking fact familiar to anyone who follows the history of philosophy: the many different ways in which that history has been interpreted.

The history of philosophy is one history.

Why, then, are there so many different ways of explaining it?

There may be more than one reason.

One reason may be the obvious complexity of the history of philosophy itself and the difficulty of fully tracing the many overlapping relationships between causes and events within it.

But from our point of view, the strongest reason is the difference in the indirect aims of historians of philosophy.

We should not treat these aims as purely private or personal.

When the different ways of interpreting the history of philosophy are classified scientifically, their differences fall into broader currents and schools rather than into isolated personal opinions.

This supports the conclusion that ideological starting points are the main reason these different forms of “knowledge” take different directions and use different methods to interpret the history of philosophy.

These differences in direction and method even affect the way historians divide the history of philosophy into periods.

The great majority of historians of philosophy who begin from bourgeois ideologies use different measures when they divide philosophical history into stages.

Very often, these measures are fundamentally unhistorical.

They may divide philosophy simply by centuries, by the dates of royal dynasties, by the rise and disappearance of particular schools, or by the appearance and disappearance of particular ideas, and so on.

By using measures of this kind, they avoid seeing the specific material and historical basis behind changes from one stage of philosophy to another.

To begin from that material and historical basis means recognizing that philosophy appears in developed societies as an indirect and highly developed reflection of material existence.

Because philosophy has this character, its development corresponds, to one degree or another, to the historical development of social existence itself[^V1-21].

This means that when we divide the history of philosophy into stages, we should begin from the same basic measures used to divide the history of human society.

In other words, we begin from the rise and development of different social formations and from the replacement of one by another.

On this basis, the materialist view of history divides the history of philosophy into the following stages:

1. The philosophy of slave society.
2. The philosophy of feudal society.
3. The philosophy of the transition from feudalism to capitalism.
4. The philosophy of the age of imperialism and proletarian revolutions, from the late nineteenth century to the October Socialist Revolution in Russia.
5. The philosophy of the age of building socialism and communism, beginning with the appearance of socialism in one country and its later development into a world system.

Dividing the history of philosophy in this way does not mean that the materialist view of history ignores the separate stages within each social formation, or the smaller stages within each historical period.

For example, it recognizes the different stages in the development of capitalist relations in Europe: the early bourgeois revolutions of the seventeenth century, the preparation for the French Revolution and the revolution itself in the eighteenth century, and the period leading up to the more advanced revolutions of 1848–1849.

It also recognizes that philosophy itself develops through different levels within each of these smaller periods.

This is how we should understand the special place Marxism gives to **classical German philosophy**.

While always stressing that all historical periodization is relative, Marxism still treats this German philosophical tradition as having a certain degree of independence of its own[^V1-22].

We have gone into some detail about these different ways of dividing the history of philosophy into stages, and about the different intellectual and methodological assumptions behind them, for one reason: to stress that differences of this kind ultimately rest on ideological differences—that is, on an implicit form of class “partisanship.”

This partisanship appears in interpretations of the history of philosophy just as it appears in philosophy itself. At every stage in the development of society—whether in Europe, the Arab-Islamic world, India, or China—philosophy developed through the struggle between materialism and idealism. The history of philosophy is interpreted through the same struggle.

Whether bourgeois philosophers and historians admit it or not, they too begin from partisan positions: from the standpoint of the interests of one class or social group rather than another. Materialists, for their part, must not respond by ignoring idealist thinkers or simply dismissing them. A materialist must treat idealists and their philosophies, first, as historical realities that need to be understood, and second, as ideas that must be subjected to constructive criticism.

This was precisely the attitude Marx and Engels took toward Hegel, and it reflects the partisan character of philosophy.

The partisanship of idealist histories of philosophy usually appears in a different form. Idealist historians often avoid an open confrontation with materialism altogether. They ignore materialist thinkers, or they try to distort the materialist content of their philosophy.

The same thing happened to the materialist elements of Arab-Islamic philosophy, and to ancient Indian and Chinese philosophy. Idealism tried to exclude materialism from philosophy by relying on a simple formula: materialism is hostile to religion; philosophy and religion are one; therefore materialism does not belong to philosophy and should not be treated as one of its subjects.

This position is itself one form of the partisanship of idealist philosophy, even though idealist philosophers deny that philosophy is partisan at all and refuse to recognize its division into materialism and idealism. They therefore classify philosophy according to standards that appear “non-partisan”—in other words, free of class interests—and divide it instead into different schools.[^V1-23]

When materialism insists that idealism cannot simply be ignored, it is also recognizing the role of historical necessity. Idealism arose under particular historical conditions because those conditions made its appearance necessary.

Behind this position lies a basic principle of historical materialism: the way a society produces its material goods plays the decisive role in the rise and development of social ideas, including philosophical ideas. Class struggle, in turn, inevitably affects the development of ideology, philosophy included.

## 4

Everything we have said so far about understanding the intellectual heritage points to an important fact. The method we use to understand that heritage, and the scientific tools we bring to it, are shaped less by the heritage itself and the social conditions of its own age than by the time in which our new understanding is produced and by the social position of the people producing it.

As we have already seen, these present-day conditions form the ideological basis of the particular way in which the heritage is understood.

This means that every view of the heritage contains, within it, a view of the past from the standpoint of the present—whatever historical period that “present” happens to be. Our understanding of the heritage is therefore a product of the present, not a product of the past in which the heritage itself was created.

This applies to every way of looking at the heritage, whatever ideological form that understanding takes.

Even the rigid traditionalist outlook that has become so prominent in recent ideological struggles in the Arab world does not escape this rule.

Traditionalists may insist on seeing the present through the past rather than the past through the present. They may try to carry ideas from the past—with all the social meanings they had in an earlier age, meanings that historical development has already left behind—into the present, and put them in place of the new realities created by that development.

But even when they insist on looking at the heritage in this way, they are in fact starting from the opposite direction.

Their real starting point is the place occupied in the present social structure by a particular class whose ideology they express. They may belong directly to that class, or their position may result from other factors connected with their intellectual formation and with the character of their political and class consciousness.

In other words, the real content of their traditionalist view of the heritage—their attempt to impose the past on the present—has its roots in the present itself. It grows out of the soil of the present.

It is one form taken by the ideological conflicts of our own time. It reaches into the “museum” of the past for ideas that have hardened there, and uses them to shore up a class position that is becoming unstable within a social structure being broken apart by the pressures of the present.

The point, then, is that there is no single relationship between the present and the heritage, because the present itself is not one single thing. And because the heritage is viewed from within the present, it too does not appear as one single thing.

The class structure of Arab societies today takes different forms from one society to another. The struggles taking place within them also differ in character. Yet across these different societies, one new reality has become increasingly clear: the growing conflict between different positions on the central questions that now demand answers—the national question, the social question, democracy, and intellectual life.

As these questions have become more closely connected, and as the boundaries between them have almost disappeared, the conflicts around them have grown sharper. The differences between opposing positions have become wider and deeper.

This has made one fact increasingly clear: the meaning of the “present” is not the same for every class and every social group.

Each occupies a different position within the process of change now shaking existing social structures. Each also understands differently where this process is heading and how it is moving. And for each class or group, the direction of that movement may fit—or conflict with—its own ambitions, interests, and future.

The “present” experienced by classes and groups whose positions are weakening and becoming unstable is therefore not the same as the “present” experienced by those whose position is becoming stronger and more deeply rooted in the current Arab liberation movement.

Each has its own distinct “present.”

The first has a **past-oriented present**. The second has a **future-oriented present**.

The first relates to the past like a drowning person clinging to a piece of wood. The second relates to it as the coming age relates to an earlier age that is being transformed through the movement of the present.

And just as the “present” of one class position differs from the “present” of another, and just as each relates differently to the past, the “heritage” itself also takes a different form for each of them.

The heritage appears within each ideological outlook in the same way that the present appears within it, and in the same way that its relationship with the past is understood.

This is how we discover that the heritage is not, in this sense, one single thing.

It becomes many different heritages because it is viewed from the present, and—as we have seen—the present itself is divided.

What we mean here, of course, is that there are many different ideological and class views of the heritage. As a historical reality, the heritage itself remains one.

## 5

The revolutionary forces within the Arab liberation movement therefore have their own future-oriented “present,” distinct from the past-oriented “present” of backward-looking forces.

They also have their own “heritage,” distinct from the heritage seen by those other forces.

What, then, are the main features of this heritage as it appears to revolutionary forces? What kind of understanding allows them to grasp the intellectual heritage of the medieval Arab-Islamic world? And how does the heritage look different from this revolutionary perspective than it does from a backward-looking one?

These questions raise two main issues:

First, the revolutionary method for understanding the heritage.

Second, the picture of the heritage revealed by that revolutionary method, as compared with the picture produced by other methods.

### A — The Question of Method

If we describe a method of understanding the heritage as revolutionary, it must rest on an intellectual foundation that expresses a revolutionary ideology.

We have already established that every understanding of the heritage begins from intellectual assumptions that form its ideological basis. For that reason, there can never be only one way of understanding the heritage. In a class society, there are as many forms of understanding as there are competing ideologies.

Each class has its ideology, and each ideology produces a particular way of understanding the heritage.

A revolutionary ideology is the ideology of the revolutionary forces within a society: the classes and social groups whose interests and ambitions, at a particular historical moment, are tied to the demand for revolutionary change.

By revolutionary change we mean the transformation of economic, social, and political conditions and institutions that can no longer meet the demands of development and progress in the interests of the most advanced social forces. These are the forces that play the central role in society’s material and intellectual production.

If we return to the basic content of the Arab liberation movement in its present stage, as we defined it earlier, we can say that the immediate requirements of revolutionary change are expressed in the achievement of a national-democratic revolution. Once its tasks are completed, this will provide the foundation and starting point for the socialist revolution.

At this particular moment in Arab history, the social and political forces objectively and subjectively capable of carrying out the national-democratic revolution are the progressive, national, and democratic forces joined in alliance: parties, organizations, institutions, and individuals united by broadly shared short-term goals, and in some cases by common long-term goals as well.

But the question that concerns us here is the place of scientific revolutionary thought within this alliance, and the place of the progressive forces that use this thought to guide their political activity and struggle.

Looking realistically at the Arab revolutionary movement at its present level of development, we can say that scientific revolutionary thought and the forces that put it into practice already occupy a particularly active place within the movement. They also benefit from favorable internal and external conditions—national, Arab, and international—which are helping them move with increasing momentum toward a position from which they can play a decisive role in determining the movement’s direction.

Seen in this light, the central ideology of the Arab revolutionary movement in its present historical stage becomes clearer.

It is the ideology of the movement’s basic forces: the classes and social groups that are most revolutionary and that have the greatest need for a transformation reaching down to the foundations of the existing economic, social, and political order.

These forces suffer from many forms of material and spiritual hardship. At the same time, they face national oppression, the seizure of their land and wealth, and the loss of control over their homeland and its history through imperialism and Zionism.

The scientific revolutionary thought of this ideology is, specifically, the thought of scientific socialism, with its two main foundations: dialectical materialism and historical materialism.

Of these two, historical materialism provides the basic method for producing a revolutionary understanding of the heritage.

### B — The Picture of the Heritage

What picture of the heritage emerges from the method of historical materialism?

Its main outlines become clear through a dialectical view of the relationship between present and past, and of the relationship between our modern understanding of the heritage and the intellectual and social content of the heritage itself.

For our purposes, this dialectical view rests on two objective facts.

The first is that our understanding of the heritage is produced by contemporary science and contemporary ideology.

The second is that although this understanding begins from the standpoint of the present, both scientifically and ideologically, it can understand the heritage only by seeing it in its own historical setting.

In other words, we must understand the heritage as something that moved and developed within the historical time to which it belonged. More precisely, we must understand it through its relationship with the earlier social structure that produced it, and with the historical conditions that in turn produced that social structure, with all the particular features of that society and that age.

At first, these two facts may seem to contradict one another.

If we understand the heritage from the standpoint of the present, does that not mean dragging the past into the present? And would that not contradict our insistence that the heritage must be understood within its own historical setting?

This apparent contradiction comes from confusing two very different things: using modern knowledge to understand the heritage, and **modernizing the heritage itself**.

There is no necessary connection between them.

In practice, it is modern traditionalism that tries to make this connection. It pulls concepts from the past into the present by claiming that all the knowledge of our own age was already present in the past, that the past contained the same ideas we have today but expressed them in different language, and that nothing in modern knowledge is truly absent from the heritage.

This attempt to “modernize” the heritage has become increasingly common in recent years among some thinkers of the Arab bourgeoisie.

They are driven by an urgent need to repair a collapsing ideology and repaint it in bright “modern” colors while preserving its original substance: the class concepts that imply that the bourgeoisie can continue to exist forever as a class.

Quite apart from the class interests behind it and the illusion that bourgeois society can exist eternally, this attempt to modernize the heritage by treating past and present concepts as essentially identical directly contradicts the historical-materialist method of understanding the relationship between present and past.

The philosophical position behind this approach is, as we have already said, a metaphysical or static view of history. It imagines history moving in an empty circle.

Historical materialism, by contrast, sees history as moving in an upward spiral. That movement is governed by the general laws of human social development, interacting with the internal laws that shape the development of each particular society.

The idea of “modernizing” the heritage is therefore fundamentally different from our own proposal: to use contemporary scientific methods to produce new knowledge about the heritage.

The first major difference is that the bourgeois approach projects the past onto the present. It treats the present as nothing more than a continuation of the past—a rigid, metaphysical continuation that ultimately makes past and present identical.

Our approach is the opposite.

We see their relationship as one of historical development, whose content includes both continuity and breaks, as quantitative changes give way to qualitative ones within the constant movement of history.

The second difference can be seen by comparing two very different goals.

The first approach tells us that we should “take from the ancients their points of view after separating them from the particular problems they were discussing,” and that we should “look at things in the same way they did. Or, to put it differently, we should judge our solutions to our problems by the same standards that they used.”[^V1-24]

Our own approach, based on historical materialism, understands “the problem of our position toward the heritage” as “the problem of the relationship between thought within this present social structure and the thought that preceded it within an earlier social structure.”[^V1-25]

Our aim, then, is not to “take from the ancients their points of view after separating them from their particular problems.”

The issue is not whether we should take ideas from the ancients or refuse to take them.

The real question is to determine “the form in which present thought understands its relationship with past thought”—that is, “the form in which this thought reveals itself to that thought.”[^V1-26]

And we must do this **without** separating past thought from the particular problems the ancients themselves were trying to solve.

In fact, the opposite is required.

We need to see the thought of the ancients alive, with its flesh and blood still on it.

If we strip their thought of “their particular problems,” we strip it of its life, its flesh, and its blood. We remove its human dimensions. We destroy the vitality it had as a form of thought connected with a particular kind of social activity at a particular moment in history.

In the end, we also strip it of its value as heritage.

That is the first side of the question.

The second is that we need to approach the heritage in a way that allows us to achieve two goals.

First, we need to understand the heritage in a new way.

Second, we need to use this new understanding to help free contemporary Arab thought from its dependence on colonial thought and bourgeois ideology, which have historically become intertwined within the modern Arab social structure.

We have already explained many of the methodological and scientific principles involved in developing this new understanding.

As for how we put that understanding to use, the first requirement is to place the heritage back into its historical setting.

We must see it as the intellectual expression of medieval Arab-Islamic society, connected to the particular history of that society and to the complete structure of its material life.

If we place the heritage within that framework, using the scientific tools available to us today and approaching it from our revolutionary ideological position within present Arab society, we can begin to uncover the real social sources and origins of our intellectual heritage.

This allows us to develop a scientific view not only of the social forces that struggled against one another within that society, with all their specific historical features, but also of the intellectual and ideological forms taken by those struggles.

And we can understand those forms as historically specific forms, shaped by the level that human knowledge had reached at the time.

This allows us, first, to uncover the real relationship between the heritage and the historical conditions in which it arose.

Second, it allows us to uncover the objective relationship between the present Arab liberation movement and both the revolutionary and non-revolutionary elements within the movement of medieval Arab-Islamic history.

The main purpose of this double discovery is to reveal the historical dimensions of the present Arab revolutionary movement.

It allows us to see the elements of continuity between its earlier historical dimensions and its new dimensions in the present. It gives its modern character a sense of historical rootedness.

In other words, it allows us to see authenticity and modernity not as opposites, but as things that can exist together and interact.

This directly challenges the illusion, deeply reinforced by colonial thought and by Arab bourgeois thought, that authenticity and modernity must necessarily conflict.

When we use our understanding of the heritage in this way, we reach an especially important conclusion.

The heritage stops being a question about the past for its own sake. It also stops being an attempt to impose the past on the present.

Instead, it becomes a question about the present itself.

We reach this point by seeing the present as part of an ongoing process of change in which the achievements of the past and the possibilities of the future interact dynamically and move development forward.

There may be breaks in this process. Some arise from the dialectical character of historical development itself. Others are forced interruptions imposed by forces hostile to the content of the present Arab revolutionary movement.

Once we understand the heritage and the use of that understanding in this way, it becomes clear that the issue is not, as others have claimed, that we should “judge our solutions to our problems by the same standards that they”—the ancients—“used.”

That way of thinking is both unhistorical and irrational.

There are two connected reasons for this.

First, the problems faced by the ancients differ from the problems we face today because their historical conditions differed from ours.

Second, the “standards” they used grew out of those particular problems and conditions.

And as we have said, their problems and conditions were neither identical nor even similar to ours.

Their standards were also shaped by the relatively limited development, in their age, of the tools, material, and forms of knowledge available to them.

Those standards were therefore appropriate to that historical level of knowledge. They are not appropriate to the level knowledge has reached in our own time.

Our standards must therefore differ from theirs as well.

How, then, could it make sense for us to solve our problems by returning to the very same standards used by the ancients?

Our present has moved far beyond them. The distance involved cannot be measured simply in years.

What matters much more is the enormous difference between the nature of their problems and ours; between the economic, social, and political conditions of medieval Arab-Islamic civilization and those of our own age; and between the level and forms of consciousness available in their society and those available in Arab society today.

Once we see the difference between our method of approaching the heritage and the older and newer forms of traditionalism, we can also see the difference between the picture of the heritage produced by our method and the pictures produced by those traditionalist approaches, despite the differences among their theoretical currents.

The traditionalist picture of the heritage is generally marked by an emphasis on supernatural, idealist, and fatalistic thought.

Arab-Islamic society therefore appears in this picture as a completely fatalistic society in which human will has little or no active role.

The creative social forces within that society also disappear—the forces that actually produced its material needs. Indeed, these forces barely appear in its history at all, even though in reality they were the source of the processes that drove that history forward.

When older and newer traditionalist approaches draw the heritage, and the society that created it, using these features alone, they produce an ideological picture.

That picture indirectly—and sometimes unconsciously—reflects the character of present Arab bourgeois ideology, intertwined with colonial ideology through a long historical relationship between the material foundations of the two.

The picture changes when we look at the heritage through a scientific revolutionary method and through the ideology behind that method—the ideology of the central revolutionary forces in the Arab liberation movement.

Here the heritage comes alive with the movement of the history that produced it.

Its main features are the features of thought in its objective, though indirect, relationship with the movement of that particular society: with its problems, its historical conditions, its contradictions, and the intellectual forms through which different social and ideological struggles were expressed.

Those forms possessed different degrees of relative independence, but they were still connected with the conflicts that produced them.

In this picture, we can see the human forces that act and make history.

We see change and development taking place according to the general laws of social development, interacting in a living way with the internal laws specific to the history of this particular society.

History is not driven by supernatural or fatalistic forces outside human and social action.

At the same time, this picture of the heritage also contains something of the present.

The present appears in it in two connected ways.

First, it appears through the scientific method that allows us to illuminate the heritage within its own historical setting.

Second, it appears through the revolutionary ideology rooted in the social basis of that method.

## 6

Traditionalist methods concentrate almost entirely on the supernatural and idealist side of the heritage.

In other words, they look at it from only one side.

Does the scientific method—historical materialism—simply make the opposite mistake? Does it concentrate only on the materialist side of the heritage and fall into the same kind of one-sidedness?

We must take this question seriously if we want to make the method of this book completely clear.

The first thing to remember is that the method is described as **historical materialism**.

That description itself helps us answer the question.

The fact that the method is materialist does not mean that it looks only at materialist thought or materialist philosophy while ignoring idealist thought and idealist philosophy.

In fact, this kind of exclusion and neglect is characteristic of idealist methods of interpreting history in general, and the history of philosophy in particular, as the work of idealist historians of philosophy in many different periods shows.[^V1-27]

Historical materialism works in the opposite way.

Precisely because it is a historical and materialist method, it looks at history as a whole. It does not examine one side and ignore another. It tries to understand all of them.

Idealism is one of the historical forms taken by human thought. Historical materialism must therefore study it just as it studies materialist forms of thought, whether philosophical or otherwise.

Both are historical realities.

Ignoring either of them would be a mistake in the use of the method itself. A scientific study cannot truly be scientific if it leaves out part of its subject.

There is another reason as well.

Idealist forms of thought, like materialist forms, are ideological products shaped by a class position toward material social reality. In that sense, both ultimately arise from that reality.

Historical materialism is defined, both in content and direction, by its attempt to explain[^V1-28] history—whether the history of society or the history of thought—on the basis of human material and social activity, rather than treating history as merely the history of human consciousness.[^V1-29]

It therefore follows from the nature of the method that idealist forms of thought must be studied just as seriously as materialist ones, since both ultimately arise from material and social reality.

When we say that they arise from it, however, we must distinguish between direct material production and indirect intellectual production.

Intellectual production does not arise from social reality in a simple or mechanical way. It develops through a complex process of reflection with its own internal laws, and those laws possess a degree of independence from the more general laws governing the direct development of material and social activity.

Our work in this book is based on this broad and realistic view.

We have not limited ourselves to searching for materialist tendencies in the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage while ignoring the idealist forms that dominate much of that heritage.

In fact, even if we had wanted to limit ourselves in this way, it would have been impossible in practice, quite apart from being methodologically wrong.

There are several reasons for this.

First, in Arab-Islamic philosophy in particular, materialist and dialectical tendencies are often so closely intertwined with idealist and metaphysical elements that we cannot identify the former without studying all the philosophical currents in which they appear, and without examining each of those currents in its own historical form and with its own particular features.

Second, purely idealist philosophies are rare, whether in the ancient or modern world, East or West.

Many idealist philosophical systems contain materialist or dialectical elements.

The reverse is also true of materialist philosophies that came before Marxist dialectical materialism.

A researcher must therefore examine such philosophies from all sides, reconsider them critically, and identify the elements of materialist dialectics within them after removing the mystical and idealist coverings around those elements.

Third, philosophy must be understood as an objective historical process that develops through the constant interaction of different ideas.

Materialism and idealism struggle with one another within this process, as do dialectics and metaphysics.[^V1-30]

The history of philosophy must therefore be understood as a system of interacting schools and intellectual currents, all of them tending, through their development, to move from the simple to the complex and from lower forms to higher ones.

All these general features of philosophy also apply to Arab-Islamic philosophy, together with the particular features created by its own historical setting.

For all these reasons, our task has been to uncover materialist tendencies within this philosophy even when they appear inside idealist forms, and to study the relations of conflict between the two.

## 7

There is another methodological question that we have had to keep in mind throughout this work.

How should we identify the forms taken by materialism, or by idealism, within an Arab-Islamic philosophy that appeared and developed during the Middle Ages across many different Islamic states—states whose conditions and characteristics differed not only from one another, but even from region to region within the same state and during the same historical period?

We raise this question because of an important historical and methodological fact.

Philosophical materialism, like philosophical idealism, has never existed in one single fixed form throughout the history of philosophy.

It has taken different forms as human societies moved through successive stages of development.

A study of the history of philosophical materialism shows that it developed as a growing movement. At each later stage, it overcame some of the weaknesses of the stage before it.

The changing forms of philosophical materialism can be understood through several general principles.

**1.** Despite their differences, the various forms of materialism share a basic position toward the world.

They hold that the material world exists before consciousness and independently of it. The material world is objective reality, existing in its own right and independently of any power outside it.

The different forms of idealism share the opposite general position.

Subjective idealism denies that the material world exists independently of consciousness.

Objective idealism denies that it exists independently of some eternal power outside it.

**2.** Even though the different forms of materialism share this basic view of the material world, each form must also be studied in relation to the social order of its own historical period.

That relationship affects the particular character materialism takes at that stage.

**3.** Each form of materialism must also be studied in relation to the natural sciences and to the level those sciences had reached at the time.

This relationship also helps shape the form taken by philosophical materialism.

A clear example is the historical connection between mechanical materialism and the science of mechanics during the period when mechanics became one of the defining sciences of its age.

With these three principles in mind, we can classify some of the forms that philosophical materialism has taken in the history of world philosophy.

**Naive materialism:** This was the earliest form of materialism known to the history of philosophy.

It was based on a spontaneous dialectical view of the phenomena of the world.

At this stage, materialism formed part of a still-undivided body of human knowledge about the world, at a time when the different “sciences” were still mixed together and had not yet become separate fields.

This early form of materialism expressed the outlook of the progressive forces within slave society, the forces once described as slave democracy.

Its best-known representatives include Thales,[^V1-31] Anaximenes,[^V1-32] Anaximander,[^V1-33] Heraclitus,[^V1-34] Democritus,[^V1-35] and Epicurus.[^V1-36]

**B — Metaphysical materialism:** This was the materialism of European thinkers in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and the early nineteenth century.

It began from a metaphysical, or static, view of the phenomena of the world, based mainly on the mechanical understanding of nature then available.

During this period, philosophy drew heavily on the natural sciences, and mechanics had developed further than the other sciences. It therefore exercised a strong influence over the natural sciences as a whole.

This metaphysical materialism expressed the ideology of the rising bourgeoisie and of the other progressive forces of that period.

**C — The materialism of the revolutionary democrats:** This form appeared during the nineteenth century in a number of countries in Eastern Europe and Asia as those countries moved from feudalism toward capitalism.

The materialism of the revolutionary democrats contained elements of a dialectical view of the world.

It expressed, above all, the ideology of revolutionary peasant forces.

**D — Dialectical materialism:** Historically, this is the most recent form of materialism up to our own stage.

It is Marxist materialism, expressing the ideology of the proletariat—the class whose historical task is the revolutionary transformation of the world.

We should add that this classification of the historical forms of materialism is neither final nor complete.

First, our knowledge of all its forms is still incomplete.

Second, some forms never developed into fully clear and independent systems, but remained at an early or embryonic stage.

For example, we did not include the forms of materialism that existed during the Middle Ages in the classification above.

In medieval Europe, the conflict between materialism and idealism appeared mainly in the struggle between nominalism (*Nominalisme*) and realism (*Réalisme*).[^V1-37]

Neither the materialist nor the idealist side developed into a form clear enough to be separated out as one of the major historical categories listed above.

This is why the German historian of materialism Friedrich Albert Lange[^V1-38] argued that medieval materialists became extremely skilled at hiding their real ideas. They developed materialism and atheism within works that, outwardly, appeared to defend God, religion, and theology.

Materialism within Arab-Islamic philosophy resembles medieval European materialism in this respect.

It too often appeared in unclear forms hidden within Islamic theological writing.

This made it easier for historians and researchers of Arab-Islamic philosophy—Arab, Muslim, and Orientalist alike—to find “justifications” for suppressing it, ignoring it, or distorting whatever signs of it did become visible.

One of the tasks of this book must therefore be to identify the forms taken by materialism within our philosophical heritage, as well as to uncover its materialist elements.

In doing so, we must try, if possible, to give a decisive answer to an important question.

By what standard should these forms be judged?

Should we measure them against the forms of materialism found in our own age—the age of dialectical materialism?

Should we compare them with the materialism of ancient Greece, with its forms of naive materialism?

Or should we judge them according to the age of al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, and Ibn Rushd?

And if so, what is the proper standard for **their** age?

To begin answering this question, we had to rely on the three principles mentioned earlier (pp. 40–41), because they follow from the requirements of the method we are using.

Along with the basic position toward the material world shared by the different forms of materialism, we must consider two other things.

First, we must examine the relationship between the materialist tendencies in our heritage and the social order that is reflected in them in one form or another.

Second, we must examine their relationship with the level reached by the natural sciences during the same historical period in which that heritage developed.

Once we accept these principles—especially the last two—we have to reject any attempt to judge the forms of materialism in our philosophical heritage by the standard of modern dialectical materialism, by the standard of ancient Greek materialism, or by any other standard disconnected from the social order within which Arab-Islamic philosophy developed.
