Questions such as divine decree, justice, and injustice also directly affected people’s lives, their attitudes, and their relationship with political power.”

Third, the denial that human beings have a real presence and an active role in the world, or that they can act freely.

Fourth, the idea that men and women differ by nature.

Ibn Rushd instead saw the difference between them as one of degree. That degree, he argued, “is determined by the type of work a woman performs, and the measure is her ability to endure its difficulties. When that ability is present, a woman may surpass a man.”

This study of Ibn Rushd by Salah Hazin, summarized here in a way that does not alter its essential argument, represents the new direction that has emerged in recent years for studying the heritage through a scientific historical method.

It also contributes to dismantling the myth that Arab-Islamic philosophy was essentially a philosophy of “reconciliation.” The traditionalist method imposed this idea on Arab-Islamic philosophy without any real basis beyond ideological motives—motives that often remained hidden beneath the heritage studies of traditionalists and other representatives of contemporary bourgeois thought.

□

When discussing modern studies of the heritage that represent this new direction, we should not overlook the serious attempt made by Ahmad Abbas Salih in a series of articles published in the Egyptian magazine *al-Kātib* between 1964 and 1965, and later collected in a separate book under the title *The Struggle Between the Right and the Left in Islam*.

The importance of this attempt comes, first, from the conditions in which it appeared. Egypt at the time was moving economically, socially, politically, and intellectually toward the building of a socialist society and a socialist ideology under the leadership of the revolutionary Gamal Abdel Nasser during the 1960s.

Second, Salih tried to use modern concepts and terms—such as the right, the left, and socialism—to describe social phenomena in Arab society shortly before and shortly after the rise of Islam. This too grew out of the conditions in which his study was written.

But from the beginning, the author carefully defines what he means when he applies these terms to the past.

He says that he uses “the term *right* to refer to conservatives, and the term *left* to refer to revolutionaries.” By the left, he means “those who were concerned with the social side of Islam.”

The left of that period, in his definition, consisted of those who sought to remove injustice from the poor and oppressed and to establish equality in rights and duties among the members of a single society.

By the right, he means “the tendency opposed to this: the tendency that allowed enormous differences to grow among members of Islamic society and fought against the left so that a small group could continue to possess wealth and control the political and social life of the Muslim majority.”

The author also defends his use of the phrase “socialist tendency,” even though, as he acknowledges, some readers may think he is using it where it does not belong.

He argues that the word *socialism* “has been used in many senses far removed from its modern meaning.” In his own study, those whom he calls socialists are simply “those who support a collective orientation,” while those who support an individual orientation are the non-socialists.

He finally defines his terms in this way:

> “The Islamic left (...) is the tendency with a collective orientation, which on the basis of what has already been said may be called the socialist tendency. The Islamic right, by contrast, is the tendency with an individual orientation, which seeks the good of the individual before it seeks the good of the group.”

By defining the terms in this way, the author removes the modern meanings from all the modern terminology he uses in the study. He openly admits that applying these terms to early Islam with their full modern meanings would be something that “has nothing to do with science.”

But this raises an obvious question: why use this unnecessary terminology at all?

He could have kept his modern perspective on these historical phenomena while also preserving the particular historical conditions in which they existed.

Still, this criticism is relatively minor compared with the positive qualities of the study: the importance of the questions it raises and the sharpness with which it approaches them from a progressive intellectual standpoint closely connected with the movement of present-day Arab reality.

The study begins from several methodological “principles.”

1 — Islamic civilization must be viewed as a whole. It is an “organic unity.”

2 — Every civilization rests on roots that are closely connected with it:

> “When we search for the ancestry of Arab civilization, we do not want simply to go back fourteen centuries. We want to discover how this civilization continues within us, and from its essential roots move toward the birth of a new civilization directed not only toward ourselves, but toward the whole world.”

3 — “A civilization is not driven forward by a single idea. Rather, after many struggles with rival principles, one general principle comes to dominate it.”

4 — Rationalism, according to the author, was the general principle that continued to dominate Arab civilization, even though:

> “the Islamic world knew more than one of these tendencies. It knew rationalism, and it knew a sensory tendency that looked down on reason. It knew individualism, and it also knew collectivism (...) Yet through all of this it moved within one general framework: the struggle between stagnation and progress, a struggle shaped by the social and political conditions through which society passed.”

The study does, however, show some confusion in its use of several concepts.

At one moment our civilization is called Arab; at another it is called Islamic. Ideology is sometimes separated from its class content. Conflicts between religious schools are often treated separately from class conflict. The individual is emptied of his social meaning, while collectivism is largely confined to one side alone—even though the opposing side is also collective in character and is not purely individual, as the study sometimes seems to suggest.

□

To conclude this critical survey of the positions taken by modern Arab researchers toward the intellectual heritage, we should finally consider the criticism that one of these researchers directs against the scientific historical method.

He claims that the method narrows the field of research for those who use it and that it offers a “one-sided interpretation of history.”

This criticism comes from Mahmoud Zayed in his introduction to the Arabic translation of Belyaev’s book on Arab-Islamic history.

The introduction says of the book’s author[^V1-188] that he follows “the Marxist historical framework” in studying and interpreting the events of Islamic history.

According to Zayed, this framework is both a source of strength and a source of weakness.

It is a strength because it led the author to concentrate on economic questions, popular movements, and revolutions and to shed revealing light on them.

But it is also, Zayed argues, a weakness:

> “He narrowed the horizons of his own research, even though those horizons are broad and many-sided. Islamic history did not arise entirely from those factors.
>
> “It is generally accepted that any one-sided interpretation of history must be incomplete. Even if the person offering that interpretation follows a scientific method, respects the principles of historical writing, and remains faithful to them, he still finds himself forced to pour history into a mold too small to contain it.
>
> “History, as the record of humanity, is as broad as life itself. Anyone who undertakes to write it must therefore possess a view as comprehensive as life. Otherwise he cannot avoid forcing reality and the available evidence to support one particular doctrine or one particular message, whether he intends to do so or not.
>
> “The author of this book is at least honest with himself. He does not hide from the reader that he is committed to a Marxist interpretation. Yet the reader will find it difficult to understand the author’s aims and intentions behind a number of his terms unless he already has some knowledge of the Marxist historical framework.”

What concerns us here is not the criticism directed at the author of the book as an individual.

What is clear, however, is that the criticism begins, both in principle and in substance, from an objection to his “Marxist historical” method itself. This is the same method that we adopt and argue should be used in studying our intellectual heritage.

Answering this criticism is therefore necessary if we are to complete the discussion begun in this introduction.

We agree with the critic that “any one-sided interpretation of history must be incomplete,” and that “history, as the record of humanity, is as broad as life itself, and anyone who writes it must possess a view as comprehensive as life.”

But that is exactly why it makes no sense to say, as the critic does, that an interpretation can be one-sided while at the same time following “a scientific method.”

A scientific method is incompatible with a one-sided interpretation of history. The two contradict one another.

For this reason, the “Marxist historical” method, precisely because it is a scientific method, rejects idealist bourgeois interpretations of history. Those interpretations are among the clearest examples of one-sided approaches.

There is also something strange in the critic’s claim that the very feature that gives the “Marxist historical framework” its strength is also the source of its weakness.

If concentrating on economic questions, popular movements, and revolutions, and shedding new light on them, is what gives this framework its strength, how can the same thing also narrow the scope of research and force Islamic history into “a shirt too small for it”?

Are we supposed to understand from this that Islamic history developed apart from economic life, popular movements, and popular revolutions?

Is it really an act of forcing “reality and the evidence to support one particular doctrine or one particular message” merely to say that Islamic history was organically and objectively connected with these things?

That would mean that such a connection did not really exist, and that concentrating on it has no basis in historical reality. The only reason for doing so would then be the desire to defend “a particular doctrine or message.”

If this is what the critic means—and this does appear to be the meaning of his argument—then it is his own interpretation of “Islamic history” that becomes one-sided in the clearest possible sense.

To separate history—any history—from its economic conditions and from the popular movements and revolutions fundamentally connected with those conditions is to look at history from only one side. Worse, it is to look at it from one of its least important sides, the side with the weakest influence on the way history moves and develops.

This one-sided outlook is one of the main features of the idealist methods preferred by the bourgeoisie in the study of history.

The wording of this criticism of the “Marxist historical” method also suggests that the critic understands Marxism as explaining history through economic factors alone. This may be why he describes it as one-sided.

It may also explain his remark that “the reader will find it difficult to understand the author’s aims and intentions behind a number of his terms unless he already has some knowledge of the Marxist historical framework.”

Perhaps, then, the critic’s own incomplete understanding of this “framework” is one reason his picture of the author’s method is inaccurate. We say this, for the sake of argument, even if we temporarily set aside the critic’s ideological starting point.

In any case, it is difficult to accept such a claim from a contemporary university professor and researcher, whatever his intellectual or ideological position and whatever method he personally uses to interpret history.

The “Marxist historical” method, or historical materialism, has become one of the best-known research methods of our time. Those who use it can be found throughout the world—in universities, academies, and other scientific institutions in East and West alike, in America and Western Europe as well as Eastern Europe.

They meet and debate with supporters of other methods at international and regional conferences held continually in different parts of the world to discuss the major questions of the age: social, economic, intellectual, philosophical, and scientific.

They are also present in large numbers in the Arab world itself, including at the American University where the critic himself teaches and carries out academic research.

Nor is this true only of historical materialism as a method of research.

Marxist thought more broadly has also become one of the basic elements of contemporary world thought. Any intellectual who genuinely wishes to be considered contemporary must understand these major currents of modern thought, whatever position he may ultimately take toward one or another of them.

No one is asking the critic to adopt the method of historical materialism in his own interpretation of history. That is a matter for his own scientific judgment.

But at the very least, he should know the method accurately—its foundations as well as its terminology—so that he can criticize the method that actually exists, rather than another method created by an inaccurate picture of it.

To understand historical materialism accurately is to understand that it does not explain history through economic and social factors alone.

It takes a broad view of the many different forces that affect the course of historical development. What distinguishes it is that it regards economic and social factors as decisive, while recognizing that many other factors also exert influence and that the strength of this influence varies according to the historical character of each society and each period.

The critic is entirely free to argue against this basic principle.

What he cannot reasonably do is accuse historical materialism of a one-sidedness that is completely foreign to the method itself.

Debate over the real foundation of the theory—the claim that there is a “decisive factor” in the movement of history—is perfectly legitimate. Indeed, that question has its own history.

Throughout the history of intellectual and ideological conflict, this is one of the basic points at which two lines of thought begin to separate and eventually develop into two different ideological traditions: the materialist line and the idealist line.

As for the criticism that Mahmoud Zayed directs at Belyaev himself, there is also room to question its objectivity because it begins from a position already decided in advance against the method Belyaev uses.

This is why the critic’s view of the book conflicts with the view presented by the “publisher” on the inside front and back covers.

While Zayed accuses the author of giving a one-sided interpretation of Islamic history, the publisher says that Belyaev “offers a comprehensive study of that vast and far-reaching state...”

The writer of the introduction also criticizes Belyaev because he “believes that the Arabs, like other peoples, passed through the following stages in their history,” after which Zayed lists the stages given in the book.

But the critic never tells us exactly what is wrong with this account, or what alternative stages he thinks should replace it.

Nor does he answer another obvious question: does he believe the Arabs were an exception to the historical pattern followed by “other peoples,” or not?

Instead, he simply comments:

> “This is the historical framework to which the author committed himself in advance, and he was consequently led to force the facts and evidence to conform to it.”
> —Introduction, pp. 8–10

But how exactly did Belyaev force the facts and evidence into this framework?

The critic gives only a few examples that have nothing to do with the question of historical stages itself.

Still, alongside this negative attitude toward historical materialism, we should also record another, more positive side.

The professor who wrote the critical introduction and his colleague who translated the book were both willing to present an Arab readership with a study based on historical materialism.

That fact offers another sign that this method continues to break through barriers, including ideological ones. It continues to establish its broad presence in the modern age and to reach us as a method for studying our own historical and intellectual heritage—after idealist and supernatural methods have exhausted their ability to strip that heritage of its history and its connection with real life.

## - 13 -

### C — The Orientalist Movement

The earliest beginnings of Orientalism in its second form were closely connected with Orientalism in its political and military form, whose own first nucleus was the “Crusading” movement.

Contact between Arab-Islamic culture and the culture of Western Europe, however, had begun before the Crusades.

It developed through the Arab-Byzantine wars and through the long Arab presence in both al-Andalus and Sicily. In these regions, Europeans increasingly encountered Arab-Islamic culture and began absorbing its achievements. Many of those achievements—especially in philosophy and the experimental sciences—were translated into Latin and Hebrew.

European philosophical schools and intellectual movements also appeared that were influenced by Arab-Islamic philosophers such as al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, Abū Bakr al-Rāzī, al-Ghazālī, and Ibn Rushd.[^V1-189]

From the time of the Crusading invasions of the East, however, the Orientalist movement acquired two distinctive features.

The first was that European scholars now came into direct contact with original sources that had not previously made their way westward.

The second was that Orientalism began to develop along two lines. At times these lines ran in parallel; at other times they became closely intertwined.

The first was political and colonial. Its beginnings were tied to the Crusading invasions, which sent repeated waves of fighters and occupiers into large parts of the Arab East for almost two centuries, from 1097 to 1291.

These invasions had colonial aims, even though they were carried out under the banner of the “Cross,” which concealed their real objectives behind a religious cover.[^V1-190]

The second line grew from the effect that Arab-Islamic philosophy, including the philosophical traditions of al-Andalus, had already had on European intellectuals, thinkers, and scientists.

That influence created a desire to discover more of the sources and achievements of Arab-Islamic culture in its different branches of knowledge.

Religious motives also found their way into both of these lines.

This helps explain why some of the earliest Orientalists known for translating large numbers of Arab-Islamic works were monks and churchmen, among them Peter the Venerable (1092–1156), Gerard of Cremona (1114–1187), Albert the Great (1193–1280), Michael Scot (d. 1235), Roger Bacon (1214–1294), and Llull (1235–1315).[^V1-191]

The positive results of the Orientalist movement cannot—and should not—be denied.

The most important of these results are:

1 — Orientalist scholars preserved many of the original texts of our cultural heritage and helped save them from disappearance or loss during the dark centuries when that heritage was cut off from educated people in the Arab world. Those were the same centuries in which the people of these countries were themselves largely cut off from the wider course of human historical development.

During this long period of isolation, many original texts were in danger of decay and destruction. Earlier, many had also been burned, mistreated, deliberately hidden, or distorted in meaning. Whatever we may think of their motives, modern Orientalists searched for these texts in the corners of private homes, neglected libraries, and book markets across cities and capitals, and even in villages and remote places throughout the Arab world and other parts of the East. They collected whatever they could obtain, by various means.

In our view, despite the roughness that sometimes accompanied this work, it saved treasures that might otherwise have disappeared. They survived, even if outside their own homeland, and their survival was what mattered most.

2 — Orientalists also published these works using modern printing methods. Sometimes they prepared critical editions, checking both the wording of the texts and their historical background. At other times they translated them into many European languages.

This work too had serious flaws. There were many errors in understanding the texts, as well as poor choices about what to translate, whether deliberate or not.

3 — The study of the heritage by Orientalists is the issue that concerns us here.

It would be wrong to claim that their contribution in this area was as positive as it was in the two areas just mentioned. In fact, the positive side was quite limited compared with the much larger negative side.

It was no accident that Western Orientalist studies of our intellectual heritage began to become active in the second half of the nineteenth century, or that Orientalism expanded enormously during the first quarter of the twentieth:

> “Some Western scholars travelled to the East, studied in its institutions, and came into direct contact with its intellectual and spiritual life. European and American capitals competed to promote Arab culture. Schools of Oriental languages and institutes for Islamic studies were established in Berlin, London, Paris, and Rome. Scholarly and historical societies were founded to study questions concerning Arab civilization. Congresses of Orientalists were held from time to time, encouraging study and providing material for research. Academic newspapers and journals devoted themselves to the East and its peoples, becoming places where opinions were exchanged and questions debated, examined, and tested.”[^V1-192]

We repeat: it was no accident that this activity began only in the second half of the nineteenth century and then grew so rapidly in the first quarter of the twentieth, even though Orientalism itself had existed for centuries.

This development was connected to particular historical circumstances and causes.

During the second half of the nineteenth century, capitalism was approaching a new stage: the age of imperialism. It was beginning to move away from a system of open, free competition toward one dominated by concentrated monopolies. This pushed capitalism into a new form and led to a new division of the world designed to provide those monopolies with places abroad to invest finance capital, sources of raw materials, and markets in which to sell their goods.

The signs of this transformation became increasingly clear and intense during the final quarter of the nineteenth century. By the beginning of the twentieth century, the transformation had become a reality.

As part of this process, capitalist states competed ever more fiercely to seize new parts of the “backward” world and to redistribute territories that had already been taken.

Under these same conditions, and for the same reasons, the Ottoman Empire—including the Arab lands under its rule—became one of the main arenas of this growing struggle. The Arab region offered both existing and potential advantages that attracted imperialist monopolies and suited their economic and political strategies. After the First World War and the Great October Socialist Revolution, the region became even more important to their military and energy strategies.

The “Eastern Question” was one expression of this struggle. Another was the plan for the B–B–B railway—Berlin, Baghdad, Basra—which formed part of the international imperialist race to control the wealth of Mesopotamia and secure access to the Indian Ocean.[^V1-193]

It was during this transition into the imperialist age—an age of redistributing old colonies and competing for new ones in the interests of the great monopolies—that Orientalism also began to turn in a new direction. It gave growing attention to Arab-Islamic studies, and especially to the philosophical heritage.

This activity increased further during the first quarter of the twentieth century, after the imperialist transformation had become an established reality and the Arab countries had come directly within the reach of imperialist ambitions.

The First World War gave its victors the opportunity to turn those ambitions into direct power. And the war also produced the first socialist state in history, lying along the northwestern borders of the Arab world. The Arab countries therefore acquired a new and extremely important place in the calculations of world imperialism. Their strategic importance grew still further when the sources of “black gold”—oil—began to emerge.

Some readers will ask: what does any of this have to do with Orientalist studies of our intellectual heritage, and especially our philosophical heritage?

Our answer is this: if we look at these studies apart from their historical beginnings, and strip away any connection between those beginnings and the conditions we have just described, then we are treating the issue in an abstract and ahistorical way.

An issue of this importance cannot be understood through an abstract approach, still less an ahistorical one. The same is true of other questions involving thought and culture.

The connection between the beginning of Orientalist studies of our heritage and the approach of the imperialist age needs to be explained. So does the connection between the rapid expansion of those studies and the beginning of the imperialist age itself. We need to examine these connections in their real historical setting.

We will uncover many of these dimensions later, when we look more closely at the positions taken by Orientalists in their treatment of the intellectual heritage. For now, we will try to identify the basic foundation of these relationships.

As capitalism was moving toward its new imperialist form, imperialism’s growing drive to control the Arab world required a related cultural drive as well. Political and economic control had to be accompanied by an attempt to influence Arab culture and shape its modern development.

This served two main purposes.

The first concerned the Arab bourgeoisie.

The Arab bourgeoisie was capable of moving into a position of dependence on imperialism because this could serve its class interests. But such a move required an ideological change. The bourgeoisie had to reshape an ideology that no longer fitted the conditions of the imperialist age.

This change therefore had to be prepared culturally. The bourgeoisie needed cultural tools that could help it rebuild its ideology.

The thinkers of rising capitalism understood that building—or rebuilding—an ideology was a complicated process. It depended on a whole network of real historical, social, and cultural relationships.

The bourgeoisie, for example, could not simply abandon its connection to its national history and national culture.

At the same time, it was not in imperialism’s interest for the bourgeoisie that depended on it in a colonized or semi-colonized country to become completely cut off from the national feelings shared by large parts of the population.

Nor was it in imperialism’s interest for this bourgeoisie to become unable to restrain those national feelings when they came into conflict with imperialist interests.

If the bourgeoisie became completely separated from the general feelings of the people, this would do more than expose its dependence on imperialism and its betrayal of national interests. It would also weaken the ability of bourgeois ideology to attract the middle social groups.

Because their class position can shift, these middle groups can sometimes serve as a reserve ideological ally of the bourgeoisie during social conflict. At other times, the bourgeoisie can lose that alliance—for example, when a national liberation struggle is rising in the country.

The thinkers of capitalism took all this into account as capitalism moved into its imperialist stage. When economic and political imperialist expansion toward the Arab region began, it had to be accompanied by a cultural and ideological approach directed at the Arab bourgeoisie.

For this purpose, imperialism needed a cultural tool connected to national history and national culture. But that history had to be interpreted in a way that was not progressive, and the culture had to be viewed through methods that suited this class-based and fatalistic interpretation.

This was the first purpose behind the imperialist attempt, through Orientalism, to influence Arab culture and shape its modern direction. The study of its intellectual heritage in general, and its philosophical heritage in particular, became one of the means by which this influence could be exercised.

The second purpose concerned the general ideological formation of those sections of Arab society that were most closely connected to culture and the intellectual heritage, and that had the greatest opportunity to shape new Arab thought: intellectuals, students, teachers, professors, writers, and researchers.

Orientalist studies of the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage began to expand precisely as the imperialist age was beginning. Their dominant tendency was to emphasize the idealist and supernatural elements of that heritage above others, while relying on subjective and ahistorical methods of interpretation and analysis.

All this shows that these studies were not separate from the wider development of capitalism into its imperialist stage. Nor were they separate from the ideological preparation taking place in countries that were becoming targets of imperialist control.

The aim was to support that control with intellectual and ideological foundations built partly from the national culture and intellectual heritage of the countries themselves.

It also meant creating a body of thinkers and ideologues drawn from the local bourgeoisie, or from sections of the lower and middle bourgeoisie moving toward it. These people could then establish those ideological foundations in their own countries, using the methods and approaches introduced by Orientalist scholarship.

In fact, the methods Western Orientalists used to study our intellectual heritage greatly impressed modern Arab thinkers, writers, and researchers when they first encountered them in Western universities.

They saw methods of research that were new to them, and they were drawn to them. They began to promote these methods and criticize the formal and traditional approaches that had been used in our own countries during the early stages of the modern Arab revival.

They then moved beyond simple admiration and advocacy and began to use these methods themselves.

Ṭāhā Ḥusayn was perhaps the boldest among the generation that had studied at Western universities under leading Orientalist professors.

He applied the Orientalist method in one of the most sensitive and controversial areas possible: his study of pre-Islamic poetry. He approached that poetry with systematic doubt and emphasized the role of religious factors in producing poetry that was later attributed to the pre-Islamic period.

Although Ṭāhā Ḥusayn remained within the framework of idealist thought in this study, his first attempt to apply this method provoked a fierce reaction.

Even so, the road had begun to open. A whole generation of researchers followed, including Manṣūr Fahmī, Ismāʿīl Maẓhar, Aḥmad Amīn, Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq, ʿAlī ʿAbd al-Rāziq, and others who came with them and after them, continuing down to the present.

There is no doubt that the methods of research used by this pioneering generation of Arab scholars were a necessary revolution against the empty, backward, descriptive style that had dominated before them.

Here we can clearly recognize a positive effect of Orientalist methods in our intellectual life—if we are looking only at the practical style of research.

But the situation is different when we look at the deeper method behind that research: its intellectual and ideological outlook.

The appeal of Western Orientalist scholarship came partly from the fact that its new research methods seemed so striking and unfamiliar to Arab scholars. They impressed intellectuals and educated readers.

But this attraction also drew generations of writers and thinkers toward the intellectual and ideological content that came with those methods: toward a particular way of looking at the world, especially society and thought, and toward a particular way of looking at the national intellectual heritage and studying it.

We have already seen enough evidence of this in our earlier discussion of modern Arab writers.

This means that Orientalist studies of the heritage have served—and continue to serve—the ideological purposes built into their method.

But new developments have also appeared.

As the Arab liberation movement has developed, and as scientific socialist thought has won victories on a world scale, scientific awareness, national liberation consciousness, and class consciousness have all deepened.

This has prepared the way for a new approach to understanding the heritage: an approach based, as we said earlier, on a scientific historical method.

## 14

### D — The Position of the Orientalists

To identify the main positions Orientalists have taken toward the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage, we first need to identify the major tendencies around which those positions have developed.

If we look at the earliest Orientalist studies and those that followed them, we can group their main approaches as follows.

**First: the approach based on “race theory.”**

This means studying the heritage from a racial point of view.

Arabs, or the “Semitic race,” or Eastern peoples in general are compared with Western peoples and described in one of several ways: as naturally and completely incapable of intellectual creativity; as capable of only one particular kind of thinking, such as analysis or synthesis, but not others; or as naturally limited to spiritual matters in the supernatural sense and incapable of dealing with material reality.

There are many similar claims.

All of them are arbitrary attempts to divide the peoples of the world and rank them according to supposedly natural differences in their intellectual and cultural abilities.

The “theoretical” basis of this approach is not only unscientific. In ideological terms, it is one of the positions most hostile to the development of peoples living under imperialist domination, including the Arab people.

It directly challenges their hopes for national liberation by presenting them with what is supposed to be an inescapable wall of fate. It tells them that they cannot transform their backward conditions into more advanced ones because their weakness is built into their very nature and is therefore permanent.

The bourgeois ideological meaning of this “race theory” is also clear. It suggests that differences between human beings come from differences in their intellectual and moral nature rather than from class divisions.

This approach appears in Orientalist studies in several forms.

(a)

Heinrich Becker (1886–1933) compares the effect of the Greek cultural heritage in the East with its effect in the West.[^V1-194]

In doing so, he presents ideas that assume a basic difference between East and West in the way they responded to ancient civilization. By “the East,” he means the Arabs in particular.

For Becker, the key difference lies in what he calls **humanism**: a sense of the self, or the presence of a distinctly human and subjective emotional life within a people’s cultural and civilizational production.

This becomes the decisive basis of the distinction he draws between East and West.

The East, in his view, has a rational and logical tendency but does not possess “humanism.”

The West, by contrast, had already produced the idea of humanism through Christian thought, and this humanism was bound to reappear later. In Becker’s view, it is deeply rooted in the West. It appeared in the Roman period, returned during the Renaissance, and still appears today in different forms in different European countries.[^V1-195]

According to Becker, this “decisive difference” between East and West explains why they responded differently to the heritage of Greek civilization:

> “Differences of type and race, differences in geographical environment, and the independent historical development of each side mean that the heritage of the ancients”—by which he means the Greeks and Romans—“produced in the West a form of development completely different from the one it produced in the East.”[^V1-196]

But what was it about the heritage of the ancients that supposedly produced such different reactions?

Becker answers through Werner Jaeger, who describes humanism as:

> “the idea of civilization based on the ideal of the pure cultivation and education of the human being, an ideal created by the Greeks when they reached the highest stage of their development.”[^V1-197]

For Becker, then, humanism in this sense is the central feature of Greek civilization.

Since he believes the East lacks this humanism while the West possesses it naturally, he concludes that the two regions had to respond differently to Greek civilization.

Becker says much more along these lines.

He denies that the Arabs created a civilization of their own or added anything fundamentally new to the civilizations of the countries they conquered. He argues that practically everything remained as it had been before, except that official and administrative documents that had once been written in Greek, Persian, or Coptic were now written in Arabic, while “nothing essential in the administration itself was changed.”[^V1-198]

In other words, Becker sees no real human creative process in the relationship between the Arabs and the civilization of the ancients.

From this point of view, the East was interested in Greek writings only when they suited what he calls its “rational and logical tendency.”

But the “Greek spirit”—by which he means humanism—remained closed to the East. This included Greek lyric poetry, imaginative literature, and everything he regarded as most purely Greek.[^V1-199]

So, in Becker’s formulation, the Greek heritage met **ideas** in the East, but in the West it met **human beings**.[^V1-200]

To reinforce this argument, Becker turns to Goethe’s famous statement:

> “East and West can no longer be separated.”

Becker interprets this to mean that the general view of the world and of life found in East and West is fundamentally very similar because both came from the same source.

By that source he means the Greek heritage.

So even the similarity between East and West, in Becker’s view, does not come from the historically and scientifically sound fact that human societies in different ages can share common forms of thought.

Instead, the similarity comes from the claim that both Eastern and Western views of life descend from the same Greek origin.

But even this similarity is only superficial for Becker, because he still believes that East and West responded to the Greek heritage in fundamentally different ways.

The idea that one part of humanity has a special claim to rational thought or humanism while another part does not is itself an ahistorical assumption.

And because this assumption rests on an unscientific theory of race, it is false at its foundation.

Becker refers more than once in his lecture to the factor of “race.”

But both rational thought and humanism are forms of consciousness shared by humanity as a whole.

Every human society is capable, simply because it is human, of developing both forms within its social consciousness and national culture. At a particular historical moment, one may become more dominant than the other.

But what determines this balance is not race or geography.

The decisive factor is the historical situation of each society: the form of its social relationships and the psychological outlook produced by its culture as a whole.

And historical conditions are never fixed. They are always moving and changing. As they change, they inevitably change the many relationships and factors that depend on them.

Becker’s judgments, however, appear to apply equally to East and West under all conditions and in every historical period.[^V1-201]

It is true that Becker sometimes mentions “historical factors” alongside racial ones.

But what does he mean by “historical” in the first place?

When we look at his argument as a whole, these supposed historical factors appear frozen, static, and permanent.

In that sense, they are not historical at all.

(b)

Before Becker, the French philosopher Ernest Renan (1823–1892) had already made “race theory” the direct basis of his well-known judgments about “Arab philosophy.”[^V1-202]

Renan carried conclusions from his comparative study of the Semitic languages into his study of philosophy.

As a scholar of Semitic languages, he followed a classification common among European linguists of his time, who divided peoples into “Semitic” and “Aryan” groups.

They based this distinction on similarities they believed they had found between Sanskrit and European languages.

Peoples whose languages they traced back to Sanskrit, including groups such as the Brahmins of India, were placed within the “Aryan” family together with European peoples.

Other peoples whose languages came from different linguistic roots, including the Arabs, were placed in another human family that they called the “Semitic race.”

Renan then added something further to this linguistic classification.

He turned it into a theory of hierarchy between the two supposed racial families in terms of cultural level and intellectual ability.

He placed the “Aryan race” above the “Semitic race.”

Renan says this quite openly. He even claims that he was the first to establish that the Semitic race was inferior to the Aryan race.[^V1-203]

This theory of hierarchy between human “races” later became part of the theoretical foundation of Hitler’s Nazi ideology, an ideology hostile both to science and to humanity.

Renan’s judgments about Arab philosophy became widely known.

He may have been the first person in nineteenth-century Europe to popularize the claim that it was wrong to call the Greek philosophy transmitted into Arabic “Arab philosophy.”

According to him, what was called Arab philosophy was really no more than a body of writings produced as a reaction against Arabism in the regions of the Islamic Empire furthest from the Arabian Peninsula—places such as Samarkand, Bukhara, Córdoba, and Marrakesh.

These philosophical works were written in Arabic only because Arabic had become the language of science and religion throughout the Islamic world. In Renan’s view, that was the whole story.[^V1-204]

Renan even rejects the claim that the Arabs preferred Aristotle to other Greek philosophers.

He argues that there was no genuine preference, because preference requires choice, and the Arabs had made no deliberate choice after reflection.

Instead, he says:

> “The Arabs simply adopted Greek culture in the form in which it reached them…”[^V1-205]

In the note that introduced the second edition of his book *Averroes and Averroism*, Renan repeated the same position:

> “The Arabs did nothing more than adopt the whole Greek encyclopedia as the world encountered it around the seventh and eighth centuries.”

What concerns us here is not the judgment itself about Arab philosophy.

What matters at this point is the basis on which that judgment rests.

Renan makes that basis clear in the introduction to the first edition[^V1-206] of his book, where he says openly:

> “It is not from the Semitic race that we should expect lessons in philosophy. One of the strange ironies of history is that this race, which was able to give its religious creations such extraordinary power, produced almost nothing original in philosophy. Among the Semites, philosophy was little more than something borrowed from outside, without great fertility of its own—essentially an imitation of Greek philosophy…”[^V1-207]

(c)

The danger of this racial “theory” lies in the fact that it became a wider intellectual current.

Renan was only one of its most prominent theorists.

After him, racial ideas became one of the foundations used in a number of Orientalist studies and formed part of imperialist ideology.

Among the Orientalists who continued this line of thought was Léon Gauthier, formerly a professor of history at the University of Algiers and a “well-known enthusiast for colonial rule.”[^V1-208]

Gauthier added new claims to Renan’s distinction between Semites and Aryans.

He argued that the “Semitic mind” could see things only as separate and unconnected, while the “Aryan mind” was able to bring things together, connect them, and form them into a coherent whole.[^V1-209]

Starting from this arbitrary racial distinction, he presents Islam as a strongly Semitic religion standing in opposition to Greek philosophy, which he presents as strongly Aryan.

He then places the Islamic philosophers between these two supposedly opposing worlds.

According to him, they tried with great skill to bridge the gap, but even the tools they used came from Greek philosophy itself.

Their work, on this account, was simply “Aryan” thinking trying to create a gradual connection between two opposing forms of thought: Islamic thought, supposedly based on separation, and Greek thought, supposedly based on connection.[^V1-210]

Gauthier uses the same colonial racial framework when judging the Moroccan people.

Among the white peoples of the Mediterranean basin, he describes Moroccans as the culturally different group that had “remained far behind.”[^V1-211]

Other Western Orientalists followed the same general current.

One was the German Orientalist Christian Lassen (1876), known for dividing peoples into Semitic and Aryan groups and for his hostility toward the “Semitic race.”[^V1-212]

Another was Émile Bréhier, professor of the history of philosophy at the Sorbonne, who also supported the distinction between Semites and Aryans.

Starting from this idea, Bréhier speaks about the philosophers of Islam in much the same way as Renan.

He argues that although they wrote their philosophical works in Arabic, most were not Semitic in origin but Aryan. This, according to him, explains why they looked for their philosophical subjects in Greek thought and also in the Mazdakite ideas of Persia, which in turn were mixed with Indian ideas.[^V1-213]

The Orientalist Stanla, known for his lectures at the Egyptian University on the history of philosophy, followed a similar approach.[^V1-214]

He too begins with racial assumptions when explaining the history of philosophy and of Islam.

In discussing the meaning of Islam, for example, he says:

> “…This absolute submission in everything, which is often an original characteristic of the Semites, is the defining principle of Islam and distinguishes it among peoples. Perhaps a vague awareness of a similar connection between this opposition and the religious instinct characteristic of the Arab people was what led Muḥammad to proclaim that he was the revealer of the true and original religion of Abraham and the Seal of the Prophets…”[^V1-215]

Modern science has made the falsehood of dividing humanity according to “race” and racial characteristics so clear that there is no need for us to discuss the question at length here.

Specialized scientific works provide detailed evidence against it.

A readily accessible Arabic source on the subject is the recently published book *The Racial Problem in Islam*.[^V1-216]

It summarizes the findings of modern anthropologists, sociologists, and psychologists—even bourgeois scholars—who have rejected the foundations of racial theories.

But we need to be careful here.

The fact that bourgeois scholars have been forced by modern scientific evidence to abandon racial theories does not mean that they have abandoned the social uses those theories served.

Those uses continue to appear both in the field of class struggle and in the struggle between imperialism and peoples seeking national liberation.

**Second: the view that philosophy has its true center in the West, not the East.**

This may be another form of the racial classification of the world’s peoples, but it has its own distinctive basis.

Its intellectual roots are different from those of explicit “race theory,” even though its class and political roots are much the same.

The theory of a Western center of philosophy begins from a real feature of human cultural history: the unity of human culture appears in forms that can look contradictory.

Because of this, it is very easy to treat the distinctive features of each national culture as absolute, and then to treat the differences between national cultures as absolute as well.

From there, a complete “theory” can be built.

This is exactly what happened among a number of European philosophers and thinkers in the nineteenth century.

Hegel (1770–1831), for example, passed the following judgment on Eastern philosophy:

> “What we call Eastern philosophy consists essentially, and to a very great extent, of the religious form of ideas and beliefs found among Eastern peoples—ideas and beliefs that at first sight we take to be philosophy.”[^V1-217]

We need to remember that Hegel’s judgment had another basis as well: his view of the relationship between religion and philosophy.

Hegel believed that religion appeared historically before philosophy.

Through religion, peoples expressed their ideas about the essence of the universe, the nature of the world, Absolute Spirit, and the relationship of human beings to all of these.

Because religion came before philosophy historically, Hegel regarded it as the first form through which Absolute Spirit came to know itself.

Even so, Hegel did not believe that the history of philosophy should include the history of religions.

Religion and philosophy may share certain features, but he believed there were also important differences between them.

Most importantly, philosophy approaches its subject through thinking consciousness, while religion approaches it through an immediate relationship to a higher reason.

Hegel says that the form through which the content of “science” properly enters the field of philosophy is **thought**—the universal and absolute form of thinking.

Religion, by contrast, presents the same content through artistic form, through direct outward contemplation, and then through representation and feeling.[^V1-218]

For Hegel, philosophy therefore stands above religion because it understands “Absolute Spirit” in a form more appropriate to spirit itself.

As for philosophical elements that may be hidden inside religion, Hegel does not consider them part of philosophy proper.

As he explains, his concern is philosophy itself, not philosophical elements in the abstract and not ideas that remain hidden inside myths.

This is why Hegel argued that Eastern philosophy should be removed from the history of philosophy.

Eastern philosophy may contain profound ideas, he says, but those ideas remain hidden within other forms.

He continued to insist on this position.

On another occasion he said:

> “Eastern thought must be removed from the history of philosophy. I will nevertheless make a few remarks about it. In the past I remained completely silent about it. Only recently have we been given the possibility of judging it.”

We do need to take this background into account when examining Hegel’s judgment on Eastern philosophy.

But there is another factor behind that judgment as well.

It may seem that Hegel simply lacked enough knowledge of the original sources of Eastern philosophy.

If that was indeed the case, however, it does not excuse him.

By the first quarter of the nineteenth century, when Hegel was delivering his lectures on the history of philosophy, enough information about Eastern cultures and their philosophical traditions was already available in Europe to allow a more accurate judgment and a sounder understanding of how philosophy had developed in the East.

The problem, then, was not simply a shortage of sources or ignorance of them.

It lay in Hegel’s philosophical method and in the way he approached the subject.

His strict definition of philosophy was also influenced by positions common among the bourgeois philosophers of Western Europe in his time, especially their views about the supposed difference between the ways people think in Eastern and Western societies.

For many decades, bourgeois European writing was dominated by the claim that Eastern and Western people had fundamentally different ways of thinking.

According to this view, Eastern thought was irrational, synthetic, and intuitive or sensory, while Western thought was rational and analytical.

Once that distinction had been accepted, it naturally followed that the intellectual products of each side would also be treated as fundamentally different from those of the other.

Philosophy was inevitably included in this distinction.

The American social thinker F. S. C. Northrop followed this line in his book *The Meeting of East and West*. The German writer W. Haas did the same, as did many others.

The problem with Eurocentrism in philosophy is, first, that its supporters turned the relationship between Eastern and Western ways of thinking into an opposition. Second, they ignored the basic unity of human thought and treated the real differences within it as absolute differences, as we will explain.

But was this theory of philosophical centrality based only on problems of knowledge—on the complex and contradictory nature of knowledge itself—or did it also rest on an ideological foundation? Problems of knowledge alone cannot fully explain this trend. The theory of centrality also had, above all, class roots. In other words, it had an ideological basis.

As capitalism developed into imperialism, it needed an intellectual and ideological justification for its domination of Asia and Africa even more than it needed a political one. In those conditions, the bourgeois claim that Eastern culture was generally irrational, sensory, and religious served a particular political purpose. It naturally gave the “rational” European a justification for ruling the “irrational” Asian.

Today, bourgeois philosophers such as Northrop still hold to the theory of Eurocentrism. But its supporters now have to find new arguments in its defence. In its classical form, the theory can no longer justify itself under new conditions simply by appealing to Eastern “irrationality.”

Earlier changes had already forced some adjustments to the theory. New standards appeared for deciding where the centre of philosophy lay. America could not simply be treated as part of Europe, yet there was a desire to include it within the philosophical centre, and America could not plausibly form a separate centre of its own. So the idea of “Western-centrism” replaced “Eurocentrism,” allowing the supposed centre to include both Europe and America.

But with the broad rise of national liberation movements in Asia and Africa, another trend naturally appeared. It answered “Western-centrism” with an opposing form of centrality: “Eastern-centrism,” or “Asian-African centrism.”

This opposing trend also has both intellectual and social roots. Its intellectual roots resemble those that produced Western-centrism. Its social roots lie in the rise of the peoples of Asia and Africa, regions that had been major centres in the early development of human civilization.

But we should note that the people who represent this Asian-African form of centrism are not, of course, representatives of the working class. They represent the bourgeoisie, the petty bourgeoisie, the feudal class, and large landowners.

Asian-African centrism appears mainly in two forms. The first is an exaggerated account of the role played by Eastern culture and philosophy in the development of European philosophy—even in the development of Marxism. The second is the tendency to treat the religious and mystical elements within the national cultures of Asia and Africa as absolute.

We have already mentioned one example: the report presented by the Pakistani scholar Sharif to the Twelfth World Congress of Philosophy in 1951. Another can be found in the ideas of the poet and philosopher Léopold Senghor, who is currently president of Senegal.

In explaining his idea of **Négritude**, Senghor describes it as the complete set of cultural, economic, social, and political values that distinguish the Black world, or the African Black world. He says that these values were created mainly by a sensory form of reason—a form of reason that enters into things and expresses itself through emotion, through self-surrender, through the merging of subject and object, and through myths, which he regards as archetypes of the collective spirit.

To all this he adds a primal rhythm in harmony with the rhythm of the universe. In other words, there is a feeling of connection with nature, the symbolism of myth-making, and rhythm. These, Senghor says, are “the essential elements of Black philosophy, whose traces you can find in every work and every activity of the Black person.”[^V1-219]

Having quoted this, we are faced with a question. Given Senghor’s definition of Black philosophy, how does he judge rationalist philosophies that differ from it?

Senghor says that “the civilization of analytical reason proves capable of creating a world of machines deprived of human warmth.” Or, as he puts it elsewhere, Black philosophy is a human philosophy, while European philosophies are essentially anti-human. He then places Marxism at the very summit of European rationalism.[^V1-220]

One Soviet philosopher[^V1-221] comments that the danger of such ideas appears when they are raised to the level of a general law. If they are made absolute in the way Senghor’s words suggest, then that danger is real: one racist position may arise to fight another racist position.

That makes it difficult to accept Jean-Paul Sartre’s interpretation when he comments on Senghor’s own account of the African tendency, given in 1948. Sartre acknowledges that “Négritude is racist,” but describes it as “anti-racist.” In his view, it “represents a moment of negation and a synthesis (*Synthèse*) produced in reaction to white superiority and privilege. It is the antithesis (*Antithèse*) in a dialectical sequence that leads to a final synthesis, which in turn gives rise to a universal humanity free of racism.”[^V1-222]

But racism is racism, and it can never be anything else. It is poetic fantasy to imagine that an equation of this kind will somehow produce a humanity free of racism. Senghor’s own statements about Négritude, and his absolute rejection of European philosophies, support this conclusion.

In fact, the appearance of a theory of Asian-African centrism under present world conditions—the conditions of national liberation movements and of labour movements in capitalist countries—does nothing to help unite the worldwide revolutionary movement.

The basic mistake in this whole approach, the approach of seeking a “centre of philosophy,” is its failure to understand the two-way relationship between national philosophy and world philosophy.

The answer to the Eurocentric or Western-centric theory of philosophy promoted by Western Orientalism—and also to its opposite, “Eastern” or “Asian-African” centrism—is that humanity is one, whether in East or West. Human beings share one material existence governed by the same objective laws.

This unity appears in the common conditions under which human beings came into existence and continue to survive. Above all, it appears in the shared basic conditions that make practical human activity possible.

The unity of humanity’s material existence in turn creates a basic unity in its intellectual or spiritual existence—that is, a basic unity in the ways human beings think and in the products of that thought.

For this reason, we cannot agree that Western thought is somehow more philosophical than Eastern thought, or the other way around.

The thought of Eastern peoples and Western peoples clearly shares a common human structure, and this unity appears in several ways. Human thought, whether Eastern or Western, is part of consciousness, which is itself the historical product of the development of matter. Thought, in East and West alike, is also a reflection of existence. And in both East and West, it is made up of comparable elements.

These real facts make understanding and interaction possible between the peoples of East and West and between their respective cultures.

But there is another side to the question that is just as important.

The unity of human thought does not mean that every way of thinking is completely identical or perfectly harmonious with every other. We should approach the question of different ways of thinking in terms of both unity and contradiction. Unity exists, but so do differences.

Here, however, we should speak about the distinctive features of each way of thinking rather than treating those differences themselves as absolute.

These distinctive features appear above all in the particular relationships between the common elements that make up thought. Here we see the dialectical relationship between the general and the particular. Every way of thinking is particular and distinctive, yet at the same time it belongs to something general and shared.

This brings us to the need to explain what we mean by the term **world philosophy**.

When we speak of world philosophy, we do not mean that at every stage of its historical development it was simply the sum of all national and regional philosophies, even though it was of course built from the achievements of those philosophies.

In fact, world philosophy has never, at any earlier stage or even at the present one, literally been the philosophy of the entire world.

Human societies have developed unevenly, and this uneven historical development has also produced uneven cultural development. At each historical stage, a particular group of countries has therefore tended to play the leading role in the development of human thought.

The philosophy produced in those countries comes, in a sense, to concentrate within itself the main development of philosophical thought during that period. This is why we can call it world philosophy even though it was not literally the philosophy of the whole world.

Perhaps Engels had this meaning in mind when he said that “in modern times, for example, France and Germany, and before them Britain, played ‘first violin’ in the orchestra of the development of world philosophy.”

But a closer look at the historical development of society shows us something else. As the world becomes more economically unified, contact and interaction between civilizations become more active and extensive. We can therefore conclude that we are now moving toward a point where **world philosophy** and the **philosophy of the whole world** increasingly come together.

At the same time, national and regional philosophies remain closely connected to the history of world philosophy without simply dissolving into it.

It would be a mistake to focus only on the elements through which a national or regional philosophy and culture contributed to world philosophy and world culture, while ignoring the elements that belong more specifically to that national or regional tradition.

Doing so can easily distort the history of that philosophy and culture. Every national philosophy contains elements that may have little importance for world philosophy but enormous importance within the national philosophy to which they belong.

The mistake, then, is to ignore the complete structure of a national philosophy and look only at those parts that became important to world philosophy. Many Orientalists made exactly this mistake in their studies of the Arab-Islamic philosophical heritage.

There is one final point in our criticism of this second trend in Orientalist studies.

Its representatives speak vaguely about “Eastern philosophy,” as though there were a single Eastern philosophy with one set of shared characteristics. This is not true.

It is more accurate to speak of **Eastern philosophies**, in the plural, each with its own distinct historical character.

European scholars themselves have studied these different Eastern philosophies separately. Chinese philosophy, such as the philosophy of Confucius, differs from Indian philosophy as represented, for example, by the teachings of the Buddha. Persia had Mazdakite philosophy and Zoroastrian philosophy, and so on.

It is only natural that these philosophies should differ from one another, because the Eastern societies that produced them also differed in their historical development.

The same applies to Arab-Islamic philosophy. It too developed in relation to a particular social reality and particular historical conditions, which it expressed in its own distinctive way.

□ There is another feature of Western research into Eastern philosophy and culture that we need to examine carefully before completing this discussion.

By the middle of the twentieth century, Western bourgeois philosophy—and Western culture more generally—was facing a crisis. Some bourgeois philosophers and thinkers tried to overcome that crisis by turning toward the East. They hoped to find values in Eastern philosophy and culture that could help rescue bourgeois philosophy from its difficulties.

They began preparing the ground for this project by saying that Western thinkers had previously neglected or ignored Eastern philosophy, even though the peoples of the East possessed great philosophical traditions. The West, they now argued, should study those traditions, gather the necessary material from them, and add the results to its own philosophy. In this way, a stronger philosophy might emerge, one capable of confronting Marxism.

The beginnings of this trend can be traced back to before the middle of the twentieth century.

It is worth noting that these beginnings appeared alongside the successive stages in the crisis of bourgeois philosophy. Consider the significance of the following events:

- Immediately after the First World War, a number of bourgeois philosophers visited countries of the East.
- In 1921, John Dewey published *Letters from China and Japan*. Other Western philosophers published a number of similar books.
- In 1922, Bertrand Russell published *The Problem of China* after visiting the country.
- In these works and others like them, their authors repeatedly argued that the values of the East could help the West overcome its philosophical crisis. This idea appears in writers such as Bergson, Russell, Dewey, Riecken, Petro, and others.
- After the Second World War, the issue was raised much more sharply. International philosophical conferences were held in Hawaii and Honolulu, with active participation from many leading contemporary idealist philosophers. Some attended in person, while others sent papers and reports. Dewey was a regular participant. Others included Sidney Hook, one of the leading American idealist philosophers and among the most reactionary; Radhakrishnan and Raju from India; Suzuki from Japan; Sharif from Pakistan; and Charles Malik from Lebanon.
- At more than one of these conferences, these philosophers discussed in detail the idea of merging Eastern and Western philosophy. They also suggested that if Marxists wanted to develop Marxism further, they too should turn to the East and incorporate teachings drawn from Eastern values.
- One striking feature of this trend is that petty-bourgeois thinkers in Asia and Africa have been among the strongest advocates of merging Marxism with Eastern philosophy. Why? Two opposing reasons come together dialectically. First, they find a number of attractive elements in Marxism. Second, like other sections of the petty bourgeoisie around the world, they are afraid of Marxism in its genuine form. They therefore propose what is called an “Eastern Marxism.”

Whatever we think of this proposal, it raises several questions:

1. Can the traditional and contemporary philosophies of Eastern countries enter into active interaction with contemporary world bourgeois philosophy and have a productive influence on it?

2. Must such influence necessarily lead to the creation of a merged Eastern-Western philosophy?

3. Can Eastern philosophy influence Marxism? And would that influence take the form of a merger?

We can answer these questions, in the same order, as follows.

- Even under capitalism, the conditions are developing for greater unity across the world. Modern communications make the world smaller and, in practice, reduce the isolation of what might once have been regarded as the world’s distant “countryside.” As communist relations develop, this process of unification becomes faster.

  Under such conditions, cultural unification will naturally become broader and deeper. The cultures of different peoples and continents will move closer together, and cultural cooperation and interaction will become increasingly urgent, especially in intellectual and philosophical work. This process will speed up as social relations develop more rapidly in different countries.

- As development accelerates in these countries and deep social changes take place, cultural development will also change. Contemporary philosophy in these countries will naturally develop a character of its own.

  When this philosophy begins to raise questions that are not purely local but broader and more universal, it will inevitably influence Western philosophy. We can already see signs of this today. Over the last fifteen or twenty years, hundreds of studies on Eastern philosophy have appeared in Western Europe and America. Some ideas from these philosophies will inevitably spread beyond specialist circles and enter ordinary thought.

  But this does not mean that Eastern and Western philosophy will merge into a single philosophy. Such a merger is not realistic.

  Idealist philosophers have already tried to bring it about. In 1949, the Second East-West Philosophers’ Conference was held in Honolulu. Some expected its participants to agree on a formula for combining selected elements from both sides into a single Eastern-Western philosophy—a kind of philosophical Esperanto.[^V1-223]

  But the expectation that such an artificial agreement could succeed was itself an idealist illusion.

  Philosophy is a product of the historical development of human societies. The advocates of philosophical merger ignored this fact. They also ignored the class character of philosophy.

  They further ignored the fact that Eastern philosophy can influence Western philosophy only through a natural historical process shaped by the development of Eastern societies themselves. Conscious social activity can speed up or slow down this process, but it cannot be produced through some artificial operation imposed from outside. A natural historical process does not happen simply because a group of philosophers decides that it should.

  Attempts to create an agreed philosophical merger by arbitrary selection can therefore produce only an eclectic philosophy, dominated by the idealist elements of the philosophies being combined.

- The idea of merging Marxist philosophy with Eastern philosophy is even further removed from reality.

  Marxism itself has no need for this kind of artificial merger. If Marxism is to spread to new countries and become useful and practically applicable in the countries of the East, what it needs above all is a precise understanding of the concrete conditions of each individual country. That matters far more than merging Marxism with the philosophies of those countries.

  But this does not mean that Marxism cannot develop by drawing on elements from Eastern cultures. It means that, as Marxism is applied to the concrete conditions of each country, it will develop through its engagement with those elements.

  Take, for example, the well-known Marxist theory of historical socio-economic formations. If we apply this theory to the development of Eastern countries when analysing their history, we will inevitably encounter new phenomena, such as the Asiatic mode of production.

  Further research into this question must in turn enrich Marxist-Leninist theory concerning socio-economic formations.

  What does the study of Asian societies from the standpoint of this theory require? Above all, it requires us to begin from the actual social activity of the countries of Asia. That is the basic way to approach the problem.

  In any case, we can already reach one conclusion. Marxist philosophy is not a fixed doctrine. It is a guide to action. Every Marxist teaching is therefore capable of development.

  The cultures and philosophies of the East are among the sources through which such development can take place when Marxism is applied to real social relations. They can contribute new forms and insights that make Marxism richer and more productive.

  Studying the intellectual heritage of the East—including the Arab-Islamic heritage—in relation to its social and economic foundation and according to the Marxist method of research is one form of precisely this kind of application.

**Third —** This is the third trend in Western Orientalist studies of the heritage.

This trend concentrates on the most conservative and reactionary aspects of that heritage, especially those most deeply immersed in the supernatural and the realm of the absolute. At the same time, it obscures the aspects that contain materialist tendencies, or hides the social dimensions that can exist even within apparently supernatural forms, as we find in the philosophical Sufism of figures such as al-Ḥallāj and the martyred al-Suhrawardī.

Many Orientalists have even tried to reinterpret the philosophical systems of thinkers such as al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and Ibn Rushd in ways that remove their materialist dimensions. The result is to turn them into purely Sufi, Illuminationist, or religious systems.[^V1-224]

□ We find one example in Carra de Vaux,[^V1-225] in his treatment of Sufi terminology in al-Fārābī’s writings.

Carra de Vaux tries to show that this terminology is a dominant feature of al-Fārābī’s philosophy. He then uses this supposed feature to pull these terms away from their rational philosophical content and to cast doubt on al-Fārābī’s place within the rationalist tradition.

Yet a systematic scientific study shows that rationalism is the defining character of al-Fārābī’s philosophy as a whole, whether we look at his theory of knowledge, his philosophy of existence, or his social philosophy.

Massignon followed a similar path by placing al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, Ibn Sīnā, and other Islamic philosophers among the Sufis.[^V1-226]

We find the same tendency in Gilson, who regards Ibn Sīnā as the founder of the theory of Illumination.[^V1-227] The Danish Orientalist Mehren also paid particular attention to Ibn Sīnā’s mystical writings, publishing and translating them.[^V1-228]

□ This brings us to a problem that occupied an extraordinary number of pages in the writings of many of these Orientalists: the supposed Illuminationist mysticism of Ibn Sīnā.

The whole problem begins with a passing phrase at the start of Ibn Ṭufayl’s introduction to his famous philosophical story *Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān*.

Ibn Ṭufayl begins his introduction by saying:

“You asked me, dear and loyal brother, ... to share with you as much as I can of the secrets of the *mashriqī* wisdom mentioned by the Master Abū ʿAlī Ibn Sīnā.”

Elsewhere in the introduction, Ibn Ṭufayl reports something Ibn Sīnā had said in the introduction to *The Healing*. The point is that *The Healing* was written according to the Peripatetic school, while Ibn Sīnā’s own true position, he says, should be sought in another work, his *al-Falsafa al-Mashriqiyya*.

It was the word *mashriqiyya* in these two passages, attributed to Ibn Sīnā, that created the problem for the Orientalists.

The question was how the first vowel should be pronounced. Should the word be read with a **u** sound—*mushriqiyya*—or with an **a** sound—*mashriqiyya*?

The difficulty was that Ibn Sīnā’s book bearing this title, *al-Ḥikma al-Mashriqiyya* or *al-Falsafa al-Mashriqiyya*, had not survived in a form available to them.

For these scholars, the question was extremely important because changing that single vowel produced two very different meanings. Read with the **u** sound, the expression meant **Illuminationist wisdom**. Read with the **a** sound, it meant **Eastern wisdom** or **Eastern philosophy**.

If the first meaning could be established, they could then argue that Ibn Sīnā was an Illuminationist, in a sense connected with Sufism.

So this was not merely a question about a word. For Western bourgeois Orientalists, much more was at stake.

It mattered greatly to them that the book Ibn Sīnā supposedly regarded as the true expression of his own position, rather than *The Healing*, should turn out to be an Illuminationist work.

That would remove Ibn Sīnā once and for all from the camp of defenders of Aristotelian rationalism and place him instead among the irrational, metaphysical Illuminationists associated with al-Suhrawardī.

It would also change how his position on the **primacy of existence** could be understood, at least in the theory of knowledge. One might still speak of such a position among some Peripatetic philosophers, but not in relation to the “real” Ibn Sīnā—the author of *Illuminationist Wisdom*, whose leading principle would then have to be the **primacy of essence**.

For bourgeois ideology—and still more for imperialist ideology—what matters in our age is not to uncover, in the brightest parts of our intellectual heritage, philosophical teachings that point toward the materialist tendency contained in the idea of the primacy of existence. It is far more useful to present that heritage to us stamped with the seal of “Illuminationist lights,” deepening our alienation in the modern world.

This is why we say that the enormous effort spent by so many Western Orientalists trying to establish a **u** sound in the first syllable of *mushriqiyya*, in the title of a lost book by Ibn Sīnā, was not pointless. It was not wordplay. It was not a storm in a teacup, as some might imagine.

It was another expression of their ideological approach.

Some of them therefore went beyond the question of the vowel itself. Even if the word were read with the **a** sound, meaning “Eastern,” they still tried to classify Ibn Sīnā’s unseen book as an Illuminationist or “spiritualist” work.[^V1-229]

□ Western Orientalists’ strong attraction to the Sufi currents in our heritage brings us to another phenomenon. At first sight, it seems like one of the strangest contradictions in Orientalism.
