One explanation lies in what we discussed in the previous section: at that stage, the new message did not yet offer an immediate material solution for the weak, the oppressed, and the exploited among the people of Mecca.

For that reason, these groups largely stood apart from Muhammad and his small number of followers. Their attitude was almost one of indifference as to whether the movement succeeded or failed.

This was despite Islam’s declared opposition to usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver. Such principles directly challenged some of the main foundations of aristocratic Quraysh power in Meccan society.

A realistic explanation of this situation suggests that the main reason the oppressed people of Mecca, as social groups rather than as individuals, held back from supporting Islam before the migration was the way they understood the Qur’anic promises of reward and punishment.

They understood these promises as postponing the issue to the next world. Reward and punishment seemed to belong to a moral and otherworldly realm rather than to the immediate material conditions of life.

This explanation therefore rejects the view of some biographers of Muhammad,[^V1-671] who argued that the Quraysh leadership frightened these oppressed groups into staying away from the new religion by persecuting Muhammad and his followers.

According to that view, fear prevented these groups from taking the role they might otherwise have played in securing the movement’s victory, even though some of its principles were close to their own interests as broad social groups—especially its opposition to usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver.

But the reality, in Muruwwa’s view, is that these oppressed groups could not yet see in the movement a material gain that would rescue them from their present hardship.

In the verses promising reward and punishment, they could see only a reward postponed until the “Day of Resurrection.”

So we have to ask: if they had found in Islam, during the Meccan period, an immediate way out of their present material suffering, would they still have held back from supporting it?

Or would they have supported it enthusiastically, no matter how harsh Quraysh persecution became?

We can ask the same question in another way:

Could the promise of future reward and punishment in the afterlife, by itself, have attracted these deprived groups during the early Meccan period while also acting as a deterrent to the ruling Quraysh aristocracy?

At this point, the question is mainly about consciousness.

Were both sides of this social conflict intellectually prepared to understand reward and punishment in the afterlife as forces that could attract one side and restrain the other?

Let us allow one modern biographer of Muhammad to answer in his own way.

Discussing one of the reasons Quraysh refused to accept Muhammad’s message, this writer says that they were driven by “their fear of resurrection and of the punishment of Hell on the Day of Judgment.”

He continues:

> “Here is Muhammad proclaiming to them, in terrifying verses that make hearts tremble with fear, that their Lord lies in wait for them, that they will be raised again on the Last Day in a new creation, and that their deeds alone will speak for them.”[^V1-672]

But after quoting these frightening verses, the writer adds:

> “...They did not know resurrection, and they did not accept what they heard about it. None of them imagined that he would be rewarded or punished for the deeds of this life after leaving it. Their fear of the future concerned this life. They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of standing and prestige (...). As for reward after death, resurrection on the day when the trumpet is blown, Paradise prepared for the righteous, and Hell prepared for the unjust—none of this entered their minds...”[^V1-673]

Dr. Haykal clearly falls into a contradiction here.

On the one hand, he speaks of “their fear of resurrection and of the punishment of Hell on the Day of Judgment.” On the other, he says that they did not know resurrection and did not accept the idea.

Even so, he reaches the heart of the matter when he identifies what actually frightened the leaders of Quraysh.

As he says, **their fear of the future concerned this life.**

They feared illness, loss of wealth and children, and loss of status and prestige.

In other words, they feared for their material interests and for the privileges they had gained through a long history of commercial, political, and religious control over the central institutions of Mecca.

That is the real issue.

On the other side, the deprived groups of Mecca had fears of their own.

They feared that postponing reward and punishment until the Day of Judgment would also mean postponing the solution to their own problem: the material suffering they faced under the absolute power of usury and monopoly.

Their fear too was ultimately “of the future in this life.”

That, here as well, is the real issue.

If this is the heart of the matter—and Muruwwa argues that it is—then the main factor determining the position of the two sides in the central social conflict of Meccan society was not whether they knew about resurrection or did not know about it.

It is correct to discuss the matter at the level of consciousness.

But what kind of consciousness?

The negative reactions that shaped the attitude of the Quraysh merchant aristocracy toward Islam throughout the thirteen years before the great migration to Medina were an early and undeveloped form of class consciousness.

They resembled an instinctive reflex.

The initial Islamic call produced a shock. It demanded the complete rejection of idols and insisted that religious belief be directed entirely toward the one and only God. At the same time, it openly mocked the idols the Meccans worshipped and condemned their worship without compromise.

These teachings immediately made the great merchants of Quraysh feel that their material interests were under threat.

The worship of idols, many of which were gathered in the Kaʿba at Mecca, was one of their important sources of profit. It made Mecca a destination for tribes from at least the north-west and north-east of Arabia.

The pilgrimage seasons around the Kaʿba, where these idols were gathered, also concentrated some of the most profitable commercial and moneylending activity in Arabia. This activity strengthened the leading figures of the Meccan Dār al-Nadwa, the emerging form of “political” authority through which they exercised their commercial and financial power.

That was one side of the danger perceived by the Quraysh leadership.

The other came from the broader moral and humanitarian teachings of the early Islamic message.

These teachings called for the material suffering of the lower social groups to be eased. They called for justice toward the poor, the weak, and the needy. They taught that people were equal in standing before God regardless of race, color, blood, or ancestry.

Other Qur’anic verses condemned usury, the monopolization of basic necessities, the hoarding of gold and silver, and similar practices.

Most of these Meccan teachings were moral rather than legal in character.

Even so, they gave the leaders of the Dār al-Nadwa the impression that Islam had arrived to place its full weight on the opposite side of the emerging balance of social forces in late pre-Islamic society, which we discussed in the previous chapter.

That opposite side was the side of the lower social groups: those being oppressed and exploited by the commercial and tribal leaders of the time.

But this early and undeveloped class consciousness, expressed in the tense reaction against Islam, was historically unable to see that this opposition was not actually in the long-term interests of the Quraysh merchant leadership itself.

In fact, Muruwwa argues, the opposite was true.

If that leadership had been able, during the early Meccan period, to see the historical direction in which Arab society was moving, and to see that Islam was moving in the same direction, it would have recognized that Islam was also opening the path to its own future development.

The Quraysh merchants were already forming the nucleus of a class that was capable of playing a major role in the new social order that was about to emerge.

It is enough here to say that Islam appeared at a historical moment when the tribal framework had reached the point where it had to break apart.

A single unifying framework now had to replace it.

Only such a framework could create the conditions needed for the rise of a genuinely new Arab society—not simply a larger collection of tribes, but a society different in quality, with new relations of production, a new social structure, and new institutions created to organize those relations and develop their material foundations.

That society appeared later.

But at the moment when Islam emerged, it was only beginning to take shape within the new historical horizon opened by the Islamic message.

It is therefore correct to say that breaking apart the tribal frameworks and establishing a single unifying framework—the first major task of the historical stage opened by Islam—did not actually conflict with the interests of the very group that spent thirteen years fighting Islam with fierce hostility.

Without realizing it, the Quraysh leadership was delaying the beginning of its own development: its transformation into a major class that would later help build the Arab-Islamic society that followed.

This was the mistake in the Quraysh leadership’s view of its own “class” interests and their supposed conflict with Islam.

The direction of historical development was not toward the contradiction they imagined.

On the contrary, the logic of that development eventually required what happened after the conquest of Mecca: the Quraysh leadership joined the historical transformations set in motion by Islam after its victory in Arabia and its expansion onto the wider world stage of the time.

### B — The Universe and the Human Being Within the Framework of Monotheism

#### 1 — The Intellectual Dimension of Monotheism

The historical need to break apart the tribal framework and replace it with a unifying one arose, in Muruwwa’s view, from the laws governing social development at that particular historical moment.

Islamic monotheism was the central religious expression of the relationship between Islam and the social conditions of that particular time and place.

But this relationship also appeared in other forms. The different institutions and teachings of Islam were connected in different ways to the particular historical features of the society in which Islam emerged.

One of the most important of these was the intellectual dimension of monotheism.

This would have a deep effect on the later relationship between two processes: the development of Arab-Islamic society and the development of Arab-Islamic thought.

The interaction between these two processes would help create a common intellectual world whose roots lay in a common ground: Islam itself.

The intellectual dimension of monotheism began to appear in the earliest Islamic teachings.

These teachings offered forms of knowledge about the universe, including knowledge of nature and of the human being’s place, role, and responsibilities within it.

Everything Islam taught about these subjects through the language of the Qur’an served the central issue of the Islamic message: establishing monotheism as a religious belief and as the foundation of the ideological system that would later develop around it.

#### 2 — The Universe and Nature

Many of the Qur’anic verses revealed during the early Meccan period, before the great migration to Medina, were concerned with this intellectual dimension.

They presented the “metaphysics” of Islam as a complete system centered on the idea of one God.

This divine unity gave the universe its unity and also gave human understanding of that universe a single organizing principle.

At the foundation of this system stood the idea of creation.

The universe as a whole, and everything within it, was created by the one God, who has no partner.

Creation was preceded by nonexistence.

In other words, the universe was created from “nothing.”

This means that the world had a beginning. It was not eternal.

If the world had a beginning, then matter, motion, time, and space also had beginnings. None of them is eternal.

And anything that is not eternal in the past is not everlasting in the future, because whatever has a beginning must also have an end.

All created worlds therefore pass away.

No person and no thing lives forever in this earthly life.

But the idea of immortality remains.

If immortality does not belong to this life, then it belongs to what comes after death: the second life, where every person receives the result of what they did in the first. Good is answered with good, and evil with evil.

Our earthly world—the world of nature that we experience through our senses—is to be known from the divine source of knowledge, revelation.

Its story is this: it existed first in the darkness of nonexistence. God created it. And it will return to the darkness of nonexistence, to annihilation.

The natural world is neither eternal nor everlasting.

God’s will is absolute in both its creation and its destruction.

The old theory of “coming-to-be and passing-away” therefore takes a particular form here in Islamic religious thought.

Things come into being from outside themselves, through God. Then the will of the Creator brings every created thing eventually to corruption and annihilation.

#### 3 — ...And the Human Being

In the source of his coming-to-be and passing-away, the human being is no different from other created things.

But his place among them is different.

The human being is the highest of created beings.

“The Qur’an made Adam’s creation from the substance of life a symbol of the appearance of the human being on earth and of his elevation above the angels.”[^V1-674]

> And when We said to the angels, “Bow before Adam,” they bowed, except for Iblīs. He refused, acted proudly, and became one of the unbelievers.
> *(Surat al-Baqara, verse 34)*

Can we see in this Qur’anic human being—formed from the “substance of life” and placed above the angels—a clear sign of Islam’s grounding in earthly reality?

Let us look again at this Qur’anic picture of the human being:

> And when your Lord said to the angels: “I am creating a human being from dry clay, formed from dark mud. When I have shaped him and breathed into him of My spirit, fall down before him in prostration.” Then all the angels prostrated together, except Iblīs, who refused to join those who prostrated. He said: “Iblīs, why are you not among those who prostrate?” He replied: “I would never prostrate before a human being whom You created from dry clay, formed from dark mud.” He said: “Then leave this place, for you are rejected.”
> *(Surat al-Ḥijr, verses 28–34)*

> When your Lord said to the angels: “I am creating a human being from clay.”
> *(Surat Ṣād, verse 71)*

So the human being is made from earthly clay, formed from the substance of this earth.

And yet this earthly human being is worthy of receiving the prostration of the angels, who in Qur’anic language are spiritual beings.

This comparison, followed by the elevation of the human being above the angels, allows us to see an inner connection between Islam’s “metaphysical” world and its world of earthly reality.

The same connection also links monotheism as a purely religious belief with monotheism as a social framework for the world of human beings made from clay.

And through this hidden connection, the human world is tied to the unity of the universe as a whole.

According to Qur’anic logic, the human being, born from earthly clay, is raised above the angels and the rest of creation. Everything in the heavens and on earth is even described as being placed at humanity’s service.[^V1-675]

This special status may itself be one expression of the connection between the human world and the unity of the universe as a whole.

But this view of the human being immediately raises another question:

If the human being holds such a high position, does this mean that he acts—or chooses not to act—through his own will?

Is he free from a compulsion that would cancel his own will?

In other words, can he freely choose to act or not to act and therefore be responsible for what he does, whether good or evil?

Or does Islam place this question under the broader principle that links the entire universe to one supreme will, the will of the one God, just as the universe is also linked by the unity of its existence through its single Creator?

This question would confront Muslims later as Arab-Islamic society developed.

It would become a major intellectual and ideological problem occupying Arab-Islamic thought throughout the Middle Ages.

During the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the problem began as a quiet dialogue between thought and social reality.

Under Umayyad rule, that dialogue increasingly became an open conflict between thought and political power.

Later still, the struggle over the same problem increasingly took place between one body of thought and another.

Its social and political roots almost disappeared behind the dust of the intellectual and philosophical struggle—first between the Muʿtazila and their opponents, and later between philosophy and its opponents.

We will return to this problem in a later section of the book dealing specifically with divine decree.

For now, what matters is its connection with the question of the human being as Islam presented it during the period of Muhammad’s mission.

The issue is the basic place Islam gave the human being within its unified vision of the world.

Within that framework, what position did Islam take on human freedom of will?

And what follows from that freedom: is the human being responsible for every action and every form of behavior that comes from him?

The foundational texts—the Qur’an and the Sunna—do not give one absolute and unambiguous answer.

On the surface, the relevant texts point in two different directions.

Some appear to affirm that human beings are free to act or not to act.

Others appear to deny that freedom and to connect every human action to the will that is the source of every other will in the universe: the will of the one God.

This question too therefore becomes connected to the central issue of the Islamic message: establishing monotheism as a religious belief, as a social framework replacing the tribal framework, and as the theoretical basis of the ideology of the social order that would emerge as Islam triumphed, spread, and built lasting institutions.

Consider, for example, these Qur’anic verses:

> Whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.
> *(Surat al-Zalzala, verses 7–8)*

> Whoever does good does so for himself, and whoever does evil does so against himself.
> *(Surat al-Jāthiya, verse 15, and Surat Fuṣṣilat, verse 46)*

> Whoever wishes may believe, and whoever wishes may disbelieve.
> *(Surat al-Kahf, verse 29)*

The first two passages plainly say that every person must bear responsibility for what they do, whether good or evil, small or great.

And the logic of responsibility seems to require that human action be connected to freedom of action.

The third verse appears to strengthen this conclusion. On its surface, it leaves belief and unbelief to the choice of the person who believes or disbelieves.

But alongside verses like these, we find other Qur’anic passages whose apparent logic points in a different direction:

> Whoever God wishes to guide, He opens his heart to Islam; and whoever He wishes to lead astray, He makes his heart tight and constricted, as though he were climbing into the sky. In this way God places defilement upon those who do not believe.
> *(Surat al-Anʿām, verse 125)*

> You do not will unless God wills.
> *(Surat al-Dahr, verse 30)*

Early Muslim scholars devoted enormous effort to this apparent conflict between Qur’anic verses.

They tried to bring all the texts together under a single logic in which no contradiction remained.

That great intellectual effort grew out of political conflicts that produced an increasingly active world of ideas. Different views, schools, and ideologies struggled with one another until the Muʿtazila gave these debates a more developed form of rational inquiry.

From there, the debate moved more specifically into philosophy.

And from this atmosphere of intellectual and ideological conflict emerged the philosophical movement whose highest expression was what we call **Arab-Islamic philosophy**.

We can therefore see how a creative intellectual movement, in both its foundations and its later developments, arose and grew on the intellectual ground created by Islam.

This is why, as we said earlier, the basic unity of Arab thought rests on the common ground from which this entire movement emerged, even though its different currents later came to disagree with one another in fundamental ways.

Islam was that common, unifying ground.

### C — The Development of Islamic Legislation

#### 1 — The Great Migration

The Islamic mission spent thirteen years in Mecca without achieving victory. One reason was that the commercial leadership of Quraysh, as a social group developing into a class, was unable to understand its own long-term class interests. It did not yet see that those interests would not ultimately conflict with the social order Islam would create once the Islamic faith had won.

But those thirteen years were filled with an enormous struggle between two forces. One drew its strength from traditional authority and material power. The other drew its strength from an unshakable belief in the new message and an extraordinary ability to endure fierce persecution without giving way.

Those years prepared the founder of the new faith and his companions, and they prepared the movement itself, for the much greater struggles still to come. Islam would face many more battles before it could establish itself firmly enough to move in step with the course of human development for an entire historical stage.

The struggle between Mecca and Islam eventually had to take a new direction. After thirteen years, the conflict could no longer be settled within its old limits. The great migration to Medina opened the way to this new phase.

How did that road open, and how did the new phase begin?

To answer that, we first need to understand how Medina, the new destination of the migration, differed from Mecca at the time.

As we have seen, Mecca was a barren town in a “valley without crops.” Yet it had grown into an important commercial center and a religious center. Its great merchants had turned its religious importance to the advantage of their own interests as the group that controlled the town’s material, social, and religious life.

Because of Mecca’s special circumstances, together with the wider historical conditions of the Arabian Peninsula that we discussed in the first chapter, this rapidly growing commercial center developed a distinctive class structure. Sharp contradictions emerged within it. These conditions were likely to create a setting in which a movement could arise in Mecca and address the whole peninsula, answering the historical need for a major transformation of pre-Islamic Arab society.

The Islamic mission appeared in precisely this setting.

But it met resistance from the very social group that, historically, was destined to play a leading role in the coming change. That group had a distorted understanding of its own interests.

Medina was fundamentally different.

It was an agricultural town, and its people had long worked mainly in farming. It had no large agricultural estates. Nor did it enjoy Mecca’s commercial standing or the religious importance that had helped make Mecca a major trading center. Social divisions in Medina had therefore not developed enough to create the same sharp conflicts between different groups of the population.

Permanent agricultural settlement had also led to the growth of several villages around Medina. Most were inhabited by settled tribes. The most prominent were the Aws and the Khazraj.

Before them, Jewish tribes had already settled in the area. The three most important were Banū al-Naḍīr, Banū Qaynuqāʿ, and Banū Qurayẓa.

Medina’s Jews did not work only in agriculture. They were also active in trade and in metalworking and jewelry-making as skilled crafts. They also spread the practice of lending at very high interest among poorer groups, including agricultural workers and the poor of the local tribes.[^V1-676]

#### 2 — The Struggle Between Mecca and Medina

That was the general character of Medina at the time.

The great difference between Mecca, with its commercial and religious importance, and Medina, which was mainly agricultural, may have encouraged the Aws and Khazraj—the two leading tribes of the Medina region—to raise the standing of their own town by embracing the Islamic movement after years of persecution by Mecca’s commercial leadership.

Their leaders may have hoped that by supporting Islam, they could eventually transfer some of Mecca’s importance to Medina if Islam won through their help.

Was this ambition, and this hope, behind the bold decision of the two tribal leaderships to begin negotiating—secretly at first—with the early Muslims?

There is little reason to rule this out. In fact, what happened after those negotiations fits this interpretation.

During the pilgrimage season of 621 CE, twelve men came to Mecca—ten from the Khazraj and two from the Aws. They brought Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the founder of the Islamic mission, their decision to pledge allegiance to him.

He met them at al-ʿAqaba, a pass between Mecca and Minā. The meeting ended with what became known as the **Pledge of al-ʿAqaba**. This pledge was an extremely important practical step in opening the historic road of migration to Medina.

A year later, in 622 CE, the migration began.

News had reached Mecca that the pledge had found fertile ground in Medina: conditions there were favorable for accepting Islam, protecting it, and working for its victory.

The first Muslim emigrants numbered around one hundred. They slipped out of Mecca separately and in small groups. When they reached Medina, they found safety, and the people who had made the pledge fulfilled their promises completely.

Once the migration was completed with the arrival of Muhammad and his companions in Medina, the nature of the conflict changed greatly.

It was no longer only a struggle between Muhammad and his followers on one side and the commercial leadership of Quraysh on the other. It also became a struggle between Mecca and Medina.

Yet the heart of the conflict remained the same. The Islamic movement still corresponded to the historical need to transform the foundations of pre-Islamic Arab society. At the same time, that transformation was moving in a direction that would ultimately serve the development of the very social forces that had originally placed themselves in direct opposition to Islam.

Islam’s migration to Medina was therefore a decisive historical event. It changed both the future of this struggle and the future of the larger historical project that Islam was then called upon to carry out.

The first reason the migration mattered was that Islam had now found security and stability in Medina, away from the persecution it had faced in Mecca. It could therefore begin working out the details of the new social relationships within which it would operate.

The second reason was the positive support Islam received from the **Anṣār**, the people of Medina who supported the emigrants.[^V1-677] Their support shifted the balance of power decisively toward Islam in its struggle with Mecca’s commercial aristocracy.

After the migration, fierce military battles followed between the Anṣār and the **Muhājirūn**, the emigrants from Mecca,[^V1-678] on one side, and the leaders of Quraysh who opposed Islam on the other.

The first side won repeatedly, while the second suffered repeated defeats.

Eventually the Meccan side gave in and invited the Muslims to negotiate the entry of the Islamic “army” into Mecca without a battle. In modern military language, Mecca was effectively treated as an open city to the Muslim army—and therefore to the Islamic movement itself, with everything that movement represented both as a religion and as a social order.

This happened in 630 CE, eight years after the migration.

Mecca therefore regained its privileged position. More than that, from the time of the “conquest” onward, it became a center of worldwide attraction.

#### 3 — The Beginning of Legislation

Because the great migration was such a decisive historical event, it allowed Islam to move from a stage centered mainly on calling people to faith into a new stage in which the movement also taught and organized society through a system of law.

Islam was no longer only a faith. It was also becoming a body of law.

This meant taking on the task of organizing a society that was moving beyond its tribal structure and entering a new system of social relations, more developed than those of the pre-Islamic period.

This was the beginning of the legislative stage in Islamic history.

The legislation itself developed in stages.

At first it was simple and temporary because it dealt with a simple and temporary social situation.

Later, Islamic legislation became more complex, broader in scope, and more permanent.

We can therefore distinguish between two types of legislation.

##### First — Temporary Legislation

The first practical legislation made immediately necessary by the migration dealt with the emergency problems of housing and daily life faced by the Meccans who had been forced to leave their homes and families as part of the Islamic migration.

This situation led to the institution of **brotherhood** between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār.

Calling this “brotherhood” a form of legislation means that it was not introduced merely as an abstract moral or humanitarian principle. It was a practical social arrangement designed to deal with a real but temporary situation.

The emigrants arrived from Mecca after being driven from their homes. Some had already been poor. Others had been wealthy but had been forced to leave Mecca with nothing.

They therefore arrived in Medina without the means to provide themselves with housing or food.

The system of “brotherhood” established by Islam was an urgent and necessary way of giving them shelter and support. But they were not treated simply as refugees living in the homes of the Anṣār. They were treated as their “brothers” in faith, with rights of housing and support similar to those of brothers by blood and family.

This law, however, was temporary.

It was meant to remain in force only as long as the emergency that had made it necessary continued. Once that need disappeared, the law itself would disappear.

And that is what happened.

When the circumstances that the law had been created to address came to an end, the system of “brotherhood” was abrogated.

Those circumstances began to disappear when war booty from successful attacks on Quraysh’s caravans started flowing to the Muslims. The Muhājirūn could then support themselves instead of depending on the Anṣār.

The abrogation of the law of “Islamic brotherhood” in this way was the first practical example of something important in Islamic legislation: an implicit recognition of the law of development and change.

Abrogation assumes that a law exists because an objective need calls for it. The law comes into force because that need exists, and it remains in force only as long as the need remains.

That is the first point.

The second is that this principle also recognizes that the need behind a law can change as objective circumstances change. No need is permanently fixed, because the conditions that create it are themselves not fixed.

We will return to this subject in later chapters.

##### Second — General Legislation

This second type of legislation rested on the following basis.

At the time Islam appeared, a society built increasingly around commercial relations was developing, and its material base was growing.

This development required the old tribal structures and loyalties to be broken down. The human groups living along trade routes and in commercial centers had to be brought together within a single social framework: one institution, or, in other words, one unified state.

At that time, Islam as law and social order was uniquely suited to provide this framework—to become this institution, or this “state.”

This historical task necessarily required a legal foundation and a complete system of general laws.

Some of these laws dealt with circumstances that already existed. Others dealt with situations expected to arise as the new society took shape.

In this setting, there had to be laws governing fighting under the banner of Islam so that Islam could win and spread.

These had to be accompanied by laws governing grants and war booty, laws concerning lands conquered either by force or by treaty, and laws dealing with the many new situations created—or expected to be created—by the Arab-Islamic conquests both inside and outside the Arabian Peninsula.

This body of legislation served two closely connected purposes.

The first was organization.

The second was encouragement.

The second may even have been more immediately effective, because these laws created material incentives to take part in conquest and expansion beyond the barren peninsula. Those incentives added material enthusiasm to the religious enthusiasm of the believers who fought in the armies of conquest.

The same laws also served a third purpose, this time involving consciousness.

A person who had lived in the pre-Islamic age did not instantly lose the ways of thinking formed in that earlier society simply by entering the Islamic age. Those older habits of memory and thought remained until a new Islamic consciousness became firmly established.

And that new consciousness could take root only through actual participation in the new Islamic society. By living and acting within this new historical setting, people gradually formed a new kind of social memory.

This gives the legislation we have been discussing another function.

Among Muslims taking part in expansion under the banner of Islam, it helped establish a clear understanding of what they were doing—what we might call the unifying “theory” behind their actions.

That theory rested on the following principles:

1. Fighting for one common, unifying institution instead of fighting the fragmenting and destructive wars of rival tribes.

2. Fighting in ways intended to develop human capacities and widen the fields in which people could use them, instead of exhausting those capacities in cycles of personal, family, and tribal revenge.

3. Turning the right of revenge from a right belonging to the individual or the tribe into a right belonging to society and its common institution.

4. Changing revenge from an act of personal, family, or tribal retaliation into a social punishment intended to defend the interests of society as a whole.

5. On this basis, organized warfare was established as a tool either for expanding the authority of the social, political, and ideological institution or for protecting that institution.

Islamic legislation also changed the legal basis of social organization.

Tribal customs and Bedouin traditions, which reflected the old subsistence economy, had previously formed the main “legal” foundation of society.

But the new society of commercial and social relations needed a different kind of legal foundation.

Islamic legislation was an objective response to this development.

Under the religious authority of Islam as law, a new legal order emerged. It included the idea of the “state” and the idea of an organized system of “law.”

The general rules of Islamic law therefore became a body of laws governing society as a whole, with everyone subject to decisions made under them.

Bedouin traditions had not recognized any authority beyond the boundaries of a particular tribe or its own customs.

Islam now made the authority of its law the one supreme authority above all others.

### D — Intellectual Debate and the Relationship Between Knowledge and Faith

#### 1 — The Question of Knowledge[^V1-679]

Islam’s position on intellectual debate can only be understood in relation to its position on knowledge. The question of knowledge lies at the root of the whole issue.

There are two main questions here.

First: where does human knowledge come from?

Second: how far can human beings go in gaining knowledge through their own powers of understanding?

If we approach the question only by looking at the relationship between knowledge and religious faith, we might conclude that Islam recognizes only one source of knowledge: God.

That would mean denying the ability of reason, or any other human faculty, to gain knowledge independently.

Such a conclusion might seem to follow from the fact that Islam presents divine revelation as the source of its message.

Both doctrine and law come from revelation. And Islam’s account of the world, in the details it provides, also comes from revelation.

The Prophet communicates what is revealed to him: “The Messenger’s duty is only to deliver the message” (Qurʾān 5:99). God alone, by His will, chose him to communicate it.

The foundations of belief and the rules of Islamic law are themselves forms of knowledge.

If this knowledge comes from God, and from God alone, then it might seem to follow that knowledge about the origin of the world, the problems of existence, and the laws of nature, society, and thought does not come from the human faculties of understanding or from their interaction with the world we experience through the senses.

If that were the case, then faith in the Islamic message would require people simply to accept this knowledge completely.

There would be neither a right nor an ability to debate it, because debate involves doubt, while faith appears to exclude doubt.

Our first conclusion, then, might be that Islam rejects intellectual debate.

We will now see how far that conclusion reflects the actual situation.

At first sight, some Islamic texts—the Qurʾān and the hadith—seem to support it.

For example:

> “If they argue with you, say: ‘God knows best what you do. God will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection concerning the matters over which you differed.’”
> (Qurʾān 22:68–69)

> “They ask you about the spirit. Say: ‘The spirit belongs to my Lord’s command, and you have been given only a little knowledge.’”
> (Qurʾān 17:85)

> “No one knows its interpretation except God. Those firmly grounded in knowledge say: ‘We believe in it; it all comes from our Lord.’”
> (Qurʾān 3:7)

There is also a hadith reported by Jābir.

He said:

> “Surāqa ibn Khathʿam came and said: ‘Messenger of God, explain our religion to us as though we had just been created. What are our actions based on now? On what the pens have already written and destiny has already decided, or on what still lies ahead?’
>
> He replied: ‘No. Rather, on what the pens have already written and destiny has already decided.’
>
> Surāqa asked: ‘Then what is the point of acting?’
>
> He replied: ‘Act. Each person is made ready for what he was created for, and every person acts according to his work.’”[^V1-680]

What does this hadith mean?

It deals with divine decree and destiny—in other words, with the question of whether human beings have freedom of will or whether their actions are predetermined.

Surāqa, who according to the hadith was one of the Prophet’s companions, asks a direct question.

Are our actions determined by what has already been written for us—by what the pens of the unseen world wrote before they dried, meaning that the matter has already been decided?

Or do we act according to choices we ourselves make about the future course of our lives?

The Prophet replies, according to the hadith, that people act according to what has already been written for them and has become part of their destiny.

Each person is “made ready for what he was created for.” In other words, each person is bound by what was assigned to him from the beginning of creation.

People are simply told to act, without continuing to question the matter, and each person will receive the reward or punishment for his actions.

The hadith therefore has two important implications.

The first is that one of the Prophet’s companions wanted to understand a question connected with the way people act in their individual and social lives.

He asked the Prophet about it.

The Prophet referred human affairs back to destiny and then brought the discussion to an end, telling people to leave the matter to God, who would judge each person according to his actions.

From this, we might conclude that knowledge of everything ultimately refers back to what has been written by divine destiny, leaving no room for debate.

But the hadith has a second implication.

Although the companions had been taught that knowledge came from God through revelation and was to be accepted rather than debated, we can already see someone among them wanting to move beyond the habit of simply receiving knowledge through unquestioning acceptance.

That desire appeared in the form of a question containing at least the beginnings of a discussion.

But the old habit of simply accepting what was given quickly brought the attempt to an end, and the debate stopped.

Another hadith, transmitted by al-Tirmidhī from Abū Dharr al-Ghifārī, reports the Prophet as saying:

> “Gabriel came to me and gave me the good news that anyone from your community who dies without associating anything with God will enter Paradise.
>
> I said”—the speaker here is Abū Dharr—“Even if he commits adultery and steals?”
>
> He said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals.”
>
> I said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals?”
>
> He said: “Even if he commits adultery and steals.”
>
> Then, on the fourth time, he said: “Whether Abū Dharr likes it or not.”[^V1-681]

This hadith carries the same two implications, but even more clearly.

Abū Dharr is more persistent in his questioning.

And the Prophet, according to the report, ends the discussion even more firmly.

This attitude is reinforced and explained by another hadith, reported by the companion Umāma:

> “The Messenger of God said: ‘No people went astray after having been rightly guided except when they were given to disputation.’”[^V1-682]

So where did this dislike of intellectual debate come from, and why?

There were two factors: a direct factor connected with faith, and an indirect social factor.

##### First — The Factor of Faith

Here we are dealing with the relationship between knowledge and faith.

That relationship follows from the Islamic view of knowledge—the view that knowledge of doctrine and law comes from God.

A decisive expression of this idea appears in the Prophet’s sermon at Ghadīr Khumm on his return from the Farewell Pilgrimage:

> “Today I have perfected your religion for you, completed My blessing upon you, and chosen Islam for you as your religion.”
> (Qurʾān 5:3)

The verse was presented by the Prophet as words from God to the Muslims.

It told them that the religion communicated by the Prophet had now been completed, and with it God’s blessing upon them: Islam as both doctrine and law.

In this setting, according to the books of Qurʾānic interpretation, “perfection” and “completion” mean that everything Islam had brought in matters of belief and law was final. It was to be taken as it was, without alteration or change.

This means that people received knowledge of doctrine and law as something complete, through an absolute act of faith.

If people were allowed to use their own understanding to gain knowledge in this area, their role was limited mainly to understanding the texts that contained the details of doctrine and law.

Even this freedom was restricted by what was believed to have been transmitted from the divine source through the Prophet, with chains of transmission ultimately judged by specialists in hadith and its transmitters.

One example of this can be seen in the way Qurʾānic commentators explained the word **ḥikma**, or “wisdom.”

The word appears frequently in the Qurʾān.

We know that before Islam it had carried a meaning connected with a simple kind of rational reflection. It referred to knowledge gained directly from things and to general judgments drawn from personal experience.

In other words, pre-Islamic Arabs could understand “wisdom” as gaining knowledge from what could be observed through the senses and using that knowledge as a basis for thought, even if only at a very simple level.

But what does the word “wisdom” mean in the Qurʾān?

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr, who died in 463 AH / 1070 CE, reports in his *Jāmiʿ Bayān al-ʿIlm wa-Faḍlihi* that Mālik explained “wisdom” in many Qurʾānic verses as understanding God’s religion and acting according to it.

In his commentary on the verse,

> “Remember what is recited in your homes of God’s verses and of wisdom”
> (Qurʾān 33:34),

al-Ṭabarī says that “wisdom” means what was revealed to the Messenger of God concerning the rules of religion but was not included in the Qurʾān itself—in other words, the Sunna.

And in explaining the verse,

> “He gives wisdom to whomever He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has been given great good”
> (Qurʾān 2:269),

Ibn ʿAbbās said that “wisdom” meant knowing the rules concerning what is permitted and what is forbidden.[^V1-683]

According to these statements and interpretations, then, “wisdom” is limited to knowledge received from an outside source—knowledge of religion as doctrine and law.

We do not find here the older sense of “wisdom” as knowledge gained through the activity of reason as it deals with things, or as it draws ideas and concepts from that experience through its own powers and faculties.

All of this leads us to the conclusion that the relationship between knowledge and faith is central to understanding the limits originally placed on knowledge in Islam.

##### Second — The Social Factor

Here we need to return once again to the question of monotheism and its relation to knowledge.[^V1-684]

If we examine the Islamic idea of monotheism more deeply, from its different historical sides and dimensions, we are led to another question: the basic relationship between Islamic belief and Islamic law, and therefore the social basis of that relationship.

Separating belief from law is not only a methodological mistake. It also goes against the logic of the Islamic mission itself.

That logic joined faith to a social order. Faith functioned as the ideology of that order. The two were connected rather than separate.

We therefore have to understand monotheism through this connection.

It was the point at which the historical role of Islam came together.

Religious unity could not be separated from social unity.

The two depended on one another.

Their agreement was necessary for both to exist, and their existence together was necessary for the creation of a unified social framework replacing—or historically required to replace—the divided tribal structure of the time.

Seen in this way, we can understand how monotheism affected the question of knowledge.

Placing knowledge within the relationship between faith and understanding, and restricting its ultimate source to God, was the intellectual side of the principle of unity.

In other words, it was the ideological side of monotheism.

Ultimately, it was the ideological expression of a unified social institution.

Seen from this perspective, the early reluctance to engage in intellectual debate becomes easier to understand.

During the Prophet’s lifetime and through most of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, the conditions existed for this reluctance to remain firm while still retaining some practical flexibility.

But after the killing of the third caliph, ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, those conditions began to weaken.

Social and political contradictions were becoming more developed and were turning, at an increasing rate, into open conflicts.

From this historical turning point onward, reluctance toward intellectual debate could no longer stand on the same firm ground as before.

Intellectual debate began actively making its way into social and political conflict despite the powerful material and ideological forces trying to restrain it.

#### 2 — Testimony from Muslim Scholars

The picture of knowledge in Islam that we have just described is also supported by statements made by Muslim religious scholars.

We may remember, for example, the passage quoted earlier from the judge Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī in his *Ṭabaqāt al-Umam*:

> “As for the science of philosophy, God Almighty did not grant them anything of it...”

This statement clearly presents knowledge as something given to human beings by God, rather than something people gain through the effort of their own minds.

Al-Ghazālī gives us another example.

While explaining his position on the discipline of *kalām*, or speculative theology, he says:

> “Its purpose—that is, the purpose of *kalām*—is only to preserve the creed of the Sunna and protect it from the confusion caused by the people of innovation. God Almighty gave His servants, through the words of His Messenger, a creed that is the truth and that serves the good of their religion and worldly life, as the Qurʾān and the reports of the Prophet make known. Then Satan planted in the minds of the innovators ideas opposed to the Sunna. They became absorbed in them and nearly disturbed the true belief of its followers. So God brought forth a group of theologians and stirred in them the motives to defend the Sunna...”[^V1-685]

Al-Ghazālī does not merely say that Islamic beliefs were given by God “through His Messenger.”

He goes further.

He says that Satan put the ideas of the innovators into their minds, and that God brought the theologians into being and inspired them to defend the Sunna.

On this view, even rational knowledge—and especially philosophical knowledge—reaches theologians and philosophers from outside their own minds and powers of understanding.

Its source is either God or Satan.

Ibn Khaldūn also understood the question of knowledge in Islam in this way when he said that “reason is excluded from religious law and its investigations.”[^V1-686]

Ibn Taymiyya likewise says that the Muslims of early Islam

> “believed that debate and argument about matters of belief led people away from religion. For this reason, when the Prophet died, the Muslims held one creed, apart from those who secretly practiced hypocrisy. Investigation and argument over matters of belief did not appear until the time of the Companions, when innovations and doubts arose and Muslims were forced to answer them. From this came the different sects, and the discipline of *kalām* arose as an argument against innovators who had departed from the path of the early Muslims and opposed religion. *Kalām* therefore arose as a necessity and was to be used only to the extent that necessity required.”[^V1-687]

This has led some modern researchers to observe that because the Qurʾān discouraged believers from investigation and argument in matters of religion, it was natural for religious scholars later to become uncomfortable with free rational inquiry whenever it extended into religious beliefs, examined them intellectually, or reached conclusions different from those the scholars were used to.

This may also help explain their hostility toward philosophy and their attacks on philosophers.[^V1-688]

Another modern Muslim researcher makes a similar point.

He says that the early Muslims were not occupied with “the heavens”—meaning they did not debate matters of belief—because the Qurʾān had spared them that burden by setting out the foundations of belief for them.

It did not ask them to enter into questions about the causes of existence, “that tree whose branches spread in every direction.”

The people of the Qurʾān therefore did not go beyond its boundaries. They stopped with it and remained within it.[^V1-689]

What matters to us here is that this supports the picture we described earlier.

Among the earliest Muslims, the belief that knowledge in these matters came only from God led either to a prohibition on rational debate over matters of faith or to a willingness to avoid such debate.

What had already been given completely through divine revelation and prophecy was considered sufficient.

Something else is worth noticing.

Historians and scholars of *kalām* have pointed out that even during the period when this discipline flourished, theologians disagreed about the exact role of reason.

They agreed that *kalām* used rational investigation in dealing with religious beliefs.

But they disagreed over another question.

Did *kalām* actually **prove** those beliefs through rational arguments as well as defend them?

Or was its role limited to answering objections against beliefs already established by the Qurʾān and Sunna?

These researchers explain that the disagreement came down to a deeper question:

Were religious beliefs established by revealed law—that is, by revelation—with reason merely understanding them from revelation and then finding rational arguments in their support?

Or were they established by reason itself, in the sense that the religious texts had already stated those beliefs together with their rational proofs?[^V1-690]

We mention this observation because it strongly shows that even when rational inquiry flourished in the hands of the theologians, the theologians themselves remained tied to the earlier view of knowledge.

As the observation above shows, they still accepted one of two positions.

Either religious beliefs were established by revealed law and reason understood them through that revelation.

Or they were “established by reason,” but only in the sense that the religious texts had already laid down the rational arguments for them.

Even the second position therefore assumes that the rational proofs themselves were already given in advance by religious texts.

If we look for the social and ideological basis of this position in its two forms, we find it in the need to preserve and strengthen the ideology of the new social group whose position in the developing social and class structure was supported by the idea that knowledge rested on faith.

#### 3 — Rational Inquiry in Legislation

We should avoid making an absolute claim here. An absolute way of thinking is foreign to scientific method.

We therefore need to distinguish between two different attitudes in Islam and among Muslims toward knowledge.

One concerned matters of religious belief.

The other concerned matters of law and legislation, where rational inquiry was used to some extent.

There was, in fact, a difference between the two.

Questions of religious belief were centered on receiving knowledge from divine revelation without debate and without independent rational inquiry.

But in matters of law, we find some use of **ijtihād**—reasoned judgment—which in some respects is a form of rational thought.

How did Muslims distinguish between these two areas?

The distinction arose from a belief held among Muslims from the earliest period.

Everything concerning the basic principles of faith was believed to have been completely revealed by God, leaving nothing for independent reason to decide.

The position of Islamic law was different.

Its basic principles had also been completed through revelation, but reason still had a role in working out the details of those principles and applying them to particular cases.

This use of reason is what Muslims call **ijtihād**.

It means using the mind to apply general principles to new and particular situations that continually arise in the constantly changing course of everyday life.

Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr explains the difference between the two areas as follows:

> “The early Muslims—may God have mercy on them—forbade disputation about God ... and His attributes. But as for jurisprudence, meaning the science of religious law, they agreed that debate and discussion were permissible in it, because it requires particular cases to be referred back to general principles whenever necessary. Matters of belief are not like this, because according to the community—that is, the people of the Sunna—God ... may only be described as He described Himself, or as His Messenger described Him ... and as the community agreed.”[^V1-691]

Once belief and religious law are distinguished in this way, a space opens for reason to operate within one part of Islam.

Reasoning through ijtihād in matters of law is not simply a mechanical process of applying general rules to particular cases.

The process itself requires thought.

It requires finding similarities and relevant parallels between cases when reasoning by analogy, or **qiyās**.[^V1-692]

It also requires identifying the reasons behind legal rulings found in the texts and from which general principles were formed.

Then, when a new case appears, one must investigate whether the same reason exists in that case. Only then can one decide whether the general rule should or should not be applied.

Ijtihād carried out under these conditions is therefore a genuine form of thinking.

But this form of thought remains strictly controlled by rules laid down for it from outside the process of reasoning itself.

It does not work according to rules that reason discovers independently, through its own powers of knowledge, by studying the objective movement of the world.

#### 4 — A Seed of a “Theory of Knowledge” in the Qurʾān?

There is another side to the question of knowledge in Islam that may lead us to reconsider some of our earlier conclusions.

It may even allow us to accept Ibn Ḥazm’s statement that knowledge is acquired rather than simply given.[^V1-693]

A modern Arab researcher has drawn attention to this side of the question.[^V1-694]

He points to two Qurʾānic verses:

> “God brought you out of your mothers’ wombs knowing nothing, and gave you hearing, sight, and hearts, so that you might give thanks.”
> (Qurʾān 16:78)

and:

> “Have they not traveled through the land, so that they might have hearts with which to understand, or ears with which to hear...?”
> (Qurʾān 22:46)

The researcher says that these verses, and others like them,

> “show that human beings possess faculties through which they understand things, including hearing, sight, and the heart—that is, reason.”[^V1-695]

Human knowledge therefore depends on these faculties.

In this sense, knowledge is acquired.

The Qurʾān would therefore contain the seed of a theory of knowledge that we will later see developed in detail by the philosophers.

It is true that the Qurʾān clearly gives an important role to the direct senses in gaining sensory knowledge.

It is also true that these verses appear to present such knowledge as acquired, in the sense intended by Ibn Ḥazm.

That is, people gain it through experience by using their natural powers of perception in the fields appropriate to each one.

But the context in which these verses appear determines their meaning and purpose.

That Qurʾānic context shows that sensory knowledge gained through these powers of perception is meant to provide the mind with evidence from the visible world and its great observable phenomena.

This evidence is then used to support religious faith and confirm the beliefs taught by Islam as truths received through divine revelation.

Even so, this does not prevent us from making another point.

The Qurʾān’s concern with using reason to support religious belief, drawing on knowledge gained through the senses, can itself be counted in reason’s favor.

At the very least, it recognizes the need to support faith through reason.

But the question now is this: does that observation undermine the claim that the Qur’an contains the beginnings of a theory of knowledge?

It does not seem to. The social meaning of the verses we discussed still gives knowledge gained through the senses a genuine role in the process of knowing. Sensory perception forms one stage in the chain of thought. It carries the mind forward to another stage until it reaches the conclusion being sought—which, in this case, is support for faith.

#### 5 — The Question of the “Glorification of Reason” in the Qur’an

There is another question about Islam’s attitude toward knowledge that we need to examine if we want to cover the subject fully. This is the Qur’anic phenomenon often described as the “glorification of reason.” Alongside it is what one contemporary Arab researcher calls “the Prophet’s endorsement of reason in many hadiths.”[^V1-696] This is a striking question, and it deserves attention.

The Qur’an contains many verses that praise the use of reason. People are called on to think about the universe and to reflect on the great mysteries found in the heavens and the earth. Other verses condemn those who have hearts—meaning minds—“with which they do not understand.” They are compared to cattle and described as “even further astray.”[^V1-697]

So the Qur’an did not ignore reason or deny its role as a tool of thought. The many verses of this kind show quite the opposite.

But how far does the Qur’an allow reason to go in seeking knowledge on its own?

Knowledge in Islam is confined within certain limits that reason is not allowed to cross. This means that the Qur’an’s “glorification of reason,” and the Prophet’s praise of reason in the hadiths, also has a limited scope.

This gives us reason to question the claim that rational thought could never be erased from Arab-Islamic civilization for one reason alone: because it came from the earliest sources of Islam, above all the Qur’an. According to this view:

> If rational thought had been merely a passing development, or simply one result of the interactions Arab civilization experienced through contact with other civilizations, this value could have been erased or pushed aside. But because it was organically tied to the first and sacred source of Islamic thought—the Qur’an—and because the Prophet also endorsed reason in many hadiths, rational thought, and therefore philosophical thought, became an authentic value in intellectual life. It might retreat for a time, fall behind for a period, or go through moments of decline, but it could never be uprooted or made to disappear.[^V1-698]

This argument can be questioned from several directions.

First, and most importantly, it separates two elements that both helped form “rational thought in Arab-Islamic civilization”: the original source of Islamic thought, on the one hand, and “the effects of the interactions that Arab civilization acquired through contact with other civilizations,” on the other.

A sound method requires us to see both of these as organic and formative parts of Arab-Islamic civilization itself.

Second, the argument seems to treat the influence of other civilizations as something accidental or secondary within Arab-Islamic rational thought. But, as we have said, that influence was itself an organic part of the formation and unity of this thought. It is therefore unrealistic to say that the earliest Islamic sources were the **only** reason rational thought could never be erased from this civilization.

Third, we certainly need to recognize the deep influence that the earliest Islamic sources had on the formation of this rational tradition. But if we want to understand why this “authentic value in intellectual life” could not simply be uprooted and destroyed, we need to look for the real reason in the movement of society itself: in the development of Arab society and in Islam’s objective relationship to that development.

Finally, the earliest sources of Islam themselves did not allow reason to go beyond certain limits in its independent search for knowledge. Those limits were set by the relationship Islam established between knowledge and faith.

#### 6 — Knowledge in the Course of Development

After everything we have concluded and discussed about knowledge in Islam, and especially about the relationship between faith and knowledge—the relationship that tied knowledge completely to religious belief—we now need to ask:

- Do these conclusions mean that the development of Arab thought was interrupted, or even brought to a halt, during the first period of Islam?

The way this question is phrased assumes that Arab thought had already been developing before Islam and that its development had been moving forward with history.

Was that really the case?

In fact, Arab thought **was** moving through a process of historical development during the period immediately before the rise of Islam, as we explained in detail earlier. This development included its religious and metaphysical ideas.

No old or modern Muslim thinker has denied this fact. We have already seen writers such as al-Shahrastānī, Qāḍī Ṣāʿid, Ibn Khaldūn and Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq discuss different features of pre-Islamic culture and the kind of thinking found within it. Some of the examples they mention concern the metaphysics of existence.

One statement by ʿAbd al-Rāziq is especially worth noting. He says that, when the Qur’an was revealed, the Arabs “were engaged in disputes and debates over beliefs, and questions concerning the sending of prophets, life, the afterlife, and the resurrection of bodies after death were particularly debated among the different religious groups.”[^V1-699]

So Arab thought in the pre-Islamic period was moving along the path of development that we described in the first chapter.

At that stage, however, knowledge had not yet been tied by the pre-Islamic “thinker” or “sage” to one fixed and final source in the way it was during the first period of Islam. In other words, the particular relationship between faith and knowledge that we have been discussing had not yet appeared.

That is why the question we asked above is a legitimate one. Once knowledge became tied to faith in this new way, it is understandable that someone might imagine that some kind of break or pause had taken place in the development of Arab thought.

So how should we understand the problem?

The mistake in this view is that it looks at the Islamic relationship between knowledge and faith from only one side. It takes that relationship in isolation, instead of looking at the other forces affecting knowledge during the first period of Islam, or at the broader set of developments that together formed the new course of Arab-Islamic thought.

The connection between knowledge and faith—whether we call it faith-based knowledge, knowledge-based faith, or simply the combination of the two—was not, first of all, completely disconnected from the historical form that knowledge had already taken during the pre-Islamic period.

By this I mean that connecting knowledge to a world beyond nature was not something entirely foreign to late pre-Islamic thought, especially after the spread of the Hanif movement.

Second, Islam appeared under the historical conditions we examined in the previous chapter. Those conditions placed this inherited form of knowledge within a changing social reality. That social reality was drawing together a whole range of developments that historical conditions were bringing into being and combining them within one overall process of change.

If we look at knowledge within this broader movement, its connection with faith no longer appears as a break in the development of Arab thought.

This connection did not develop separately from the wider movement of history. It was itself one of the forms produced by the historical conditions we have described.

From this point of view, we also need to notice that Arab thought in the early Islamic period was beginning to move beyond the simplicity and strongly sense-based character that had generally marked it before. It was entering a more complex and structured stage.

At this new stage, the process of knowing began, relatively speaking, to move from a framework dominated by sensory images toward one that gave a larger role to mental abstraction.

Islamic ideas about the world beyond nature, in particular, formed one part of this transition.

We can therefore say that, through its engagement with Islamic concepts, Arab thought began to make its way toward a new and relatively more advanced stage.

We will later see the pace of this development increase whenever a major change took place in the social relations of the society that had come under the rule of the Arab-Islamic state.

#### 7 — Cultural Developments

During this first Islamic period, the different forms of cultural life were largely shaped by the needs of the struggle between the Islamic movement and its opponents.

Poetry, public speaking, and popular storytelling all expressed the events of this struggle or the views of the two sides.

But as Islamic victories followed one another—first after Islam became established in Medina, then after Mecca came under its authority and the new religion spread through different parts of Arabia—the voice of poetry became quieter.

Public speaking then moved to the foreground. It became the most active, effective, and widely used literary and cultural form.

Yet the most striking cultural feature of the period was the remarkable rhetorical power of the Qur’anic style. It rose above all the other literary, artistic, and cultural forms of the time. From the literary and cultural point of view, this remains one of the clearest features of the period in which Islam appeared, quite apart from the many other ways in which the period was distinctive.

The Prophet’s hadiths also have a distinctive literary style, but their artistic and stylistic value does not reach the level of the Qur’an.

For Muslims, the reason for this difference lies in the belief that the Qur’an is divine revelation—not only in its source, religious content, and laws, but also in its artistic form and unique style, which they regard as unlike anything else in Arabic literature.

The Prophet’s hadiths, by contrast, are understood as connected to a divine source only in their religious and legal content. Their literary and artistic style is the human side of them. It comes from Muhammad himself as a human being: “Say: I am only a human being like you…” (Qur’an 18:110).

There is another way to explain the difference between the style of the Qur’an and the style of the hadiths: the two had different purposes.

The Qur’an had the more important and more difficult task, and the task that most required its extraordinary rhetorical force. It was the voice of the Islamic call and its main instrument for moving people’s emotions, conscience, understanding, and awareness.

It therefore needed an exceptional power to affect its listeners and awaken a sense of wonder in them.

The Prophet’s hadiths had a different function. They were mainly concerned with teaching and law, and with particular situations in people’s lives and their everyday behaviour. They therefore had no need for the same heightened rhetorical power. Their style could remain closer to the familiar simplicity of everyday speech.

We said that poetry became quieter during this period while public speaking took the leading role.

Why did this happen?

There were two main reasons.

The first was objective. Poetry belongs to the process of artistic creation, and artistic creation does not easily or quickly adapt itself to a major new change. To produce art that feels genuine, the artist needs inner conviction and deep emotional involvement.

This inner emotional truth is an essential part of creating great art. But an artist cannot simply manufacture or force it. If it is manufactured, it is no longer genuine.

This is why literature and art often respond to major social and historical changes only after some delay. Their own role in the two-way interaction between culture and society’s underlying structures is therefore delayed as well.

This was the position of Arabic poetry when Islam first appeared.

Poetry did not respond easily or quickly to this great new development in Arab society. In fact, at first the opposite happened. A number of poets from Quraysh rose to defend the Qurayshi leadership against the Islamic movement.

The second main reason for the decline of poetry came from Islam’s own attitude toward it.

Islam brought the Qur’an with a highly developed artistic style. Its aesthetic qualities had reached a very high level and matched the development of the Arabs’ own literary and rhetorical taste during the pre-Islamic period.

Islam wanted this striking new artistic event to become the main attraction for people’s emotions and literary tastes, so that the Qur’an’s rhetorical and aesthetic appeal would itself become a path toward religious faith.

For this purpose, Islam did not rely only on the Qur’an’s own artistic power. Nor did it rely only on presenting the Qur’an as a miraculous divine phenomenon beyond human ability.

In addition to all this, the Qur’an itself launched an attack on poetry and poets.[^V1-700]

At first, this helped spread an attitude of hostility toward poetry and poets among those responding to the Qur’anic attack.

But poetry and poets had such a strong influence over the people of pre-Islamic society that it was not easy to abolish their role or turn people away from them completely.

That was a difficult and unrealistic goal.

Poets who supported the old tribal leadership continued their counter-campaign. Eventually the Prophet and his companions had to fight poetry with poetry.

They turned to Ḥassān ibn Thābit, one of the prominent poets of the pre-Islamic period who had since become a Muslim, and asked him to answer the attacks.

He began writing poems in praise of the Prophet and satirical poems against his enemies. This is how Ḥassān became known as “the Prophet’s poet.”

But if we compare Ḥassān’s poetry from this period with the poetry he had written before Islam, there is a noticeable difference in artistic quality. His earlier poetry was more creative and showed greater artistic sincerity.

All this took place during the early years of the Islamic movement.

Later, as people became increasingly occupied with the new religion and Islam spread more widely across Arabia, this poetic battle died down. The energy of poetry itself declined with it.

Poetry began to regain its force only when conflict returned to society in new forms, beginning with the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and continuing afterward.

While poetry was relatively quiet, public speaking carried out the work of “propaganda and agitation.” Both its style and its content drew heavily on the Qur’an and on its religious, legal, and moral themes.

This gave public speaking the chance to develop greatly and continuously until the Abbasid period. By then, prose writing and the production of scientific and philosophical works had begun to overshadow it. Poetry too regained a major role, shaped by the intellectual, social, and cultural development that had taken place.

All these cultural forms, as well as the Islamic texts themselves, were transmitted mainly by word of mouth.

Writing had not been widely used in pre-Islamic society, and even during the first Islamic period its spread remained fairly limited.

Writing in Arabia did, however, have a long history.

The historical evidence known so far does not reveal written remains from the ancient Arab peoples before the kingdom of Saba in southern Arabia. Saba came after the Minaean kingdom and had its own writing system, which is described as the earliest old form of present-day Arabic writing.

Its ancient name was “cuneiform writing,” and its letters were known as the **Musnad** script. Archaeologists have found examples of this writing in Sabaean inscriptions on stone and metal, and especially on copper tablets.[^V1-701]

The point is that writing in the Arabian Peninsula was ancient. It must have passed through several stages of development before reaching the form of Arabic writing known in the late pre-Islamic and early Islamic periods.

It cannot simply have appeared suddenly in those periods already in the relatively developed form it had then.

The difference between the Arabic writing we use today and the writing of the first Islamic period, judging from the handwritten documents that have survived from that time, is not extremely large.

This suggests that writing in the Islamic period must already have had a much longer history before reaching the form we find in those documents.

In general, then, writing was rare in Arabia at the time, but it did exist.

When the Prophet and his companions migrated to Medina, seventeen Muslim men and three Muslim women knew how to write. Among them were people later known as “the scribes of revelation,” including Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, and Zayd ibn Thābit.[^V1-702]

The needs of the new Islamic community made it necessary to spread writing more widely among Muslims.

They began looking for people who already knew how to write so that they could teach others.

After the Muslim victory over Quraysh at the Battle of Badr, a number of prisoners were taken. Muhammad then issued a rule that any prisoner who taught ten people in Medina to write would be released.

This differed from pre-Islamic custom, under which money had been the only ransom for release from captivity.

Writing therefore began to spread, and with it came a certain amount of religious education.

There is also a report that the Prophet once encouraged some of his companions to learn another language in addition to Arabic.[^V1-703]

## Conclusions of Chapter Two

### 1 —

We have seen that Islam appeared in the Arabian Peninsula at the beginning of the seventh century, at a time when pre-Islamic society was going through major social changes affecting the very foundations on which that society was built.

We also saw that the rise of Islam at this stage of Arab history did not take place separately from the events that were shaking the foundations of the old tribal social order and its particular historical features.

We therefore looked for the relationship between these events—which pointed toward some kind of change in the lives of the people of Arabia—and the great new development announced by Muhammad as a divine religion revealed to him by God.

We began to find the first thread leading us toward this relationship when we examined the connection, before the rise of Islam, between Muhammad himself and the religious and intellectual current that had first appeared in one of Arabia’s agricultural regions and then spread into other settled and semi-settled areas.

We mean the movement known in pre-Islamic Arab history, and in Islamic history itself, as the religion of the **Hanifs**.

It was not by chance that Islam was described in both the Qur’an and the Prophet’s hadiths as the **Hanif religion**.
