Historians tell us that Muhammad was either one of these Hanifs or was closely connected with them. We saw this as further evidence that, when Islam appeared in Arabia, it was an objective continuation, at a new stage of development, of the Hanif movement itself.

That movement had emerged during a period when social relations in the desert, the cities, and the agricultural regions were gradually beginning to undergo new changes.

We also found that the Hanif movement reflected changes taking place in the intellectual ideas and spiritual outlook of pre-Islamic society. These changes were themselves connected to the early transformation of the tribal system and its old, relatively primitive character.

### 2 —

From this, we identified several important social and intellectual roots on which Islam was built when it appeared under those particular historical conditions.

To identify these roots more precisely, we first examined the social background from which Muhammad emerged.

Second, we looked at the class structure of the population of Mecca, where Islam first appeared.

Third, we examined the general foundations and principles on which Islam built both its religious beliefs and its laws.

This led us to the following conclusions:

1 — Islam, in its essential and practical content—and even in its religious form and its metaphysical and idealist concepts—was an objective response to the historical changes needed by pre-Islamic society.

Sometimes this response was direct, and sometimes it was less visible.

It was also a response to the sharp contradictions found in some places, such as Mecca, and the milder contradictions found elsewhere, such as among unsettled Bedouin communities.

Although these contradictions appeared in different social, spiritual, and intellectual forms, almost all of them could be traced back to the same material base.

That material base lay in the gradual breakdown of the tribal system.

The old natural, largely self-sufficient economy was weakening. Trade, money, and interest-based lending were spreading. At the same time, differences between rich and poor were becoming more visible.

On one side stood the great merchants, moneylenders, and tribal chiefs.

On the other stood small traders, craftspeople, wage workers, the destitute, people crushed by heavy interest-bearing debts, and ordinary members of the tribes.

2 — The two central principles on which Islamic belief was mainly built—monotheism and resurrection—also had social roots beneath their religious meaning.

In religious terms, monotheism means belief in one God who created the universe, and then in one religion.

But behind this idea of unity we can also see what may have been an indirect reflection of the idea of **social unity**.

Pre-Islamic tribal society was fragmented. The historical need was to bring its separate tribal units together on a new basis, even if that basis was religious.

What mattered was that the breakdown and fragmentation affecting the tribal system at the time required the different tribal groups to be brought together within the framework of one religion.

In social terms, that meant bringing them within the framework of one people.

The principle of resurrection, in its religious meaning, says that another world exists beyond our material world.

But it also carries an almost direct promise to the socially deprived and oppressed: in that other world, they will find compensation for the deprivation and injustice they suffer here, and comfort for the harsh reality of their lives.

At the same time, it threatens their oppressors with punishment in the afterlife.

Yet the forces responsible for social oppression could also benefit from a belief that justice would be postponed until the next world.

3 — Islam did not stop at principles of belief. It also introduced a system of law in which the social effects were much clearer than they were in the religious doctrines themselves.

Islamic law prohibited usury, monopoly, and the hoarding of gold and silver.

It imposed the **zakāt** tax on certain forms of wealth belonging to the rich and made its proceeds the right of particular groups among the poorest and most needy.

It also introduced rules regulating certain productive and social relationships.

Yet the basic principle of Islamic law still accepted social differentiation.

Even so, these laws came as a shock to the wealthy people of Mecca and spread alarm among them.

They looked at what an Islamic victory might do to their immediate interests. They did not yet have enough class awareness to see that, over the longer term, the general direction of development would not conflict with the development of their own class position.

For this reason, Islam, Muhammad, and the first Muslims faced violent persecution from the wealthy Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.

At the beginning of the Islamic movement, however, Islam did not win many supporters among the poor of Mecca either.

The social laws we have described did not appear until after the migration from Mecca to Medina.

For these poor people, the promise of reward and the threat of punishment on the Day of Resurrection were not enough reason to endure persecution in defence of Islam.

They needed an immediate material answer to their material problems.

4 — Islam also introduced ideas about the metaphysical nature of the universe and the world, about the place of human beings within the universe, and about human responsibility for their actions.

Yet the Qur’an appears contradictory when it comes to defining this responsibility. At some points it presents human beings as free in their actions, while at others it speaks in terms of compulsion and predestination.

### 3 —

5 — In Chapter Two, we also examined the Muslim migration from Mecca to Medina, or Yathrib, along with its causes, its decisive consequences, and the conflict between Mecca and Medina that followed it.

Throughout this conflict, the basic issue remained the same: the changes that the Islamic movement was bringing to the social forms that had dominated pre-Islamic society, especially the society of Mecca.

6 — We then examined the legislative stage of Islam, which began immediately after the migration to Medina.

We saw that the laws introduced during this stage were grounded, for the most part, in material conditions and were closely connected to the practical needs created by the migration itself.

Later, they were also shaped by the victories that the **Anṣār** and **Muhājirūn** began to win against the Qurayshi leadership in Mecca.

Eventually that leadership accepted the new reality.

Mecca came under Islam and returned to its position as a religious centre, but now in a new form and under the banner of Islam.

While discussing Islamic law in this chapter, we also pointed to an important feature of its development: the existence of a principle allowing law to change and develop.

This stands in contrast to the later belief, common among some Muslim scholars, that everything laid down by Islamic law is permanent until the Day of Resurrection and may never be changed or altered.

### 4 —

7 — In trying to define a “theory” of knowledge in Islam, we found that knowledge was ultimately traced back to a divine source: revelation from God to the Prophet.

This applied whether the knowledge concerned religious belief or law.

Knowledge therefore became tied to faith.

We based this account of the “theory” of knowledge, and of the relationship between knowledge and religious faith, on Islam’s basic sources: the Qur’an and the Sunna, meaning the sayings and actions of the Prophet.

On this basis, we found that rational debate was not accepted by the Prophet. In fact, he rejected it and called on people to avoid it, especially in questions of religious belief.

We based this conclusion on Qur’anic verses, on hadiths transmitted from the Prophet by his companions, and on the views of both early and later Muslim scholars.

In this connection, we observed that the rejection of rational debate over matters of belief created a certain break in the historical development of Arab thought.

But this was not an absolute break.

An absolute break in any process of historical development, whatever the subject, would contradict the law of development itself—and development is the only absolute law.

We therefore saw that Arab thought, during this period of its history, opened another path for itself, different from the one it had been following shortly before Islam appeared.

It found this path through the use of reasoned judgment, or *ijtihād al-raʾy*, when applying general legal rules to new situations, events, and needs in Muslim life.

This form of *ijtihād* created some room for rational thought, even if that room remained limited.

In the chapters ahead, however, we will see that the development of Arab thought did not remain confined within these narrow limits.

From the end of the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs and the beginning of the Umayyad period, it began to move along several different paths.

8 — Once we had concluded that Islam’s “theory” of knowledge ultimately traced knowledge back to a divine source, we also had to examine the Qur’anic verses and prophetic hadiths that call on people “to use reason and to praise the gift of reason.”

Here we observed that the context of these texts limits the value of reason to what it can contribute in support of religious, faith-based knowledge.

Even so, we found something positive in the attention that both the Qur’an and the Sunna give to reason, even within these limits.

They recognize that religious beliefs themselves need the support of reason.

We then traced the different sides of this question back to the fact that they reflected an objective reality that could not simply be ignored.

9 — Finally, at the end of the chapter, we discussed the other cultural developments that appeared during this stage in the history of Islam.

We noted a certain decline in Arabic poetry alongside the growth of public speaking.

We explained this partly by Islam’s struggle against poetry and its attempt to direct people’s attention toward the highly developed Qur’anic style and its artistic and aesthetic qualities, in addition to the Qur’an’s religious and legal content.

# Chapter Three

## The Era of the Rightly Guided Caliphs

*(632–661 CE)*

### A — The Social and Political Conflict Erupts

#### 1 — “Muhammad Has Died”

Muhammad ibn ʿAbd Allāh, the founder of Islam, died in Medina in 632 CE, twenty-two years after he began his mission. He spent the first thirteen of those years in Mecca and the remaining years in Medina after the Hijra. He is generally said to have been born in 570 CE, which would mean that he lived for sixty-two years.

His death came as a severe shock to Muslims in general. But for some of them, it caused something deeper. They had come to see Muhammad, as a prophet, as somehow standing above ordinary human nature. In their minds, he could not simply die as other human beings did.

For a few moments, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb seems to have reacted in this way. When he saw people mourning Muhammad, he quickly went to the pulpit of the mosque and addressed them:

> “I do not want to hear anyone say that Muhammad has died. He has only been summoned away, just as Moses son of ʿImrān was summoned away and remained absent from his people for forty nights... By God, I expect that the hands and feet of men who claim that he has died will be cut off.”[^V1-704]

Abū Bakr then arrived while ʿUmar was still speaking. He told him to be quiet, and ʿUmar stopped. Abū Bakr climbed the pulpit and said:

> “As for what follows: whoever among you worshipped Muhammad should know that Muhammad has died. But whoever worships God should know that God is living and never dies.”

He then recited the verse:

> “Muhammad is only a messenger. Other messengers passed away before him. If he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?...”[^V1-705]

ʿUmar asked, “Is this in the Book of God?”

Abū Bakr replied, “Yes.”

According to another account, ʿUmar later said:

> “By God, as soon as I heard Abū Bakr recite it, my legs gave way beneath me[^V1-706] while I was still standing. I fell to the ground and knew with certainty that the Prophet had died.”[^V1-707]

This shock occurred even though Muhammad had never misled people about his human nature. Through the Qur’an and through his own words, he had repeatedly stressed that he was a human being like other human beings.[^V1-708]

But another image had taken hold in people’s minds. Muhammad was connected with divine revelation. The Qur’an was seen as miraculous. And people believed that Muhammad himself was illiterate and could neither read nor write. Together, these ideas planted the belief that the Prophet possessed a nature higher than that of ordinary human beings. Some therefore found it difficult to accept that death could reach him just as it reached everyone else.

Abū Bakr’s firm and direct intervention settled the matter. It brought back to reality those who had surrendered to this illusion, whether because they lacked understanding or because their social position gave them an interest in presenting Islam as something above ordinary human reality.

#### 2 — The Problem of the Caliphate

As soon as the Prophet’s death was announced, the leading Companions among the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār began to struggle over political power.

The struggle started immediately, before the Prophet’s body had even been taken to its final resting place in Medina. It also divided his Companions into two groups: the Muhājirūn, the emigrants from Mecca, and the Anṣār, the people of Medina who had supported them. Each group wanted control of the caliphate after the Prophet. In other words, each wanted actual leadership of the new political authority.

This division suddenly brought back to the surface old tensions between Mecca and Medina. Those tensions had been suppressed for only a few years under the authority of the single Islamic community.

At the same time, early class-like tensions between the Anṣār and the Muhājirūn also began to appear openly. These feelings had existed before, but they had not come fully into the open during the Prophet’s lifetime.

In the first years after the Hijra, a new Islamic organization had taken shape in Medina. It resembled a kind of communal order. It stood above the tribe, and Islam as a religion provided the framework that held the whole community together.

In principle, this made it different from the older forms of primitive communal life, where tribal loyalty had been the basis of unity.

Yet even within this new Islamic organization, there was a clear difference between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār. The Muhājirūn formed its leading group. They received the larger share of war booty, and the organization was largely led by their own prominent figures, especially Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. These two men appeared to play the leading role in managing its affairs.

This created a certain disappointment among the leaders of the Anṣār, who were the original inhabitants of Medina. They had invited Muhammad and his Meccan followers to migrate to their city and had supported the Islamic cause. They had expected more from this relationship.

They carried this disappointment within them and kept it under control throughout Muhammad’s life in Medina. But as soon as the news spread that Muhammad had died, those suppressed feelings came rapidly to the surface.

At the same time, another division appeared among the Muhājirūn themselves.

Old differences from the pre-Islamic period came back to life between the Banū Hāshim, the clan of the Prophet and of his cousin and son-in-law ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, on one side, and the Banū ʿAbd Shams, Taym, Umayya, and the other Quraysh clans to which the rest of the Muhājirūn belonged, including Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, on the other.

Most of the Banū Hāshim had represented the poorer branch among the leading clans of Quraysh in pre-Islamic Mecca. It was therefore natural that, after losing the Prophet, they should think about how to preserve the position they had gained through him.

Muhammad had been the greatest expression of that position. Indeed, he had given it its highest meaning.

The Banū Hāshim could now try to preserve that position through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Muhammad’s cousin and son-in-law. ʿAlī had fought courageously at Muhammad’s side in the wars against the leaders of Mecca after the Hijra. And on the night Muhammad left Mecca for Medina, ʿAlī had slept in his bed, exposing himself to the plot that Quraysh had prepared to kill Muhammad before he could escape.

#### 3 — How the Conflict Erupted

All these factors caused the struggle to erupt immediately after the Prophet’s death.

One striking feature is that the people involved did not manage to hide the real political and social motives behind the conflict beneath a religious appearance. Muslim historians themselves describe the events quite openly. In brief, this is the picture they give us.

While ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet’s uncle, and Usāma ibn Zayd, one of the Companions, were washing and preparing the Prophet’s body for burial, then carrying it to the place near the room where he had died in the house of his wife ʿĀʾisha, a spokesman for the Anṣār called out to the Muhājirūn:

> “Give us a share in the Messenger of God in his death, just as we had a share in him during his life.”

At first, this seemed to mean only that the Anṣār wanted to take part in the burial so that they too could have the honor of participating. ʿAlī therefore immediately invited one of the Anṣār, Aws ibn Khawlī, to go down into the grave with them and help bury the Prophet and say the final farewell.

But the meaning of the word “share” soon became clearer.

While ʿAlī was inviting Aws to take part in the burial, the leaders of the Anṣār were meeting at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida. There they declared the Khazraj leader Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda to be ruler of the Muslims—that is, caliph after Muhammad.

When Abū Bakr, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and some of the other Muhājirūn heard what was happening, they hurried to the meeting place. They moved the crowd away from Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda, whom the Anṣār had proclaimed their leader, and Abū Bakr made his way to the front of the gathering.

He addressed the Anṣār:

> “People of the Anṣār! The Messenger of God is from us, so we have the stronger claim to take his place.”

The Anṣār answered:

> “One ruler from us and one ruler from you.”

Abū Bakr replied:

> “The rulers will come from us, and you will be the ministers.”

The argument between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār grew so heated that open conflict almost broke out.

According to the account, the situation was saved by one of the leaders of the Anṣār, Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ. He stepped forward and pledged allegiance to Abū Bakr as caliph. The Anṣār then accepted his decisive position.

Abū Bakr thus became the first of the four men who succeeded the Prophet and who later became known among Muslims as the “Rightly Guided Caliphs”: Abū Bakr of Banū Taym, then ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb of Banū ʿAdī, then ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān of Banū Umayya, and finally ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib of Banū Hāshim.

All four were Muhājirūn.

But the struggle was not actually settled.

The Banū Hāshim—the Prophet’s own family—had been absent from what happened at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida. When they learned what had taken place, they became angry. Some of them went to the place where the decision had been made.

One of them, ʿUtba ibn Abī Lahab, stood and recited poetry praising ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. His words amounted to putting ʿAlī forward as the only rightful candidate for the caliphate.

The historian al-Yaʿqūbī, who died in 284 AH/897 CE, says that ʿAlī sent word to ʿUtba telling him to stop[^V1-709] making this appeal.

But ʿAlī himself did not immediately pledge allegiance to Abū Bakr. A group from Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayya also held back.

It also seems that some of those who were angry about what had happened went to ʿAlī intending to pledge allegiance to him instead. He told them to return the next day with their heads shaved. But when the next day came, only three men returned.[^V1-710]

It is true that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib later cooperated with the first caliph, Abū Bakr, and with the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb. It is also true that the Anṣār accepted Abū ʿUbayda’s position because of the respect they had for him.

But the conflict itself remained beneath the surface.

At first it stayed hidden. Later it returned with great force, sometimes in bloody political conflict and sometimes in intellectual and ideological conflict.

The reasons behind it had never been resolved. Its underlying social and political content had not changed.

Historically, however, this conflict played a positive role. First, it was a necessary part of the movement of social development. Second, it became a rich source of new intellectual movements. These movements later became part of the development of Arab-Islamic thought, especially its philosophical thought.

#### 4 — The Religious Form of the Conflict

Although the struggle was driven by clear social and political interests, it eventually took a religious form. In that historical period, this was the form it naturally had to take.

The visible conflict therefore shifted. What had first appeared as a struggle between the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār over political power became a struggle between the Hāshimites and the other groups over who possessed the **religious right** to the caliphate.

This question of religious right opened another major dispute. It concerned the Islamic meaning of the caliphate itself.

Was the caliphate a right granted by God?

Was the office of caliph itself a purely divine office, like the Muslim understanding of prophethood and the prophet?

If so, then God would have to choose the caliph personally, just as he chooses a prophet. The person chosen would have special qualities that made him fit to continue the Prophet’s mission. Above all, he would have to be the best and most knowledgeable of all people.

In this understanding, the caliph would also be the **imam** of the Muslims.

God’s choice would be revealed to the Prophet, and the Prophet would then be required to announce that choice to the Muslims in clear and direct words. After the Prophet’s death, Muslims would have a religious duty to accept that choice and believe in it as part of faith itself, or as one of the foundations of belief, just as they believed in prophethood and the Prophet.

On this view, the only difference between a prophet and an imam would be revelation: revelation belongs to the prophet, but not to the imam.

Or was the caliphate simply a position of political leadership?

If so, the caliph would not be chosen by God. The choice would belong to the Muslims themselves. They would decide how the caliph should be selected, and they would decide what qualities the person holding the office should possess.

Among those who rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office, another dispute then appeared.

Did the caliph have to come specifically from Banū Hāshim within Quraysh?

Did he only have to come from Quraysh in general?

Could he come from another Arab tribe outside Quraysh?

Or could any Muslim become caliph, whether Arab or non-Arab—even, as the Khārijites later said, “an Abyssinian slave”?

The view that the caliphate was a divine right was adopted by the supporters of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. It later became one of the basic principles of Shiʿi belief.

This required them to prove that God had revealed to the Prophet that ʿAlī had been chosen as imam of the Muslims, and that the Prophet himself had clearly announced this choice.

They cite several reports in support of this position. The one on which they rely most heavily, and which has the strongest historical standing in the Islamic tradition, is the report known as the **Hadith of Ghadīr**.

The story is found in both Shiʿi and Sunni sources.

According to these accounts, the Prophet was returning from Mecca to Medina after his final pilgrimage, known as the Farewell Pilgrimage, when the following verse was revealed to him:

> “O Messenger, deliver what has been sent down to you from your Lord. If you do not, then you have not delivered His message.”
> *(Qur’an, al-Māʾida 5:67)*

The Prophet ordered his Companions to gather at a place beside a pool known as Ghadīr Khumm.

He then called ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib forward and had him stand on his right. The Prophet addressed the people and said:

> “I have been called to my Lord”—meaning that his death was near—“and I will answer that call. I am leaving this world and leaving among you two great trusts: the Book of God and my descendants, the people of my household.”

He then took ʿAlī by the hand and raised it where everyone could see.

He said:

> “People! Do I not have a greater claim over you than you have over yourselves?”

They answered:

> “Yes.”

He continued:

> “For whoever I am his *mawlā*, ʿAlī is his *mawlā*. O God, support whoever supports him, oppose whoever opposes him, give victory to whoever gives him victory, abandon whoever abandons him, and let the truth follow him wherever he goes.”

When the Prophet had finished speaking, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb congratulated ʿAlī:

> “Congratulations, ʿAlī. You have become my *mawlā* and the *mawlā* of every believing man and woman.”

The Prophet then returned to his tent and ordered another tent to be set up beside it for ʿAlī. He instructed the Muslims, men and women alike, to pledge allegiance to ʿAlī as imam and greet him as Commander of the Faithful.[^V1-711]

As we have said, the different Islamic schools agree that the report itself has a historical basis. What they disagree about is what it means.

The disagreement centers on the word *mawlā*, and on the related idea of *walāya*.

Shiʿis argue that the Prophet first used the word about himself when he said, “For whoever I am his *mawlā*.” Here, they say, the word means the person who holds religious authority over someone.

The Prophet then immediately used the same word about ʿAlī:

> “ʿAlī is his *mawlā*.”

The word must therefore carry the same meaning in both cases. On this reading, the Prophet appointed ʿAlī to exercise authority over the Muslims just as he himself had done. In other words, he appointed him their imam.

ʿAlī could not, of course, become a prophet like Muhammad, because Islam holds that Muhammad was the final prophet and that no prophet would come after him.

Other Muslim groups interpreted the word differently. They argued that *mawlā*, *walāya*, and the other forms of the same word used in the report refer only to friendship, loyalty, and affection. In their view, the report does not appoint ʿAlī to the imamate.

This was one side of the religious dispute over the caliphate.

Within the same debate, some Muslims argued that the Prophet had indirectly indicated that Abū Bakr should succeed him, rather than ʿAlī.

They pointed to the fact that during his final illness the Prophet ordered the Companions to perform the communal prayer with Abū Bakr leading them.

They argued that leading the prayer was the “minor imamate,” and that this suggested that the Prophet also intended Abū Bakr to receive the “major imamate”—general leadership over Islam and the Muslim community.

ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb used this argument when he called on people to pledge allegiance to Abū Bakr at the Saqīfa.[^V1-712]

Another report used to support Abū Bakr’s claim was transmitted from Muhammad ibn ʿUmar ibn Qatāda. According to it, the Prophet once bought a camel from a man on credit.

The man asked:

> “Messenger of God, what if I return and do not find you?”

He meant: what if the Prophet had died?

Muhammad replied:

> “Then go to Abū Bakr...”

The report continues from there.[^V1-713]

Other reports of this kind are found in greater detail in collections of hadith and biographies of the Prophet.

The other main side of the dispute rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office at all. According to this view, it belonged to the Muslims themselves to choose whoever they believed was best suited to manage their affairs.

Here a tribal problem appeared, and in some respects it may also have been a class problem.

We have already seen how both the Muhājirūn and the Anṣār claimed the right to the caliphate.

The issue had something close to a class dimension because, as we noted earlier, the Anṣār had developed something like class resentment toward the Muhājirūn. There was a clear difference between them, and the Muhājirūn had become the leading group within what we earlier called the Islamic communal order in Medina.

Other groups also entered the competition for supreme political leadership.

When Abū Bakr became caliph at the meeting of the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida, for example, Abū Sufyān ibn Ḥarb—the father of Muʿāwiya, founder of the Umayyad state—refused at first to pledge allegiance to him.

He accused the leaders of Quraysh, saying:

> “Are you satisfied, people of ʿAbd Manāf,[^V1-714] to let someone outside your own group rule over you?”[^V1-715][^V1-716]

The sources say that Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayya, despite their differences with one another, were both angry that a man from Banū Taym—Abū Bakr—had become caliph.

This produced several different views.

Was the caliphate restricted to Quraysh?

If so, did all of Quraysh have the right to it, or only Banū Hāshim?

Or did the right belong to all Muslims, Arabs and non-Arabs alike?

Throughout this conflict, the arguments took a religious form, and every side used religious evidence.

But in its substance and underlying content, the conflict was social and political, with something close to a class character.

On one side were wealthy merchants. On another were people hoping to gain wealth and expand their interests through the wars of conquest. Both could see control of the Islamic caliphate as a way of advancing the interests of their own social groups.

#### 5 — The Problem of *Shūrā*

We have said that some Muslims rejected the idea that the caliphate was a divine office.

They argued that the Prophet had left the matter to the Muslims themselves, who were to choose the person they thought best qualified to manage their common affairs.

But this immediately raised another question: how should the caliph be chosen?

Should he be appointed or elected?

Who had the right to make the appointment?

And who had the right to take part in the election?

In practice, events themselves answered these questions before any clear theory had been settled.

The meeting at the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida, which ended with Abū Bakr becoming caliph after a personal initiative by ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, became the first historical model for deciding how a caliph might be chosen.

Then Abū Bakr personally selected ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb to succeed him.[^V1-717]

ʿUmar later used a different method, which became known as *shūrā*, or consultation.

After he received the wound that eventually killed him, he was asked to appoint a successor. Instead, he chose six men from among the Companions[^V1-718] and instructed them to meet for three days after his death and select one of themselves as caliph.

He laid down the procedure in considerable detail.

Indeed, the arrangement was so carefully directed that ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, who was one of the six, seems to have expected the outcome from the moment he left ʿUmar’s meeting after the plan was announced.

He told a group of Banū Hāshim who were with him:

> “If your people have their way, none of you will ever be given power.”

Al-ʿAbbās met him and said:

> “It has been turned away from us...”[^V1-719]

That is what happened.

ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf carried out the plan that ʿUmar had drawn up before his death, and the members of the *shūrā* eventually chose ʿUthmān as the third caliph after ʿUmar.[^V1-720]

After ʿUthmān was killed during the well-known uprising against him, the process became much more spontaneous.

At that point, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib was the obvious candidate. Some people pledged allegiance to him, others fought him, and still others remained neutral, as we will see.

#### 6 — A Closer Look at *Shūrā*

A great deal has been written about the principle of *shūrā* in Islamic literature. The period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs has even been called the “age of *shūrā*.”

But what exactly does this principle mean?

Some modern Muslim scholars define *shūrā* as consultation among Muslims in choosing the caliph and in dealing with public affairs and the government of the Islamic state.[^V1-721]

Did the way the Rightly Guided Caliphs were actually chosen match this definition?

The historical picture we have just described answers the question.

It shows what actually happened, step by step, from the caliphate of Abū Bakr to that of ʿAlī.

Can we really see in these events a practical application of *shūrā* in the sense described by many modern Islamic writers?

On the basis of this historical example, the answer seems clear.

The principle of *shūrā* was not actually applied as a general rule in the government of the Islamic state. In practice, the system took other forms that did not match the meaning that Muslim scholars later gave to the term—even during the reign of ʿUmar, which is often regarded as the golden age of the Rightly Guided Caliphate.

That is the general picture when we look at how *shūrā* worked in practice.

Now let us look at its legal status.

The primary Islamic texts—the Qur’an and the Sunna—do not contain any clear statement making *shūrā* a binding principle of law. In other words, it is not explicitly presented as part of Islamic law in the same way as other rules that Muslims are required to follow.

The clearest Qur’anic text on the subject says:

> “Their affairs are conducted through consultation among themselves.”[^V1-722]

But the verse does not present consultation as a legal rule. It appears as part of a description of the moral qualities and conduct of believers.

Nor does the verse say that it applies specifically to government.

If it did clearly lay down a system of political rule, it would be difficult to explain why the Rightly Guided Caliphs were chosen in the ways we have just described.

Some of those choices were shaped by family, tribal, and group interests, if not by interests with something close to a class character.

Others were shaped by personal positions.

Still others involved a kind of *shūrā* from above, in which the people allowed to take part were limited to a small number of individuals.

And it was already known that these men were unlikely to agree on the person most qualified to become caliph. They had political conflicts among themselves. Each had his own ambition for the office. And most of them had already agreed, in practice, to keep ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib away from leadership of the caliphal state.

The principle of *shūrā* that can be drawn from the Qur’anic verse is therefore broad and unrestricted. It is not defined in enough detail to serve as a binding legal rule that determines the specific form of government in Islam.

Muslim scholars themselves acknowledge that Islam did not specify a particular method for carrying out *shūrā*.[^V1-723]

It can still be said, however, that the general spirit of Islamic law rules out the hereditary system that Muʿāwiya later adopted.

One piece of evidence is a saying attributed to the Prophet in which he rejects a system he calls *mulkan ʿaḍūḍan*—literally, a kingship that “bites” or clings tightly.

The expression is figurative. It can mean a ruler who grips power tightly and keeps its privileges for himself and his heirs. It can also mean a ruler who forces his rule upon the community and holds it there by force. This is how one modern scholar explains the phrase.[^V1-724]

But even this prophetic saying is not enough to give the principle of *shūrā* a clearly defined legal status.

The only other possible basis would be actual practice: the conduct of the Prophet and of the Rightly Guided Caliphs.

The Prophet often consulted his Companions on matters for which no revealed text had given a direct ruling.

Before deciding to fight the Battle of Badr in 624 CE, for example, he consulted them at length until he received their agreement.

Similar examples can be found in the conduct of all the Rightly Guided Caliphs except ʿUthmān.

But these examples generally concern legal, administrative, or military matters. They do not establish *shūrā* as a binding principle covering the entire system of government.

We can therefore conclude that Islam does not prescribe one particular form of government that Muslims must follow and no other.

In the end, *shūrā* is best understood as a recommended principle. Islam encourages Muslims to use it when the public interest requires it.

In other words, the public interest is what should ultimately guide the choice of a system of government.

### B — The Ridda Wars

#### 1 — Islamic Policy in the Arabian Peninsula

During the first years after the Hijra, much of Islamic law and policy was directed toward the immediate tasks facing the new movement.

The first goal was to bring all the regions of the Arabian Peninsula under one authority and unite them within a system that went beyond the tribal order, which had already exhausted its historical role.

Islam aimed to establish a social order at a higher stage of human development and to turn Mecca and the Kaʿba into an Islamic center that would attract the Arabs of the entire peninsula.

When the Prophet died, this policy had not yet fully achieved its aims.

The people of Mecca and Medina were by then fully under Islamic authority, as were some of the tribes living nearby.

But the population of other parts of the peninsula—especially Yemen, Ḥaḍramawt, and Oman in the south—had not yet submitted completely to the Islamic movement.

The Ridda Wars revealed this historical reality, despite the way Arab historians of the ninth and tenth centuries later described the situation.[^V1-725]

It is true that during the “Year of Delegations,” after the Muslims had defeated the leaders of Quraysh and returned to Mecca as conquerors, delegations came to the Prophet from different parts of the peninsula. They announced either their acceptance of Islam or their submission to the authority of the new religion.

But this appearance did not tell the whole story.

Even tribes such as Asad and Ghaṭafān, which lived near Medina—the Islamic capital after the Hijra and the first center of Muslim power—took advantage of the revolt in other regions and joined it themselves.

They were also encouraged by the military situation at the time, because the main core of the Islamic army was outside the peninsula fighting the Romans.

The revolt stretched from Bahrain and Oman along the coast of the Arabian Gulf in the east and southeast, then through Ḥaḍramawt and Yemen in the south, and from there to al-Yamāma.

It therefore formed something close to a semicircle around a large part of the Arabian Peninsula.

These conflicts became known as the “Ridda Wars,” or wars of apostasy.

But the word *ridda* covered more than one kind of break with Islamic authority.

Some tribes were refusing obedience to the new tax system, especially the payment of zakāt.

Other tribes, particularly in al-Yamāma, rejected Islam itself.

Taken as a whole, these wars could be described in modern language as wars of **counterrevolution**.

Their main social character was reactionary because, in their general direction, they stood against the progressive side of the Islamic movement.

#### 2 — The Social Causes of the Ridda Wars

The Ridda Wars represented the social side of the reaction that immediately followed the Prophet’s death.

It would therefore be wrong to explain them simply as a religious return from Islam. That would be a one-sided and idealist explanation.

Social factors also lay behind the movement.

We have already discussed the growing differences in wealth inside the tribes.

At one end were poor tribespeople who owned almost nothing—not even livestock in many Bedouin areas.

At the other end were tribal chiefs.

Besides holding money earned through services provided to trading caravans, these chiefs possessed expensive household goods associated with a more settled way of life: carpets, vessels, fine wool and silk fabrics, and jewelry.

They also owned large herds of animals, controlled the grazing lands used by them, and kept the benefits for themselves.

Meanwhile, poverty among ordinary tribespeople became so severe that a completely destitute group known as the *ṣuʿlūk* emerged.

These people were forced to wander through the desert away from the settlements of their own tribes. Some survived by attacking roads, caravans, and travelers.

Poor groups like these looked toward Islam when it first appeared.

The new movement condemned monopoly, usury, and social injustice. To the poor, it seemed to offer hope that their situation might change for the better.

Tribal chiefs reacted differently.

They approached Islam with hesitation and anxiety because they wanted to protect their privileges and interests.

Their concern grew when they understood that Islam aimed to break through the closed structure of tribal unity and replace it with a broader community.

Inside this larger community, the chiefs would lose their absolute authority over their tribes. They would now have to submit to a higher power that came from outside the narrow world of the tribe itself.

For this reason, many tribes delayed submitting to Islam until the movement had become the victorious political power after the conquest of Mecca.

The delegations that traveled to Mecca in the “Year of Delegations” to announce submission, obedience, and acceptance of Islam therefore seem to have been responding mainly to the new balance of power.

They were accepting a reality they could no longer avoid, or they feared that the growing power of Islam would sweep over them if they continued to resist.

In general, this means that the Islam of these tribes—or, more precisely, the Islam of their chiefs—had weak foundations from the beginning.

In some cases, submission was simply a way of dealing with the stronger power and avoiding conflict with it.

In others, the chiefs were attracted by the booty Muslims gained in war and distributed among the fighters.

All this applies mainly to the Bedouin tribes.

But there was another group in the peninsula whose position was different: the settled populations of Yemen and al-Yamāma.

These people lived under stable agricultural conditions.

For that reason, they were more strongly attached to their traditions, their settled way of life, and their own religious beliefs. Their outlook was more firmly connected with the conditions in which they lived.

They were therefore more resistant to change and less attracted to new ways of life.

There was another difference as well.

Unlike Bedouin tribes, they did not have the same powerful incentive to seek war booty. Doing so would have required them to leave their settled life, migrate, and take part in military campaigns.

A third factor was the presence of people claiming prophethood in these settled regions: Bahrain, Ḥaḍramawt, Oman, and al-Yamāma.

These were local figures who claimed to be prophets.

One was Musaylima in al-Yamāma, known in Islamic tradition as “Musaylima the Liar.”

Another was a woman from the Banū Taghlib tribe named Sajāḥ, who also claimed to be a prophet. Both played a part in the Ridda Wars.

Musaylima had considerable personal influence in al-Yamāma.

Before the rise of Islam, he seems to have represented the Ḥanīf religion in that region, and there appears to have been some contact between him and Muhammad before Muhammad publicly began the Islamic mission.

Musaylima succeeded in bringing a large part of the population of al-Yamāma under his influence.

During the Ridda Wars he led what, in his own region, amounted to a counterrevolution against Islam. Muslims therefore called him “Musaylima the Liar” because of his claim to prophethood.

Muslim historians say that he tried to imitate the Qur’an by producing rhymed speech in something like the Qur’anic style.

But it is not certain that the words they attribute to him are really his.

The texts preserved by these historians often sound so much like nonsense that serious historical research has good reason to doubt that they came from a prominent Arab leader of that period.

Musaylima had enough standing among his people to organize a powerful resistance to Islam that continued into the reign of Abū Bakr. He even defeated the caliph’s armies twice.

The resistance was finally crushed only after Abū Bakr sent a large army under Khālid ibn al-Walīd.

Khālid defeated the movement and killed Musaylima, but his army lost many fighters from both the Anṣār and the Muhājirūn in the process.

After this, the people of al-Yamāma were brought under Islamic authority.

Yemen came under Islamic rule during the Ridda Wars under different circumstances.

At the time, its people were heavily occupied with resisting Persian rule.

The local leader of this resistance, another man who claimed prophethood, was killed at night in his room by his wife. She was the daughter of the Persian governor, whom he had killed before forcing her to marry him.

These conditions made it easier for the Islamic army to defeat those in Yemen who had rebelled against Islam.

Afterward, Yemen came under Islamic authority without further resistance.

The Ridda movement continued to occupy much of the attention of the first two caliphs, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

But the second caliph, ʿUmar, used skillful political methods to bring it to a final end.

He negotiated peacefully with the chiefs of rebellious tribes and used force only when negotiation failed.

In practice, the areas that resisted most strongly were the agricultural regions.

This is why Banū Ḥanīfa in al-Yamāma, the region of Musaylima, were the last to submit to the caliph’s authority by force.

Defeating this storm of rebellion became one of the decisive developments that allowed the Arabs to move beyond the Arabian Peninsula.

They were now able to begin a huge historical process.

Its result was not only the creation of a state and then a vast empire.

One of its greatest consequences, made possible by the rise of that state and empire, was the birth of a civilization that became a major force in social, political, and cultural history.

This historical process is what we call the **Arab-Islamic conquests**.

### C — The Arab-Islamic Wars of Conquest

#### 1 — The Beginning of the Conquests

When the Prophet died, Islam as a political system had not yet moved beyond the borders of the Arabian Peninsula.

As a religious message and belief, however, it had already reached some neighboring countries.

The Prophet had sent several delegations to kings and rulers, especially the kings of Persia and Abyssinia, inviting them to accept Islam.

These missions were peaceful. They presented the basic beliefs of Islam and some of its general social principles.

None of the rulers accepted the invitation. The king of Abyssinia was the only one who received the Arab Prophet’s delegation with warmth and friendship.

But the Prophet was already preparing the way for Islam to move beyond its Arabian setting and enter the wider world.

In the autumn of 629 CE, he sent a military expedition to Syria that became known as the expedition of Muʾta.[^V1-726]

It was led by Zayd ibn Ḥāritha[^V1-727] and consisted of three thousand fighters.[^V1-728]

This was intended as the first military encounter between the Islamic army and the Roman forces that then controlled Syria.

But the expedition withdrew and returned to Medina under the command of Khālid ibn al-Walīd after its commanders were killed one after another: Zayd ibn Ḥāritha, Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib—known as Jaʿfar al-Ṭayyār—and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa.

The Muslim force was simply not strong enough to face an army that was incomparably superior in both numbers and equipment.

This happened before the conquest of Mecca.

After that conquest ended in a historic victory, followed by victory at Ḥunayn and the defeat of al-Ṭāʾif, the Prophet returned to the idea of confronting the Romans in Syria.

Preparations began again.

Then came the expedition of Tabūk in the ninth year after the Hijra, 630 CE.

This time the Prophet himself led the Muslim army.

It was the height of summer, and the heat was severe. The Islamic army also lacked enough money to support a long war against the Roman forces.

The expedition returned from Tabūk without fighting the Byzantines.

Even so, it achieved two important things.

First, it gave the Muslims useful experience and helped prepare them psychologically for the wars of conquest that would follow.

Second, during the expedition the Prophet made peace agreements with the inhabitants of some of the oases along the road to Syria. This made the route safer for future Muslim armies.[^V1-729]

A third attempt to prepare for expansion took place during the Prophet’s lifetime.

The Prophet gave Usāma ibn Zayd ibn Ḥāritha command of a military unit that was also to march toward Syria.

But the force had barely assembled outside Medina to prepare for departure when the Prophet became ill with the sickness that caused his death.

When news of his death spread, the Companions hesitated.

Should the expedition continue as the Prophet had ordered, or should it be delayed?

The first Rightly Guided Caliph, Abū Bakr, decided that it should continue in order to carry out the Prophet’s wishes.

In practice, the expedition rode among the tribes of Quḍāʿa, attacked Balal on the approaches to Syria in the land of Jordan, took some booty, and returned safely to Medina after being away for forty days.[^V1-730]

It is therefore accurate to say that Islam did not move beyond the Arabian Peninsula during the Prophet’s lifetime.

But these three attempts prepared the way.

The time had now come for the movement of conquest to begin.

Two events delayed it for a while: the Prophet’s death and the outbreak of the Ridda Wars.

The Arab-Islamic conquests beyond the peninsula began decisively during the reign of the second Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

In the autumn of 633 CE, shortly before ʿUmar became caliph, the armies of conquest had already begun moving through the Syrian desert toward Syria and Palestine.

They were organized into three divisions, each containing 7,500 fighters.

In the first year of ʿUmar’s caliphate, 634 CE, the first truly decisive battle in Arab history took place: the Battle of al-Qādisiyya.

It was fought west of the city of Najaf, around eighteen miles west of Kufa, in the region where the Arab state of al-Ḥīra had once stood.

Al-Ḥīra had been one of the centers of Persian control over Mesopotamia, or Iraq. Its rulers were the Arab Lakhmids, known as al-Manādhira, who were subjects of the Persian Empire.

The Arab victory at al-Qādisiyya opened the way to the conquest of all Iraq and the final removal of Persian rule from Mesopotamia.

Between 635 and 638, the conquest of Syria and Iraq was completed.

The victories of the Arab armies continued.

By the end of the ten years in which ʿUmar held the caliphate, Syria, Egypt, Palestine, Iraq, and a large part of Persia had come under Arab-Islamic rule.

By the 650s, the conquests had reached parts of North Africa and the island of Cyprus.

This marked the end of the first of the two main stages of Arab expansion.

The second stage stretched from the late seventh century into the early eighth century.

By then, the Arab state had gained control over vast territories in Asia, Africa, and Europe, after a movement of conquest that had continued for more than seventy years.

#### 2 — Western Explanations for the Conquests

At this point, we should look at some of the explanations given by European scholars in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries for the Arab-Islamic conquests and for the remarkable victories they achieved.

One explanation claimed that Islamic religious fanaticism drove the Arabs of the peninsula to wage wars against non-Muslim countries.

Another said that Arabia contained too many people and too little food, so conquest was a way of solving this imbalance.

In the twentieth century, some Orientalists argued that drought had left the Arabian desert short of water and grazing land. The people therefore lacked enough food, and their animals lacked enough pasture. According to this view, they left Arabia in search of a better life in more fertile countries.[^V1-731]

The explanation based on religious fanaticism can be rejected for a simple reason.

For large numbers of the soldiers in the Arab-Islamic armies, Islam had not yet taken such deep root in their minds that they would willingly risk their lives for the sole purpose of forcing the Islamic faith on the people of the countries they conquered and abolishing the religions those people already followed.

If that had really been the purpose, the conquerors would have accepted nothing from the defeated populations except conversion to Islam.

But the historical record clearly shows otherwise.

The Arab conquerors allowed the people of the conquered lands to keep their religions and beliefs in return for paying the *jizya* tax.

They were also allowed to continue practicing their religious rituals.

Indeed, religious freedom was included among the protections granted to them, and Christian clergy in particular were often treated well.

The reality is that tribal loyalties were still more deeply rooted than Islamic ideas, beliefs, and principles among many of the soldiers taking part in the conquests.

Many of them also knew very little about those ideas and principles.

How, then, can anyone reasonably explain the wars of conquest mainly through religious fanaticism while ignoring the material conditions behind them?

Two of those material conditions were already recognized in the explanations mentioned above: the imbalance between a growing population and limited food supplies, and the harsh climate of Arabia, which encouraged people to seek better living conditions in fertile lands beyond the peninsula.

But there was another historical factor that made these pressures much more powerful.

Trade inside Arabia had been developing.

Between the sixth and seventh centuries CE, a class of wealthy Arab merchants had begun to grow rapidly.

Their rise contained the beginnings of a new society built around commercial social relations.

This group was the earliest class form of that new society.

By the time Islam appeared, the group was growing so quickly that the internal limits of the Arabian Peninsula were becoming too narrow for its development.

Expansion beyond Arabia was therefore becoming a necessity.

Islam, as a universal movement, helped awaken and strengthen these ambitions for expansion.

In this sense, it appeared as an objective response to that historical need.

#### 3 — Why the Conquests Succeeded

We now face a major question.

How were the Arabs able to win such great victories against the huge regular armies of the two most powerful and highly developed states of the seventh century, Persia and Byzantium?

The Arabs were leaving their peninsula for the first time as conquering soldiers.

Their own society had also not reached the same level of development as some of the peoples whose lands they were now conquering and bringing under Arab-Islamic rule.

This question was asked long ago.

And the answer has also existed for a long time in the form of historical facts that point directly toward the real explanation.

These facts give us an almost complete picture of the economic, social, and political conditions facing the two great empires on one side, and the peoples confronted by the Arab conquerors on the other.

They also help us separate two sides of the explanation.

First, there were **objective conditions**—conditions independent of what the Arabs themselves wanted or intended.

Second, there were **subjective factors** on the Arab side: the qualities and motivations that allowed them to take advantage of those conditions.

What were these objective historical conditions?

And what were the subjective strengths of the Arabs?

Let us begin with the first question.

When the Arab-Islamic conquests began, Byzantium and Persia had already been badly weakened by long wars against one another in regions lying around or near the Arabian Peninsula.

These regions included Mesopotamia, or Iraq, and Persia on one side, and Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Turkey, and North Africa, which were then under Byzantine control, on the other.

The long wars had weakened both empires.

In addition, the Byzantine state and the church connected with it were carrying out a form of religious persecution in Egypt, Syria, and Palestine.

At the time, the Byzantine emperor Heraclius was in Syria and was imposing extremely heavy taxes on the population.

Bitterness against these conditions had spread widely, and people could see no clear way out.

Feudal exploitation of those who produced society’s wealth became mixed with religious persecution.

The Syrian clergy faced pressure from the Byzantine Church, which had made Syria one of its major centers.

This produced opposition among Syrian churchmen to foreign Byzantine rule.

Different local Christian sects and communities gathered around this opposition.

The movement therefore had a social content expressed through a religious form.

Peasants and craftsmen were drawn to it, and it gradually took on a class character as well.

Economic, social, political, and religious conditions like these made war much harder for a regular imperial army.

That army now had to face an advancing force of irregular conquerors without being able to rely on support from the local population.

Quite the opposite.

It was surrounded by a hostile population.

This created conditions for an internal psychological war among its own soldiers against the state whose oppressive rule they were being asked to defend.

We can therefore make three comparisons.

First, compare the morale of an attacking army with the morale of an army forced onto the defensive.

Second, compare forces carrying the energy of something new and growing with forces carrying the decline of something old and dying.

Third, compare fighters driven by powerful hopes of reaching a richer life with soldiers who have been forced into service while suppressing their own resentment against the state they are defending.

Ibn Khaldūn tried to explain why Muslim armies, despite their small numbers and limited equipment, defeated “the armies of Persia at al-Qādisiyya and the armies of Heraclius at al-Yarmūk,” even though those opposing forces were incomparably larger and better equipped.

In substance, his explanation is not very far from the three comparisons we have just made, even though the historical form in which he understood the issue was naturally different.[^V1-732]

We should add another factor.

Because they lived nearby, the people of Syria and Mesopotamia must have heard something about Islam’s call to reduce the material suffering of the poor, the destitute, and the oppressed.

The peoples of these regions must also have hoped for some movement that could free them from the unbearable conditions under which they were living.

This became visible during the Arab conquest of Syria.

Popular resentment there had already developed into political and social opposition to Byzantine rule.

That opposition had a clearly religious form.

Local Christian sects had emerged among the native population and united in opposition to the Byzantine Church, which expressed the ideology of the occupying political power in religious language.

Peasants and craftsmen supported these religious groups because of their own anger toward Byzantine rule.

Through that opposition, they also resisted, in a largely spontaneous way, the feudal ideology represented religiously by the Byzantine Church.

One fact makes this especially clear.

Under Byzantine rule in Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, local Christian clergy were prevented from holding the highest church offices.

Those positions were reserved for Greek clergy.

#### 4 — Arab-Islamic Rule in the Conquered Lands

We must also remember that when the Arabs left the peninsula as conquerors, their own society had not yet fully developed into the kind of class society that already existed in the conquered lands.

In those countries, production was already organized mainly through feudal relations of an eastern type.

This created a wide gap between the economic and social structure of the conquered societies and the political and administrative system of their new Arab rulers.

The Arab conquerors had never before governed societies with this kind of social and economic structure.

In other words, early Islamic Arab rule did not naturally arise from the economic and social conditions already present in those countries.

This raises an obvious question.

How, then, did the Arab conquerors actually govern the peoples they had defeated?

During the period of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, and especially under ʿUmar, their policy took the following form.

First, the conquerors took the booty captured from defeated enemy armies on the battlefield.

Under Islamic rules of war, this booty was divided between the fighters and the *Bayt al-Māl*, the public treasury.

Four-fifths went to the fighters, while the remaining fifth went to the treasury.

The fighters’ four-fifths were then divided among them according to a system of ranks that combined tribal status with something like class status.[^V1-733]

Second, non-Muslims—Christians, Jews, and Ṣābiʾans, the groups known as the People of the Book—were required to pay the *jizya* tax.

Those who paid this tax were known as **ahl al-dhimma**, the protected people.

The term meant that once the war of conquest had ended, or once an agreement had been made with the local population and they had accepted payment of the *jizya*, Christians and Jews in these countries came under Arab protection.

This protection covered their lives, their private property, their personal and religious freedoms, and their right to continue practicing the rituals and customs they had followed before the Arab conquest.

This gives us another reason to reject the theory mentioned earlier that religious fanaticism was the main cause of the Arab conquests.

It also shows that spreading Islam was not an independent goal cut off from the social aims we have just discussed.

We will later see that some Arab rulers in the conquered countries actually discouraged local people from becoming Muslims when they realized that conversion reduced the amount of *jizya* entering the public treasury.

Muslims, and people who converted to Islam from other religions, did not have to pay this tax.[^V1-734]

Third, the *jizya* brought enormous sums of money to the Arab conquerors.

It was said that under ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, Egypt alone sent around fourteen million gold dinars to the caliphal treasury, while Iraq sent one hundred million silver dirhams.

In the early period of conquest, Byzantine gold currency remained in use in the lands that had previously been under Byzantine rule, while Persian silver currency continued to be used in Iraq and the Persian provinces.[^V1-735]

Fourth, when one of the protected non-Muslims converted to Islam, the *jizya* was removed.

Instead, the convert became subject to the Muslim obligation of *zakāt*, which was lower in both amount and rate than the *jizya*.

If a non-Muslim peasant converted to Islam and then left the countryside for the city, he had to pay *zakāt*.[^V1-736]

If he remained in the countryside and continued farming, he instead paid the *kharāj*, a land tax taken from agricultural production at a rate of one-tenth.

Most of the population in the conquered countries were peasants, because agriculture was the main form of production.

For that reason, revenue from the *kharāj* formed a large part of the income of the *Bayt al-Māl*.

Fifth, the conversion of these populations from Christianity and other religions to Islam proceeded slowly during the early period of the conquests. The Muslim Arab conquerors did not make a deliberate effort to spread Islam through direct missionary activity.

One reason was financial. The *jizya*, the tax paid by non-Muslims, brought large sums into the state treasury. This helped weaken any incentive to encourage widespread conversion in the conquered lands.

The historical sources even mention measures intended to limit the number of local people converting to Islam. As increasing numbers of the protected non-Muslim population entered Islam, revenue from the *jizya* began to fall.

Al-Balādhurī, for example, reports[^V1-737] that officials serving al-Ḥajjāj, the Umayyad governor of Iraq, wrote to complain about this very problem:

> “The land-tax revenue has fallen, and the protected non-Muslims have converted to Islam and moved to the cities.”

They meant that these people had converted, left agricultural work in the countryside, and moved into the towns. As a result, the state lost revenue from both the land tax, or *kharāj*, and the *jizya*.

What matters here is that large numbers of people entering Islam became a cause for complaint. That complaint tells us something important: the state’s financial income came first, while the conversion of the population came second.

Sixth, the term “protected peoples” originally referred specifically to Christians and Jews, whom the Qurʾān calls the “People of the Book”—that is, the followers of the Torah and the Gospel, or more generally the followers of earlier revealed religions recognized by Islam.

Later, however, the Arab conquerors broadened this category in their treatment of local populations. Some caliphs extended it to include the Sabians and Zoroastrians as well. This was done through legal interpretation, and the purpose was to increase the number of people liable to pay the *jizya* and therefore increase the revenue it produced.

We can therefore say that the Arab conquerors’ lack of interest in rapidly expanding the Muslim population of the conquered lands had a material basis. The same material basis can also help explain the religious tolerance that marked Arab rule in this period.

Seventh, from the beginning of the conquests, the Arabs established special military settlements for their armies. These were known as *amṣār*, with each individual settlement called a *miṣr*.

These settlements later became major centers of intellectual, economic, and political life in the Arab state. Among them were Basra and Kufa in Iraq, both founded during the rule of the second caliph, ʿUmar; Fusṭāṭ in Egypt, today Cairo, also founded during ʿUmar’s rule; and Kairouan in Tunisia, founded during the rule of Muʿāwiya, the founder of the Umayyad state.

The first striking feature of these towns is that they were laid out along tribal lines. Each was divided into quarters, and each tribe was assigned its own quarter, which then took the tribe’s name.

The second striking feature is that many of the wealthy merchants of Mecca—men who had already been rich before Islam and had become highly skilled in trade and profit-making—moved to Kufa and Basra. They brought their commercial activity and capital with them.

Many craftsmen followed them to work for these wealthy groups. As a result, a clear class structure began to emerge in the new towns. Agricultural labor, meanwhile, was increasingly carried out by enslaved captives and poor free workers.

The third feature was the separation of the military commanders, wealthy merchants, and other leading figures from the local population. They lived apart in these towns, which became something like isolated strongholds: military strongholds and class strongholds at the same time.

Eighth, the Arab conquerors did not follow the usual practice of conquerors in that period by looting the cities they captured.

They generally limited themselves to taking the property of wealthy people and leading notables who fled when the conquerors entered. This property included money, movable goods, slaves, and palaces.

Land itself was not taken in this way until the reign of ʿUthmān, the third caliph. Under him, Umayyad governors from among his relatives began building up large and wealthy estates at the expense of the state treasury, poor Arabs, and the poor of the conquered lands.

#### 5 — Important Conclusions

What can we conclude when we bring these eight observations together?

In our view, they point to something extremely important.

They show that religion was not the decisive force behind the Arab conquests. If we look again at each of these observations, and then consider them together, we can see that social forces played a major and often decisive role in driving the Arabs out of the Arabian Peninsula and into a much larger world filled with economic activity, social life, and diversity.

This does not mean denying the historical role of Islam as one of the forces behind the conquests. That role was especially important for those who took part sincerely because of their commitment to Islam and their religious faith.

But our concern here is not the personal intention of individual believers. We are looking instead for the objective force that drew people from many different tribes of the Arabian Peninsula into campaigns that were close to an adventure—if not outright adventure.

When we analyze the historical facts we have discussed, it is difficult to believe that religion alone could have driven such large numbers of people so powerfully into battle and danger against the two strongest states in the civilized world at the time.

Alongside this first conclusion, we can draw several others from the same eight observations:

1. The Byzantine and Persian authorities had practiced various forms of social, religious, and sectarian persecution. When the Arab conquerors entered these lands, they presented the local population with principles and slogans that many people saw as offering hope for better living conditions.

2. The Arab conquerors raised the principle that there should be no war against those willing to make peace. They also raised the principle that there should be no compulsion in religion.

   When they entered a country, its inhabitants were to receive security and protection for their lives, property, personal freedom, and religious freedom. War booty was taken only from lands whose rulers rejected peace and chose war.

3. The booty was limited to what was found with the rear units of enemy armies, and to the wealth and palaces of rich people and nobles who fled the cities.

   Even in lands taken by force rather than through a peace agreement, the Arabs did not loot the cities or seize the property of ordinary inhabitants. The exception was the property of the wealthy and noble groups just mentioned.

4. The Arab conquerors allowed local Christian clergy to hold the highest religious offices in their own communities, replacing Greek clergy whom the Byzantine Church had imposed on religious institutions in Syria, Palestine, and Egypt.

   This won the support of the local clergy. Some of them even became advocates of Arab rule in these countries.

5. In the land tax, or *kharāj*, the conquerors treated Arabs working in agriculture in the same way as non-Arabs.

   This helped them win the support of this part of the population.

6. Local merchants made large profits from the conquerors because the Arabs often sold them captured goods at very low prices, even when the goods were extremely valuable.

   The Arabs arriving from the peninsula often did not know the true value of these objects. Local merchants therefore had a strong interest in maintaining good relations with the conquerors.

7. At the time Islam appeared, Arab society was approaching the stage of a class society, but it had not yet reached the more developed class structure already found in the conquered lands.

   For this reason, the Arabs left the existing feudal institutions of power largely in place. At first, they neither seized those institutions nor took a direct part in running them.

   Nor did the conquerors immediately enter the process of social production. They remained largely separate from it. For a time, this also kept them separate from the wider social life of the conquered countries.

   They continued to live in their military settlements—the new towns established after the conquests—and in doing so preserved many of their dominant tribal traditions. They were also afraid that the Arab element might be absorbed into the much larger non-Arab populations around them.

   The feudal ruling groups in these countries therefore kept their positions and class privileges. As a result, these landholding elites had little reason to create trouble or organize counter-revolts against the Arab conquerors.

8. During the conquests, another slogan appeared: the Arabs were the army of Islam.

   Under this principle, among the original inhabitants of the conquered lands, only Arabs were allowed to join the Arab armies operating there.

   This made it possible for Arab tribes that had been living in Iraq and Syria long before the conquests to join those armies. These included tribes that had once belonged to the Lakhmid state in Iraq and the Ghassanid state in Syria. Most had been Christian. Some later converted to Islam, while others remained Christian.

   In this way, the conquerors also secured the support of Arab tribes already living in the conquered lands. Their support may have come from ethnic or tribal solidarity, or from material interests, since joining the conquerors allowed them to preserve full equality with the victorious Arabs.

Taken as a whole, this picture gives the researcher a clearer view of many important historical facts—social, political, and intellectual.

But we should remember that these observations apply only to a limited period in the history of Arab rule over the conquered lands. We can probably say that the picture began to change during the reign of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān. We will see this shortly.[^V1-738]

One final point should be added.

Following Qurʾānic guidance and ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb’s rules for the conduct of conquest, the Arab conquerors adopted a principle that deserves attention in both their overall strategy and their conduct in particular situations.

They were not to begin an armed conflict, and were to use force only in three cases:[^V1-739]

The first was self-defense against an enemy:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. God does not love those who transgress.”

—Sūrat al-Baqara, 2:190.

The second was to protect the weak and save them from oppression or destruction:

> “Why should you not fight in the way of God and for the oppressed among men, women, and children, who say: ‘Our Lord, take us out of this town whose people are oppressors, and appoint for us from Yourself a protector, and appoint for us from Yourself a helper’?”

—Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, 4:75.

The third was when the opposing side itself resorted to arms—that is, when the other side began the fighting:

> “Fight them until there is no persecution and religion belongs to God. But if they stop, then there is to be no aggression except against the wrongdoers.”

—Sūrat al-Baqara, 2:193.

And:

> “If they incline toward peace, then incline toward it as well, and put your trust in God.”

—Sūrat al-Anfāl, 8:61.

#### 6 — The System of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb

Most of the system we have just described for the early Islamic conquests goes back to the second Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.

Drawing on the general principles of Islamic law, together with his own bold legal reasoning, ʿUmar developed a practical policy for three areas: the armies carrying out the conquests, the tribes to which the soldiers belonged, and the conquered lands themselves.

Some parts of this system were positive, while others were negative.

Among its positive features was something that, to a certain extent, can be described using Engels’s term “military democracy.”

In principle, the relationship between the commanders of the conquering armies and their soldiers rested on a fairly broad form of this democracy. In practice, however, it remained limited because tribal traditions were still powerful.

We saw this especially in the distribution of booty. The stated rules could be violated when tribal chiefs took the shares belonging to ordinary soldiers from their own tribes.

Another positive feature of ʿUmar’s system was his establishment of some of the foundations of a “state” in the legal and administrative sense.

ʿUmar created the first *dīwān* in Islam. It was a form of government administration, rather like a ministry.

Its original purpose was to record the names of those entitled to receive shares of the conquest booty and charitable funds, and to classify them according to the kind and rank of their entitlement.

The order of distribution was as follows: first the Prophet’s wives; then the Prophet’s Companions, beginning with the early emigrants; then the *Anṣār*; and finally the tribes that had taken part in the conquests and were living in the conquered regions.

This system clearly created differences in rank. Even so, the establishment of the *dīwān* was an important step in the development of organized government. It contained some of the first features of an emerging state.

This, more specifically, is what historians refer to as the “System of ʿUmar.”

But there were also negative features in the conquest system we have described—or, more precisely, in the way that system worked in practice.

One of them was the isolation we mentioned earlier.

The Arab conquerors remained separate from the process of social production and from social life more generally. Their activity stayed concentrated within the military settlements. This also reflected a sense that they stood above the local population, while their own society remained divided internally along tribal lines.

The class differences that also existed among them were another matter. These were a natural result of the stage of social development through which Arab society was then passing, as it took its first steps toward a more developed class society.

ʿUmar’s role in this transition helped prepare the way for the establishment of the state as an organized political system.

He did not allow the conquering armies simply to act as they wished. Alongside his strict instructions that they follow the rules already mentioned, and his repeated orders that the inhabitants of conquered lands be treated with tolerance, he also kept close control over the soldiers themselves.

He counted them, recorded their ranks and tribal affiliations, and entered all of this carefully in the records of the *dīwān*. Under him, the *dīwān* became an organized administrative institution, which the Umayyad caliphs later developed further.

His aim was to ensure that the booty from the conquests was distributed according to a fixed system rather than according to the wishes of military commanders.
