But whatever the form... [the source text breaks off here].

[^V1-19]: Two examples may be useful here. 1. Abd al-Rahman Badawi in his book *Aristotle* (Cairo, 1964, 4th ed.). 2. Tayyib Tizini in the work cited above. Badawi, as an idealist thinker, argues that for Aristotle true existence is the existence of essences, and that there is no difference between Plato and Aristotle in their view of the “status of existence” (p. 55). He also says that “the central idea in Aristotle, running through every part of his system, is the idea of matter and form” (p. 282). Tizini, by contrast, as a materialist thinker, argues that Aristotle’s basic principle is the objective, real existence of the material world, and that consciousness—thought or essence—derives from the existence of that material world. Tizini therefore believes that this basic principle in Aristotle must be brought clearly to the foreground, because it is here that Aristotle breaks decisively with Plato’s theory of abstract forms, with “Platonism” itself (p. 101). Tizini further argues that Aristotle’s concept of substance, insofar as it includes the eternity of matter in general, marked a major and fundamental step toward a precise dialectical-materialist concept of matter (p. 121).

[^V1-20]: For reference on this point, see the works of Ibn Taymiyya among the earlier writers, and the works of Ali Sami al-Nashshar among modern scholars, including *Methods of Research among Muslim Thinkers*, *The Rise of Philosophical Thought in Islam*, and others. By a “nihilistic” view of this relationship, we mean the attempt by this group of Salafis to deny absolutely any influence of Aristotle on Islamic logic and philosophy, and to treat both as arising entirely from purely Islamic sources.

[^V1-21]: In Marxism, the Leninist theoretical principle for identifying stages in the history of philosophy rests on the idea that philosophical development results from a unity of quantitative and qualitative change—that is, from a unity between gradual development and breaks within that development. Engels explains this unity through the law of the negation of the negation. He writes: “Ancient philosophy was spontaneous materialism. For that reason it could not explain the relation between thought and matter. But the need to clarify this question led to teachings about a soul distinct from the body, then to the claim that the soul was immortal, and finally to spiritualism—that is, the unity of soul and body. In this way ancient materialism was negated by idealism. But idealism itself, in the later development of philosophy, also proved unable to sustain itself, and it too was negated by modern materialism. Modern materialism is therefore a negation of the negation. It is not simply a continuation of ancient materialism. Rather, it adds to the enduring foundations of ancient materialism the whole intellectual content produced by two thousand years of philosophical and natural-scientific development, as well as by the development of history itself over those two thousand years” (Engels). See *Anti-Dühring*, chapter 12, “Dialectics: Negation of the Negation”; Arabic translation by Fu’ad Ayyub, Dar Dimashq, 1st ed., 1965, pp. 165–166.

[^V1-22]: Marxists explain the flourishing of classical German philosophy in the nineteenth century, despite Germany’s economic backwardness compared with other European countries at the time, in two ways. First, they see it as one expression of philosophy’s relative independence from the economic base. Second, they see it as the result of two sets of factors: external European factors and internal German ones. In Germany, quantitative changes were accumulating within a process of development. So although the country’s economic and political conditions were still relatively backward in qualitative terms, there was movement within them: a process of formation through accumulating quantitative changes. These accumulations could then turn into new qualitative forms—political, intellectual, or theoretical.

[^V1-23]: Lenin exposed the partisanship of idealist philosophers through concrete examples, despite the many masks behind which their philosophical partisanship could hide. He did this in *Materialism and Empirio-Criticism*; see especially the chapter “Parties in Philosophy and Philosophical Blockheads,” Arabic translation by Munir Shabak and Fu’ad Ayyub, Dar Dimashq, 1971, 1st ed., pp. 335–355. Lenin described neutrality in philosophy as “a disguised baseness, concealing idealism and fideism” (p. 354). In the conclusion to the book (p. 358), he wrote: “Modern philosophy is partisan, just as it was two thousand years ago, and the two parties struggling against each other are, in essence, materialism and idealism.”

[^V1-24]: Zaki Najib Mahmud, *The Rational and the Irrational in Our Intellectual Heritage*, Beirut, Dar al-Shuruq, no date, p. 7.

[^V1-25]: Mahdi Amel, *The Crisis of Arab Civilization or the Crisis of the Arab Bourgeoisies?*, p. 188.

[^V1-26]: Eduard Batalov, Doctor of Philosophy at the Soviet Academy of Sciences, in an article in *Questions of Philosophy*, Moscow, no. 12, 1964.

[^V1-27]: See the discussion on p. 28 and its footnote.

[^V1-28]: One feature of historical materialism in Marxist thought is that it is not only a method for interpreting history or the world. It is also a method for changing history and changing the world, unlike the task philosophy set itself before Marxism. This is why Marx, in his remarks on Feuerbach, said that philosophy had interpreted the world, whereas the task now was to change it. Earlier inquiry dealt with interpreting the spiritual or ideal world; now the task was to transform the objective, material world.

[^V1-29]: Each higher form of consciousness unquestionably has its own history. But since all of them are forms of social consciousness, they must also be examined in terms of their social character, which is determined in the final analysis by the mode of production through which people organize their material life.

[^V1-30]: Here “metaphysical” means the opposite of dialectical, not the opposite of natural or physical.

[^V1-31]: Thales (621–550 BCE) tried to develop a fairly integrated view of the world as a unified material whole. He believed that water was the original basis of everything that exists, and that the earth was a round cylinder resting in water.

[^V1-32]: Anaximenes (588–524 BCE) believed that air was the basis of everything that exists, and that all things in the world arise through the condensation and rarefaction of air.

[^V1-33]: Anaximander (611–547 BCE) approached the origin of the world differently. He argued that the world’s basis did not lie in a concrete material substance, but in an indeterminate substance he called the *apeiron*. Existing things arise through the interaction of cold and hot, two inseparable qualities of the infinite *apeiron*. The *apeiron* is an abstract category, comparable to the category of matter in Marxism.

[^V1-34]: Heraclitus (520–470 BCE). Materialist historians of philosophy associate Heraclitus with the emergence of dialectics as an almost fully developed method for analyzing everything that exists. Lenin believed that Heraclitus expressed some essential points of dialectics very well (*Philosophical Notebooks*). Heraclitus held that the basis of everything must be material and that fire was the primary material basis. Fire is in constant motion and change, continually coming into being and passing away. He gave a material explanation of the soul. Everything turns into something else according to the law of necessity.

[^V1-35]: Democritus (second half of the fifth century BCE), together with Leucippus and Anaxagoras, founded the atomist school. They assumed the existence of an infinite number of indivisible particles moving through empty space. These particles, absolutely dense and differing in shape and size, are atoms; atoms and the void are eternal. Against Zeno, Democritus defended the validity of sensory knowledge without setting it against rational knowledge. Nothing exists in the world except atoms and the void. He held that existence and time are eternal. Everything that exists does so for a cause and by necessity; even chance has a cause. He also explained the existence of the gods in material terms.

[^V1-36]: Epicurus (341–270 BCE). His philosophy represents the highest stage in the development of ancient Greek atomism. In his theory of knowledge he takes a sensory approach and begins from materialist positions. Like Democritus, he holds that only atoms and the void exist, and that all things and natural phenomena are different combinations of atoms. Coming into being and passing away are simply processes of atoms joining together and separating. Nothing comes from nothing, and nothing turns into nothing. He went beyond Democritus on the question of the weight of atoms, affirming that atoms have weight. He looked for the source of atomic motion within the atoms themselves—that is, for an internal, self-generated source of material motion. His idea that atoms deviate from a straight path contributed to the development of ancient Greek materialism. He linked happiness to knowledge: there can be no happiness without understanding humanity’s place in the world and freeing people from fear—fear of the gods, death, and an unseen afterlife. He denied that the gods intervene in nature, human destiny, or the world. His school was the last major materialist school of ancient Greek philosophy.

[^V1-37]: In the Christian Middle Ages, nominalism and realism were the two main currents within which the various schools of Scholastic philosophy developed. They were the historically distinctive form taken by the struggle between materialism and idealism within that philosophy: nominalism represented the materialist side, while realism represented the idealist side. The nominalists denied the real existence of universals—essences—and affirmed the real existence of individual things, arguing that the universal exists only as a name. The realists, by contrast, held that universals had real existence apart from individual things. Among the best-known representatives of Scholastic realism were John Scotus Eriugena (810–877), followed by the philosopher-theologian Anselm, Archbishop of Canterbury. Among the best-known nominalists was the French philosopher Roscelin (1050–1120), whose view that the word “universal” is merely a verbal label with no reality of its own is considered one of the earliest expressions of materialist nominalism in medieval Scholasticism. He was followed by English representatives of nominalism, the best known being Duns Scotus (1274–1208), Roger Bacon (1214–1294), and William of Ockham (–1341).

[^V1-38]: Lange was a major representative of bourgeois philosophy and a historian of philosophy. He became famous for a work described as the first major study in bourgeois materialist history. In 1866 he published *History of Materialism and Critique of Its Importance in the Present Age*. It was reissued in 1969, when bourgeois philosophers believed that the study had finally destroyed materialism.

[^V1-39]: We use “inclination” and “tendency” as synonyms. They help us distinguish between what is materialist or dialectical in the full modern scientific sense and what has not yet developed all the elements of dialectical materialism, or has not yet reached a firm and consistent materialist position. This is why the title of this book speaks of “materialist tendencies,” even though our research sometimes finds clearly materialist positions on particular philosophical questions in some thinkers from the heritage.

[^V1-40]: In the discussions of motion, time, and space by the most prominent representatives of Arab-Islamic philosophy, especially al-Farabi and Ibn Sina, we find ideas that point toward a necessary connection between matter and each of motion, time, and space. These ideas do not, however, reach the point of dialectical materialism—Marxism—which treats motion, time, and space as forms of matter.

[^V1-41]: The intended meaning is the intellectual class. (Publisher.)

[^V1-42]: Calls to break with the Arab cultural heritage appeared in different forms and within different ideological currents. They first appeared in the first third of the twentieth century as calls to replace the Arabic alphabet with the Latin alphabet, gradually cutting people off from that heritage. This appeared in two currents. One was in Lebanon, represented by Father Marun Ghusn and later Sa‘id Aql, and was driven by a sectarian political aim: isolating Lebanon from its Arab surroundings as an expression of the ideology of the colonial Lebanese bourgeoisie. The second appeared in Egypt, represented by Abd al-Aziz Fahmi and Salama Musa. This current expressed the ideology of the emerging Egyptian bourgeoisie, based on an Egyptian nationalism separate from Arab nationalism. The slogan of the 1919 Egyptian Revolution was “Egypt for the Egyptians.” After the Arab-Israeli war of June 1967, the same call appeared in another form, under the claim that the Arab defeat resulted from “civilizational” factors rooted in the country’s “civilizational” backwardness and reflected in the literature of the Arab intellectual heritage itself. This newer form appeared in two ways: in literature and in theoretical thought. It appeared artistically, for example in the poetry of Unsi al-Hajj and Nizar Qabbani, and theoretically in the Kuwait symposium on “The Crisis of Arab Civilizational Development,” held in April 1974; see *al-Adab*, Beirut, no. 5, 1974. In the papers presented at this symposium, the idea of discarding the heritage appeared only indirectly, and perhaps unintentionally, but the logic of the arguments leads in that direction.

[^V1-43]: When we speak of the originality of Arab thought—by which we mean all intellectual work originally written in Arabic, rather than translated into it—we mean that this thought is objectively connected to a particular historical and social reality, which it reflects in its own distinctive ways. We insist on this originality for two reasons. First, to affirm this connection as a methodological principle. Second, to affirm the dialectical unity between originality and contemporaneity, or modernity, and therefore to reject the colonial-bourgeois concept of “modernity” detached from originality. Colonialism spent a long period trying, in the cultural sphere, to implant this concept in the minds of the Arab intelligentsia. Its aim was to make it possible to cut modern Arab thought off from its own history—its originality—and redirect it toward ideological dependence on colonial Western thought.

[^V1-57]: Between the time of al-Ash‘ari and al-Ghazali, some thinkers fiercely opposed philosophy without this kind of intellectual understanding or clarity. Quite the opposite: they showed a striking ignorance of philosophy. One revealing example appears in Jamal al-Din Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Abbas al-Khwarizmi (d. 382 AH/993), *The Useful in the Sciences and the Destruction of Worries*, al-Matba‘a al-Sharqiyya, 1328 AH, pp. 61–62. He wrote: “They—that is, the philosophers—are a people from among the Greeks who became so confused in their doctrines that they fell into the valley of bewilderment and derangement, which resembles madness without being madness. They were perplexed in divine matters and based their views on pure whim and unsupported claims. They claim to be the cleverest of God’s creation, yet the course of their doctrine shows that they are the most ignorant of God’s creation and the most foolish of people. The foundation of atheism and heresy rests on their doctrine, and all unbelief is a branch of theirs (...) They used to experiment with preventing reproduction, and their leader Plato the atheist—may God curse him—said to Moses son of Amram, God’s messenger and interlocutor: ‘I will believe everything you say except your statement: the Cause of Causes spoke to me.’ Look at the belief of this wicked man: he called God’s messenger a liar and believed that God Most High has no speech at all (...) He also believed that the world is eternal. His companions, such as Aristotle, Socrates, Hippocrates, and Galen, are all certainly the atheists of their age and the heretics of their time (...) They are polytheists and atheists—may God curse them!”

[^V1-96]: In the terminology of early historians, classification into “classes” (*tabaqat*) was not based on social class in the modern sense. It usually meant chronological grouping. A “class” could therefore mean a generation of poets, hadith scholars, philosophers, and so on, with a generation usually spanning between ten and twenty years. Sometimes a geographical criterion was used, as Ibn Sa‘d did in his *Great Book of Classes* when he arranged biographies of the Companions according to the cities where they settled. See Ibn Sa‘d, *Classes*, Dar Sadir/Dar Beirut, 1957, Ihsan Abbas’s introduction, vol. 1, p. 12. Books of *tabaqat*, then, are specialized biographical works devoted to a particular group of historically important people. This form of writing among Arabs and Muslims goes back to the third century AH. Al-Waqidi may have been the first to write in this form, followed by his student Muhammad ibn Sa‘d; both wrote about hadith scholars. In the same century, many literary writers produced books on classes of poets, such as Ibn Sallam’s *Classes*, Ibn Qutayba’s *Poetry and Poets*, and Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s *Classes of Poets*. Later came works on the “classes” of physicians, sages, Shi‘is, Shafi‘is, and so on.

[^V1-97]: The history of Arabic literature gives us an example in which most of these personal, class, and ideological motives come together, along with a desire to flatter the ruling power. Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz (247–296 AH), whose caliphate lasted no more than a day and part of another day, wrote a book called *Classes of Poets*, containing biographies of about 127 male and female poets from the Abbasid period. Three points about this book were noted by its editors, Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj and Abbas Iqbal. First, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz ignores several of the greatest poets of his age, including Ibn al-Rumi (221–283 AH). He also ignores Ibn al-Rumi in his book *al-Badi‘*. Why, when Ibn al-Rumi was such an important poetic figure in the Arabic tradition? The editor and publisher Abd al-Sattar Farraj links this omission to two positions taken by Ibn al-Rumi. First, Ibn al-Rumi had satirized al-Mu‘tazz, the author’s father, after he was removed from the caliphate. Second, Ibn al-Rumi “was closely associated with al-Qasim ibn Ubayd Allah, one of Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s enemies, who advised that he be arrested when al-Mu‘tadid died.” Here the motive is personal. Second, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s book gives biographies of poets who praised or had connections with the Abbasid caliphs (...) and gathers poetry stamped with the outlook of poets dependent on Abbasid caliphs, ministers, and leading officials. It also tries to reveal the relationship between each poet and the person he praised (Abbas Iqbal). Here the motive is class-based and ideological. Third, the editors observe that despite Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s fame and the importance of his book, later biographers rarely mentioned it; “it was as though most of them did not know it.” Abd al-Sattar Farraj points to a convincing political reason: “al-Muqtadir returned to the caliphate and remained caliph for more than twenty years after Ibn al-Mu‘tazz was killed. There is no doubt that most transmitters do not favor someone from whom power has turned away and whom the events of time have brought down.” This is a case of flattering the ruling power. See Ibn al-Mu‘tazz, *Classes of Poets*, edited by Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, no date, pp. 10, 12, 583, 588.

[^V1-109]: The Arab world began using modern movable-type printing in the early eighteenth century. It is well known that the deacon Abdallah Zakhir of Aleppo established the first press using Arabic type in the town of al-Shuwayr in Lebanon in 1748. But Arabic movable type had already been used in Europe since the sixteenth century, beginning in 1514, when Pope Leo X opened the first Arabic press in Italy for printing religious books. Ibn Sina’s *Canon* may have been the first work from the Arabic intellectual heritage printed in Europe, in Rome in 1593. After that, Arabic heritage works continued to be published in European cities and capitals such as London, Paris, Leiden, Leipzig, Göttingen, Rome, Vienna, Berlin, and St. Petersburg—now Leningrad—before Arab countries themselves were able to make broad use of this form of printing. From the mid-nineteenth century onward, it spread through the Arab world for printing old and new books, magazines, and newspapers. See Jurji Zaydan, *History of Arabic Literature*, Cairo, 1911, vol. 4, pp. 54–56.

[^V1-165]: Some modern Salafis give a different account of the attempts by the “philosophers of Islam” to reconcile religion and philosophy. Their view contradicts the model presented here by Tawfiq al-Tawil, even though al-Tawil himself also follows a Salafi approach. Mahmud Qasim, for example, argues that Ibn Rushd merely brought religion together with Aristotle’s philosophy, without intending to defend philosophy itself. His aim, Qasim says, was to defend religion, as shown by the fact that he modified Aristotle’s philosophy and accepted from it only what he believed to be true. See Mahmud Qasim, *Ibn Rushd, the Misrepresented Philosopher*, Cairo, Anglo-Egyptian Bookshop, pp. 45–46. This disagreement among Salafis over how to understand the attempt to “reconcile” religion and philosophy in our philosophical heritage shows that the alleged reconciliation is not an objective historical reality, but a set of subjective interpretations imposed by shared ideological starting points. Most of these interpretations are also highly selective.

[^V1-173]: Plato says in his famous dialogue (4A 2): “The ignorant do not concern themselves with philosophy and do not want to become wise, because the ugliness of ignorance lies in this: a person who is neither beautiful, complete, nor intelligent is nevertheless completely satisfied with himself and thinks he needs nothing, and therefore does not desire what he believes he does not need.” The “ignorant” in Plato’s formulation here are neither the gods nor the philosophers; they are the slaves. The judgment that a human being is not beautiful, complete, intelligent, and so on excludes philosophers and places a fixed metaphysical barrier before the development of the lower classes and before any possibility that they might reach the level of philosophy. Their ignorance is therefore treated as innate and unchangeable.

[^V1-193]: This railway was built before the First World War under an agreement between the Ottoman Turkish government and Imperial Germany. Germany was among the imperial powers most eager to control this important part of the Arab region and the strategic route to the Gulf, which opened onto seas and oceans of great strategic importance. The Iraqi national movement viewed the project with suspicion and anxiety from the start. This national concern appears in some literary writing from the period. The Iraqi poet Muhammad Rida al-Shabibi, for example, wrote in 1918:

    > They laid the iron rails, but our bonds were not extended by a rope;
    > instead, a trap was laid for us.
    > When railway lines intertwine,
    > they become a net in which the East of the land is caught.
    >
    > (*Diwan al-Shabibi*, Cairo, 1940, p. 36.)

[^V1-306]: The cultural remains of the ancient East show a synthetic character in which the language of images and the language of concepts are mixed together—poetry with philosophy, as in Omar Khayyam and al-Ma‘arri, for example. This synthetic character led some Western Orientalists to conclude that philosophy was absent from these Eastern cultural works. But the decisive question is whether categories and concepts are present. Since we do find philosophical views in these works that, despite their synthetic form, take the form of concepts, there is no reason not to classify them as philosophical thought.

This is also shown by a report in which Abu Dharr insulted a man in the Prophet’s presence by referring to his mother. The Prophet said to Abu Dharr: “You are a man in whom there is still *jahiliyya*.” Muslim writers divided *jahiliyya* into a first *jahiliyya*, which they said was the age in which Abraham was born, and a second one closer to Islam, in which the Prophet Muhammad was born. [^V1-323]: The Sabaeans fought the Minaean state during its period of weakness until they destroyed it. The Sabaean state then faced internal struggles with tribal chiefs and local rulers seeking power, as well as several local revolts. It also faced external pressures, beginning with the Ptolemies’ attempt in Egypt to monopolize eastern trade and continuing with foreign intervention after internal disorder exhausted the state and weakened its economy. Eventually it lost control of the Red Sea and the African coasts, while maritime trade passed into Greek and Roman hands. The same happened to the Himyarite state. It faced a Roman invasion in 24 BCE, Ethiopian occupation in 340 CE, the diversion of trade from Ma‘rib to the Red Sea maritime route, and the expansion of Roman sea trade. All this led to neglect of the Ma‘rib Dam until it collapsed, followed by migrations and the destruction of agriculture. Same source, pp. 136, 141, 142, 147, 151, 152.

[^V1-328]: Zeno held that motion is irrational. He admitted that sensory knowledge tells us motion exists, but he did not accept sensory knowledge as valid. Thought, or rational knowledge, falls into contradiction when it tries to think motion. Motion can be thought only through the contradiction between rest and movement: at a particular point and moment, something both is and is not there. Zeno treated this as a contradiction within thought itself when it thinks motion in this way—that is, as a contradiction according to formal logic. Motion is therefore irrational and, consequently, does not exist. Zeno explained this reasoning through three proofs known as aporias: the arrow, Achilles and the tortoise, and the endless division of a distance into halves while it is being crossed. For these examples, see Ahmad Amin and Zaki Najib Mahmud, *The Story of Greek Philosophy*, 2nd ed., Cairo, 1935, pp. 46–47.

[^V1-329]: To prove that motion is impossible, Zeno imagined an arrow flying through space. At every instant during its flight, he said, the arrow must be at rest at one particular point, because it cannot occupy two places at the same instant. If the arrow is motionless at a particular point during every unit of time, then across the sum of those units it must remain motionless as well. A continuous sequence of states of rest can produce only rest. Therefore there is no motion.

[^V1-330]: Zeno tried to deny motion in another way by imagining a man named Achilles racing a tortoise. He assumed that the tortoise begins ten meters ahead and that Achilles runs ten times faster. By the time Achilles covers the ten meters separating them, the tortoise has moved one meter farther. When Achilles covers that meter, the tortoise has moved another tenth of a meter. When he covers that tenth, the tortoise has moved another hundredth of a meter, and so on without end. Achilles therefore never catches the tortoise.

[^V1-347]: Evidence for this comes from reports about the kinds of agricultural products brought to the markets of towns and settlements in the Hijaz and elsewhere. Sources tell us, for example, that the towns of the Hijaz—especially Mecca—depended on Ta’if for wheat, other grains, grapes, and honey. See Lammens, *The Arab City of Ta’if before the Hijra*, Beirut, 1922, p. 32, in French. Ta’if also produced many kinds of fruit, some dates, raisins, figs, and so on. Yaqut al-Hamawi tells us that the seeds of the *ban* tree produced in Yathrib were carried to other lands. *Dictionary of Countries*, vol. 5, entry “Yathrib,” p. 87. The point is that these products circulated through markets. Markets were naturally also held during the pilgrimage seasons, and their names are well known. “At these markets Arabs from all parts of the peninsula came with their goods to exchange and sell them” (Salim, p. 364).

The Sabaeans were also famous for producing frankincense and incense, and they gained great wealth from the perfume trade. Same source, p. 57.

Such lava fields are scattered between eastern Hawran and Medina, or Yathrib. Yaqut lists twenty-nine of them. See Salim, p. 405. They also seem to have known how to make dyes for coloring fabrics, since they cultivated plants used in producing dye materials. See Belyaev, p. 92.

[^V1-363]: The Arabian Peninsula was not fully surveyed geographically until the period between the First and Second World Wars. Even in the mid-nineteenth century, Europeans knew no more about the vast interior of the peninsula than they knew about the visible surface of the moon. Belyaev, p. 55. That concerns physical geography, which remains stable over very long periods. Economic and human geography, by contrast, changes and develops. It is still the obscure—if not missing—link in the history of the pre-Islamic period.

[^V1-399]: Belyaev, p. 136. Jawad Ali, vol. 8, p. 200 ff., says that examples have been found of local coins used by the people of southern Arabia in their transactions. Some were struck in gold, some in silver, others in copper and other metals. Museums, antiquities collections, and private collections contain coins struck in southern Arabia, some in gold, some in silver, and others in copper. Some small coins carry the name of the king during whose reign they were struck. Some, however, are ancient and go back to the period before the Common Era. Jawad Ali also argues, same source, p. 206, that the people of the Hijaz used not only Roman and Sasanian coins—dinars, dirhams, and *daniq*—but also Yemeni and Ethiopian coins in the pre-Islamic period and in early Islam before Islamic coins with Arabic inscriptions were struck. Meccans in particular traded with Yemen, Iraq, and Syria and therefore used many different currencies. Conditions in their own country were not favorable for minting coins locally.

[^V1-401]: One revealing example shows that private ownership of livestock was widespread. *al-Aghani*, vol. 16, p. 95, tells a story about Hatim al-Ta’i, who died forty-five years before the Hijra. Banu Lam wanted to compete with Hatim at the market of al-Hira by making a wager involving his horse. When Iyas ibn Qabisa al-Ta’i heard of this, he feared Hatim might be defeated and lose the wager, so he gathered his people from Banu Hayya and urged them to support their cousin Hatim. One man said: “I have one hundred black camels and one hundred reddish camels.” Another stood and said: “I have ten stallions, each with a fully armed rider.” Hassan ibn Jabala al-Khayr said: “You know that my father died and left great wealth. I will provide all the wine, meat, and food for as long as they remain at the market of al-Hira.” Iyas then said: “I will give as much as all of you together.” The story continues that Hatim’s cousin Wahm ibn Amr said: “No. This is my property, numbering nine hundred camels. Take it from him until the camels are exhausted or you get what you want.” The story also appears in *Stories of the Arabs*, by Muhammad Ahmad Jad al-Mawla and his colleagues, Cairo, 1948, vol. 3, pp. 98–99. Hatim’s own verse is significant here: “They say to me: You have wasted your wealth, so be moderate / Yet without the very things they criticize, I would never have been a chief.”

[^V1-402]: Two concrete examples illustrate this kind of ownership. 1. It is said that during the reign of King al-Nu‘man (583–605), Hajib ibn Zurara and Qays ibn Mas‘ud argued over which man among their peoples was the meanest. Al-Nu‘man sent someone to see and testify. When they reached the territory of Hajib ibn Zurara, they passed a man from his people, and Hajib said: “This is the meanest of my people.” The man was beside his water basin, watering his camels. See Mahmud Shukri al-Alusi, *Reaching the Goal*, Cairo, 1923, vol. 1, p. 286. Note the phrase “his basin”: the water source was therefore this man’s property. The rest of the story says that he refused to give these people water from “his basin” even after learning that their tribal chief Hajib ibn Zurara was among them, although the story says that they had “entered Hajib’s territory.” 2. In a story about Qays ibn al-Khatim, who died in 2 AH, when he set out to avenge the killers of his father and grandfather, he went to his water-drawing camel while it was irrigating his palm grove. A *nadih* is the camel used to turn the waterwheel. See *al-Aghani*, vol. 3, p. 3. Here Qays ibn al-Khatim clearly owns a garden, along with a well or irrigation channel from which he waters it using his own waterwheel driven by his camel.

[^V1-404]: The Basus War alone is enough to show this, even though it began at the end of the fifth century CE. As is well known, the immediate cause was the killing of Kulayb ibn Rabi‘a by Jassas ibn Murra al-Shaybani after Kulayb wounded the udder of a camel belonging to Jassas’s maternal uncle. The camel had been grazing on land that Kulayb had set aside as protected pasture, where he allowed only his own camels to graze. Jawad Ali, vol. 4, p. 355.

[^V1-405]: One of the *su‘luk* poets, Urwa ibn al-Ward, who died thirty years before the Hijra, expressed this meaning in his famous poem in *r* rhyme:

    > May God curse the poor outlaw who, when night falls,
    > goes among the butchered bones, familiar with every slaughter place,
    > counting himself rich whenever, for one night,
    > he finds enough food from a fortunate friend.

    See *al-Asma‘iyyat*, ed. Shakir and Harun, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, 1964, p. 45. Al-Muttalib then formed an alliance between Quraysh and the Ahabish—Banu al-Harith ibn Abd Manaf ibn Kinana, Banu al-Hun ibn Khuzayma ibn Mudrika, and Banu al-Mustaliq ibn Khuza‘a. [^V1-467]: In the language itself, *su‘luk* means a poor person. The well-known Arab *sa‘alik* were poor men who emerged from the social divisions discussed above. They broke away from their tribes as an expression of grievance and rebellion, and as a way to escape the poverty they suffered. Most were poor and often had nothing to eat. If they gained something through a raid or similar action, the tribal chief took the lion’s share of the booty, leaving them only scraps. See Ahmad Amin, “Su‘luk Life and Chivalry in Islam,” *Iqra’* series, no. 1, 1952, p. 27. al-Qattal al-Kilabi described their condition in lines including:

    > When he is hungry, he does not rejoice at an hour’s food,
    > nor does he despair when it is gone while he remains hungry.

    Previous source, p. 35. But the clearest picture of the rebellion and protest these *sa‘alik* felt against social inequality appears in the words of Urwa ibn al-Ward, one of their poets:

    > Let me seek wealth, for I have seen
    > that the worst of people in their eyes is the poor man.
    >
    > He is the least respected and most despised among them,
    > even if he comes from a good and noble line.
    >
    > He takes part in the gathering, yet they look down on him;
    > his own wife scorns him, and even the child rebukes him.

    Salim, pp. 429–440. Some *sa‘alik* were adventurers who turned to robbery and raiding. Others were outcasts expelled by their tribes. These were known as *khula‘a*, because their tribes renounced any bond of affiliation with them; they then attached themselves to another tribe through clientage and protection. See Salim, p. 436.

[^V1-468]: In pre-Islamic terminology, an *ashira* is a group of tribes that all trace themselves to one genealogical origin, as Quraysh did. Quraysh consisted of several tribal branches but together formed one *ashira*. The upper group—the Qurayshi commercial aristocracy—contained members from about ten of these branches.

[^V1-469]: The well-known term *mala’* of Mecca draws its historical meaning from its linguistic sense. Dictionaries define it as the nobles, leading men, and people of distinction—that is, people marked by status, appearance, and honor. [^V1-470]: In the terminology of pre-Islamic history, *Ahabish* refers to a group of dark-skinned slaves of African origin. The name came from the chroniclers’ belief that they were Ethiopian in origin. Wealthy Meccans used them for various kinds of labor and service. See Lammens, *Western Arabia before the Hijra*, pp. 244–245; and Jawad Ali, vol. 4, p. 198.

Al-Baladhuri reports an incident showing that the Ka‘ba was sometimes raided in attempts to steal the valuables it contained. He says that three men from Quraysh came one morning to the door of the Ka‘ba, which had plates of gold attached to it, and stole it. This report, which al-Baladhuri traces to Ibn Abbas, together with Lammens’s research, suggests that robbery of the Ka‘ba was familiar enough—not only for stealing a gold-plated door, but also for stealing wealth stored there by rich Meccans.

The *siqaya* meant filling leather water basins for pilgrims in the courtyard of the Ka‘ba. The *rifada* meant feeding needy pilgrims during the days of pilgrimage. The *liwa’* was the office of carrying or raising the war banner before the fighters when needed. Mecca also had the office of military command, meaning leadership of the army in war. [^V1-492]: The chroniclers often become confused and contradict themselves on this subject. They greatly exaggerate the illiteracy and ignorance of the pre-Islamic Arabs and their lack of reading and writing. Yet they also admit that when Islam appeared there were seventeen people in Mecca who could write, while claiming that Yemen did not have even one writer—despite the evidence contradicting both claims. At the same time, they speak of alliances whose agreements and charters were written down, such as the alliance between Banu Khuza‘a and Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, which they say was recorded in Dar al-Nadwa. See al-Baladhuri, *Genealogies*, vol. 1, p. 71; and Ibn Sa‘d, *Classes*, vol. 1, p. 81. They also write at length about the poetic and oratorical skill of the pre-Islamic Arabs, which itself contradicts the picture they give of total intellectual deprivation. Another contradiction is that while denying outright that the pre-Islamic Arabs knew reading and writing, they point to Qur’anic texts showing the opposite—texts indicating that reading and writing were familiar in the late pre-Islamic period. The Qur’an uses many forms of the words for reading and writing and words referring to writing materials and tools, such as ink, pens, scroll, and sheet. Izzat Darwaza, in *The Age of the Prophet*, p. 269, counted more than three hundred words of this kind.

[^V1-501]: It is historically established that pre-Islamic inscriptions used two main scripts. The first was the Musnad script, used for Minaean, Sabaean, Qatabanian, Himyarite, and Awsanian inscriptions, all in South Arabian dialects. The second was the Nabataean script, derived from late Aramaic, and used in the only pre-Islamic inscriptions that have reached us and are referred to here. Thamudic, Safaitic, and Lihyanite inscriptions were written in scripts derived from Musnad. Musnad is older than the Nabataean script, and inscriptions discovered in the Arabian Peninsula show that it was widely used in Arabia both before and after the beginning of the Common Era. See Jawad Ali, vol. 7, pp. 36–37.

[^V1-509]: Lihyan and Thamud were two tribes or peoples—the word *sha‘b*, with a short *i*, means a large tribal group—living in western Arabia before the Common Era. Each established a local government after the collapse of Minaean and Sabaean rule in the Hijaz. Both used writing derived from the South Arabian Musnad script and spoke North Arabian dialects. As for the Safaitic people, their name comes from the al-Safa region of Syria, where Orientalists found ancient inscriptions. Similar inscriptions were also discovered elsewhere in the Syrian desert and upper Hijaz, and all were called Safaitic inscriptions after al-Safa to distinguish them from inscriptions named after other places where some of them were found.

[^V1-535]: There are many examples showing that early scholars were aware of this problem. One is enough to stand for them all. al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi says that Hammad al-Rawiya corrupted Arabic poetry. He explains that Hammad knew the dialects of the Arabs, their poetry, the styles of their poets, and their meanings. Because of this knowledge, he could compose poetry closely resembling the style of an earlier, pre-Islamic poet, attribute it to that poet, and then spread it widely under that name. In this way, al-Dabbi says, the poetry of the Arabs became mixed together, and only a critical expert could distinguish the authentic from the false—and where could such an expert be found? [^V1-549]: Taha Husayn wrote in the introduction to the second edition: “This is last year’s book. One chapter has been removed, one retained, other chapters added, and the title has been changed slightly.” He did not explain what had been removed, retained, or added, or why the changes were made. In fact, what was removed was the first chapter on method. But the chapter was not really deleted except in two senses. First, it no longer appeared as the opening chapter. Second, certain phrases and words were changed, especially passages touching on some Islamic beliefs. The substance of the chapter, after revision, was divided between two new chapters: “Literature and Its History” and “The Pre-Islamic Arabs: Their Language and Literature.” He also added passages to the beginning and end of the chapter applying his method to some pre-Islamic poets, and added two chapters at the end of the book, one on the nature and forms of pre-Islamic poetry and one on pre-Islamic prose. These revisions were not made by his own free choice. He was forced into them after a campaign of intellectual and material intimidation led by rigid conservatives among Azhar scholars, university academics, and literary figures, along with members of the royal court pursuing political aims. Despite all of this, the basic argument and method of the book did not change.

[^V1-578]: Some attribute this saying to the Islamic period. (Publisher.) Others attribute it specifically to the Prophet and to Imam Ali. It is said that “the green plant on a dunghill” means a beautiful woman of bad origin and character.

[^V1-579]: “The green plant on a dunghill”: one meaning of *dimna* is a rubbish heap. Its “green plant” is the grass that grows there thick and fresh. The expression therefore describes outward beauty hiding the filth of its place of growth. The proverb warns against being deceived by an attractive surface that conceals something bad underneath. It reflects botanical observation generalized into a social rule.

[^V1-580]: *al-Ajza’* here means a raised hill of sand too barren to produce plants. The proverb is used when good comes from someone from whom good was not expected, just as one does not expect fertility or lush growth from such barren ground.

[^V1-581]: The ostrich is a bird of the ostrich family. This proverb is used of someone who has no distinct color, position, or opinion of his own.

[^V1-582]: This proverb means that miserliness does not come from a person’s nature but from lack of means. It expresses a social view.

[^V1-583]: *Khalla* means need and poverty; *salla* means secret theft. The proverb therefore says that theft is produced by poverty. Here too we find an advanced way of thinking about a social problem.

[^V1-584]: This proverb lays down a rule about punishment that is the same in principle as the rule later expressed in the Qur’anic verse, “In retaliation there is life for you, people of understanding.” The pre-Islamic proverb says that executing murderers in retaliation is the way to remove murder from society.

[^V1-585]: This proverb resembles the previous one because it also provides the basis for a legal rule: a person who abandons someone and thereby causes his death is equal to the killer—in other words, he is a partner in the killing.

[^V1-586]: This proverb expresses the idea that similarity between things in some outward features does not mean that they agree in all their other characteristics. Recognizing the logic of this proverb is important from the standpoint of knowledge.

[^V1-587]: Arabic literary works attribute this saying to Hatim al-Ta’i and say that he spoke it while a captive among Banu Anaza, after taking the place of another prisoner whom he had ransomed with himself. A slave woman struck him, and slave women among them did not wear jewelry.

[^V1-588]: Ukaz was a place between Ta’if and Nakhla on the road to Mecca. As the pilgrimage season approached, the pre-Islamic Arabs would go there and hold a market from the first of Dhu al-Qa‘da until the twentieth. They then moved to Dhu al-Majanna, where another market was held, and from there to Dhu al-Majaz for a third market. On the eighth of Dhu al-Hijja, pilgrims began moving toward Mecca. Ukaz was distinctive because people came from every part and edge of the Arabian Peninsula to trade, exchange or ransom prisoners, and hold gatherings for tribal boasting. Poetry was often recited as part of this boasting. See *al-Aghani*, vol. 2; Yaqut al-Hamawi, *Dictionary of Countries*, entry “Ukaz”; and other sources and studies.

During the rule of the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, an extremely wealthy Umayyad aristocracy also emerged among his relatives from Banu Umayya.

[^V1-735]: The *jizya* could be paid in cash or in kind, for example in clothing. The original upper limit for a cash payment was one dinar, or thirteen dirhams, per person each year. Later, this amount became the minimum, and two dinars or twenty-four dirhams could be taken, and sometimes four dinars from a wealthy person.

[^V1-736]: Zakat is due from every sane adult, provided the wealth is fully owned and the owner is able to dispose of it. The types of wealth subject to zakat are gold, silver, camels, cattle, sheep and goats, wheat, barley, dates, and raisins. The minimum amount on which zakat becomes due varies by type of wealth. 1. Gold: for every twenty dinars of gold, half a dinar is due; below that amount there is no zakat. 2. Silver: there is no zakat below two hundred dirhams; after two hundred, nothing further is due until the amount reaches forty more dirhams, at which point one dirham is due. 3. Camels: there is no zakat below five camels; at five, one sheep is due, and so on. 4. Cattle: for every thirty cattle, one yearling calf is due; below that there is no zakat. For forty cattle, one mature cow is due, with further details beyond this. 5. Sheep: for every forty sheep, one sheep is due; below that there is no zakat, with further details beyond this. Zakat on these kinds of livestock is due only under certain conditions: the minimum threshold must be reached, the animals must not be working animals, and a full year must have passed. 6. Crops—wheat, barley, dates, and raisins: zakat becomes due at roughly 910 kilograms; below that there is no zakat, provided the underlying crops are owned by the person concerned. As for the rate, if the crop is irrigated artificially, zakat is half of one tenth. If it is watered naturally by a river, spring, rain, or grows without artificial irrigation, the full tenth is due. See Shaykh Muhammad Jawad Mughniyya, *The Jurisprudence of Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq*, vol. 2, pp. 59–101.
